 SUPREME COURT OF ALABAMA
 OCTOBER TERM, 2026-2027

 _________________________

 SC-2026-0203
 _________________________

 Tony Lee and Emily Boles

 v.

 Diana Sue Vest

 Appeal from Talladega Circuit Court
 (CV-25-900090)

SELLERS, Justice.

 Tony Lee and his wife Emily Boles ("Lee and Boles") appeal from a

judgment of the Talladega Circuit Court ("the trial court"), ordering
 SC-2026-0203

specific performance of an option to purchase contained in a lease

agreement executed by Lee and Boles and Diana Sue Vest. We affirm

with instructions.

 I. Facts

 Lee and Boles leased to Vest a mobile home and property ("the

property") located in Lincoln for a term beginning on October 5, 2022, and

ending on June 5, 2024, for $1,500 per month. The lease agreement

contained the following option to purchase:

 "OPTION TO PURCHASE: Tenant, upon satisfactory
 performance of this Lease, shall have the option to purchase
 the real property described herein for a purchase price of
 $275,000.00 provided that the Tenant timely executes the
 option to purchase and is not in default of the Lease
 Agreement. Thereafter, each of the parties shall promptly
 execute any and all further instructions or other documents
 including a Sale Agreement which may be reasonably
 required for purchase of the real property.

 "….

 "OPTION CONSIDERATION: Non-refundable option
 consideration in the amount of $30,000.00 paid by the Tenant
 as consideration for this Option to Purchase Agreement shall
 be credited to the purchase price at closing if the Tenant
 timely exercises the option to purchase. If the Tenant doesn't
 exercise the option to purchase, the Tenant shall forfeit the
 nonrefundable option consideration."

 The lease agreement also contained a holdover clause, providing:

 2
 SC-2026-0203

 "HOLDOVER: If Tenant maintains possession of the
 Premises for any period after the termination of this Lease
 ('Holdover Period'), Tenant shall pay to Landlord lease
 payment(s) during the Holdover Period at a rate equal to
 150% of the most recent rate preceding the Holdover Period.
 Such holdover shall constitute a month-to-month extension of
 this Lease."

 Vest timely exercised her option to purchase the property and

tendered the nonrefundable option consideration of $30,000, and the

closing was scheduled for June 5, 2024, and extended until June 10, 2024.

According to Lee and Boles, Vest failed to tender the required funds to

close the sale of the property as scheduled, thus voiding the option to

purchase. Lee and Boles thereafter commenced an action against Vest,

asserting claims of breach of contract, ejectment, and unjust enrichment.

Vest responded with a counterclaim alleging breach of contract and

seeking specific performance of the option to purchase. At the request of

Lee and Boles, the trial court entered an order requiring Vest to pay

$2,000 per month into an escrow account, beginning June 2024, for the

use and occupancy of the property pending the outcome of the litigation.

See, e.g., Coan v. Championship Prop., LLC, 404 So. 3d 237 (Ala. 2024)

(noting that the trial court's escrow order was designed as an equitable

remedy to maintain the status quo and to protect the parties' competing

 3
 SC-2026-0203

interests to property, pending a final ruling on the issue of right to

possession). For their part, Lee and Boles continued paying the note on

the property, along with property taxes and homeowner's insurance,

pending a bench trial.

 The evidence presented during the bench trial was largely

undisputed. In early spring 2024, Vest exercised her option to purchase

the property and, as required by the lease agreement, tendered the

nonrefundable option consideration of $30,000 to be credited to the

purchase price of the property; the closing was scheduled for June 5,

2024, the last day of the lease term. According to Lee, he had insisted

that Luke Henderson handle the closing, and he acknowledged that

Henderson owed the same duty to Vest that he owed to Lee and Boles.

Lee and Boles did not attend the closing; rather, they signed the closing

documents a couple of weeks beforehand. Vest also intended to close

remotely, because she was scheduled to fly out of the country on the day

of the closing.

 On May 31, 2024, five days before the closing, Vest sent Henderson

an email, apparently one of several, informing him that she would be out

of town the following week and requesting that he send an accurate

 4
 SC-2026-0203

closing statement so that she could arrange for the payment to close the

transaction. Henderson responded to that email, apologizing for the

delay and stating that he would send the final closing documents later

that afternoon for her review and signature. Henderson thereafter sent

Vest an email attaching the final closing documents, reflecting an

amount due of $226,246.20 and informing her that she could wire the

funds via the instructions included in the closing package or send a

cashier's check made payable to Luke A. Henderson, LLC. On that same

date, Vest deposited $226,246.20 into her checking account.

 On June 1, 2024, Vest sent Henderson an email attaching the

signed closing documents. In that email, Vest reminded Henderson,

among other things, that she would be out of the country the following

week, that she felt Lee was trying to cancel the parties' contract, and that

she felt rushed to close on the property because she had only received the

closing documents on May 31, 2024. She therefore requested that the

closing be postponed until she returned from her trip on June 9, 2024.

 On June 4, 2026, the day before Vest left to go out of the country,

she informed Henderson that she had been unsuccessful in getting a

cashier's check for the closing because, she said, her bank either limited

 5
 SC-2026-0203

the amount of money she could wire or because the funds she had

previously deposited to purchase the property were still "pending." Vest

read the lease and noted that it did not require certified funds; she

informed Henderson that she was overnighting a personal check and

that, if he had not cashed her check by the time she returned from her

trip, she would send the certified funds to close to transaction.

 On June 5, 2024, Henderson sent Vest an email informing her that

he had received her check and that he had gone to her bank and

requested that the check be converted to a cashier's check, but that the

bank had declined his request because he was not the account holder; the

bank further advised that the check would not clear for 14 days.

Henderson also informed Vest that Lee and Boles had agreed to extend

the closing until June 10, 2024, and that to conclude the closing, she

would need either a cashier's check or a wire transfer in the amount of

$226,246.20 by the end of the business day on June 10, 2024.

 On June 8, 10, and 12, 2024, Vest sent emails to Henderson asking

whether her check had been destroyed and informing him that she felt

uncomfortable wiring additional funds until she knew the disposition of

her check. Vest received no response.

 6
 SC-2026-0203

 On June 10, 2024, after receiving no response from Henderson, Lee,

or Boles for two days, Vest stopped payment on her check. On that same

date, Vest sent an email to Lee stating that she had not heard from him

and that Henderson had never responded to her email about the

whereabouts of her check. Vest further indicated that, because

Henderson was no longer communicating with her, she needed to know

how to proceed with closing the transaction.

 On June 11, 2024, without Vest's authorization or consent, Lee

went to Henderson's office and demanded that he indorse Vest's check

over to him so that he could deposit it into his account. When questioned

by Vest's attorney, Lee candidly testified:

 "Q. All right. Anyway, you changed your mind [about the
 personal check] and you went to [Henderson's] office, didn't
 you?

 "A. I did.

 "Q. Okay. And you went down there and you instructed that
 attorney to endorse that check over to you and -- so you could
 deposit it in the bank; correct?

 "A. Correct.

 "Q. Okay. And tell me by what authority do you have to go to
 the attorney and instruct him to endorse that check when he
 owes her the same duty that he owes you?

 7
 SC-2026-0203

 "A. Well, it was the check meant to pay for the house that
 she's living in that belongs to me, so the check was coming to
 us anyhow, so --

 "Q. What do you mean --

 "A. -- it was my money.

 "….

 "Q. So if certified funds were required, then why are you
 changing your mind to deposit a personal check that you said
 could not be used to consummate a real estate closing
 transaction? You testified to that previously, didn't you?

 "A. Yeah.

 "Q. Well, then, why were you getting her personal check and
 putting it in the bank?

 "A. Well, we needed the money. I mean --

 "Q. You needed the money, but you said a personal check
 could not be used on a conveyance of property. Those are your
 words. I guess they were going to be if you were going to put
 it in the bank, the personal check; correct?

 "A. Yeah."

According to Lee, Henderson also gave him the entire closing file.

 On June 12, 2024, Vest informed Lee about the stop-payment order,

adding that she was uncomfortable with Henderson's "sitting on her

check" because he had been unresponsive. Vest further expressed her

willingness to wire the funds directly to Lee and Boles if acceptable. On
 8
 SC-2026-0203

that same date, Boles responded to that email, informing Vest that,

because she had stopped payment on the check, the location of her check

was irrelevant and had no bearing on her ability to wire the certified

funds. Nonetheless, Boles informed Vest that Henderson had indorsed

the check over to her and Lee for deposit. In that same email, Boles also

informed Vest that she and Lee were in the process of taking legal steps

to secure the property and that if Vest wanted to bring everything to a

closure, she could simply wire the funds to their personal account the

following day by 10:00 a.m. Although Vest expressed in one of her emails

a willingness to wire the certified funds directly to Lee and Boles, she

nonetheless testified that she did not feel comfortable doing so without

an attorney being involved.1 Lee and Boles thereafter sent Vest a letter

informing her that the option to purchase had expired and that the lease

would not be renewed. Notably, Boles testified in her deposition that,

after she and Lee commenced this action, they continued to discuss

closing the real-estate transaction with Vest because, according to Boles,

they were desperate to do so.

 1Some of the emails referenced herein were sent by Dennis
Flannagan, on Vest's behalf. It appears that Dennis was Vest's friend
and/or roommate.
 9
 SC-2026-0203

 At the conclusion of bench trial, the trial court expressed its opinion

that the closing would have occurred but for the conduct of Henderson

and Lee and Boles. The trial court asked Vest if she remained ready,

willing, and able to close the real-estate transaction, to which she

responded "yes." At that point, the trial court asked counsel for the

parties whether they could agree to a closing date if the court ordered

specific performance and, if so, whether they could provide certain

documentation allowing the trial court to make necessary calculations.

The parties agreed to a closing date and provided the trial court with the

requested do

leads.caseName: Waterworks Operating Co., LLC v. 514 W. 24th Owner LLC
leads.court: Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of the State of New York
leads.text:
Waterworks Operating Co., LLC v 514 W. 24th Owner LLC 
 2026 NY Slip Op 06036 
 October 15, 2026 
 Appellate Division, First Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 Waterworks Operating Company, LLC, Plaintiff-Respondent, 
 v 
 514 West 24th Owner LLC, et al., Defendants-Appellants. 514 West 24th Owner LLC, Third-Party Plaintiff-Appellant, 

 Decided and Entered: October 15, 2026 
 Index No. 654947/20|Appeal No. 7230-7230A|Case No. 2025-00312| 
 Before: Webber, J.P., Friedman, Kapnick, Pitt-Burke, JJ. 

 Liston LLP, New York (Joshua D. Liston of counsel), for appellants. 
 McCarter & English LLP, New York (Adam M. Swanson of counsel), for respondent. 

 [*1] 
 Judgment, Supreme Court, New York County (Joel M. Cohen, J.), entered December 5, 2024, awarding plaintiff the principal amount of $1,396,058.74, and bringing up for review an order, same court and Justice, entered June 12, 2024, which, to the extent appealed from as limited by the briefs, granted plaintiff's motion for summary judgment on its causes of action for lien foreclosure and breach of contract, unanimously modified, on the law, without costs, to vacate the judgment and to remit to Supreme Court on the issue of damages only consistent with this decision, and otherwise affirmed, without costs. Appeal from the aforesaid order, unanimously dismissed, without costs, as subsumed in the appeal from the judgment. 
 Plaintiff manufactures and supplies high-end bathroom fixtures. It commenced this action for breach of contract, lien foreclosure, and account stated against defendant 514 West 24th Owner LLC (the Owner) and its surety seeking complete payment for bathroom and cabinet materials that were delivered to the Owner for its redevelopment of a building in Chelsea. Pursuant to a series of purchase orders and change orders, the Owner agreed to pay plaintiff $2,577,166.99 (the full contract price) for the materials supplied. Both parties acknowledge that the Owner has paid plaintiff $1,608,827.37 for goods actually delivered and accepted. Plaintiff then filed a mechanic's lien in the amount of $968,339.62, which it asserts represents the outstanding balance due under the contract. Supreme Court granted plaintiff's motion for summary judgment on its breach of contract and lien foreclosure claims and dismissed the remaining cause of action as duplicative. The court awarded plaintiff damages corresponding to the outstanding balance due under the contract, based on the full contract price, plus pre-judgment interest, costs and disbursements. 
 Defendants principally advance two arguments on appeal. First, they argue that they cannot be held liable for breaching change orders totaling $390,605.51 because Michael Ohman of Sunrise Construction, LLC (Sunrise), the project's original construction manager, lacked authority to bind the Owner to those agreements. The Owner relies on a construction management agreement between the Owner and Sunrise which prohibited Sunrise from entering into change orders without the Owner's "prior written approval." Defendants' argument lacks merit because the Owner's acceptance of materials delivered pursuant to the change orders, without objection, constituted an implied ratification of those agreements ( see Matter of Cologne Life Reins. Co. v Zurich Reins. [N. Am.] , 286 AD2d 118, 126 [1st Dept 2001] ["An affirmance of an unauthorized transaction can be inferred from a failure to repudiate it"] [internal quotation marks omitted]; cf. Standard Funding Corp. v Lewitt , 89 NY2d 546, 552 [1997]). 
 [*2] 
 Defendants next argue that triable issues of fact exist as to the total damages that should be awarded to plaintiff because plaintiff did not establish that it delivered all materials required under the contract. In support of its summary judgment motion, plaintiff supplied invoices for materials delivered totaling $2,340,098 and defendants do not identify any specific items from these invoices that were not delivered or failed to conform to the terms of the applicable purchase orders. Thus, plaintiff met its prima facie burden to show that it delivered $2,340,098 in materials due under the contract. 
 Nonetheless, plaintiff did not satisfy its prima facie burden of establishing delivery of the remaining $237,069 in materials required by the contract. Plaintiff submitted an affidavit from its accounts receivable manager to demonstrate that all contract items were delivered to the Owner, but it did so only in reply in further support of its motion for summary judgment. Because defendants did not have an opportunity to rebut the evidence submitted by plaintiff in its reply papers, the affidavit must be disregarded ( see Doyaga v Camelot Taxi Inc. , 102 AD3d 594, 595 [1st Dept 2013]). 
 Accordingly, the judgment, which is premised on the unpaid balance of the full contract price, is vacated and the matter remanded for further proceedings on damages. 
 We have considered the remaining arguments and find them unavailing. 
 THIS CONSTITUTES THE DECISION AND ORDER OF THE SUPREME COURT, APPELLATE DIVISION, FIRST DEPARTMENT. 
 ENTERED: October 15, 2026

leads.caseName: Gill, P. v. Exxon Mobil Corp.
leads.court: Superior Court of Pennsylvania
leads.text:
J-A05005-26 

NON-PRECEDENTIAL DECISION - SEE SUPERIOR COURT O.P. 65.37 

PAUL GILL AND DIANE GILL, H/W 

 v. 

EXXON MOBIL CORPORATION 

 Appellant 

: 
: 
: 
: 
: 
: 
: 
 IN THE SUPERIOR COURT OF 
 PENNSYLVANIA 

 No. 2811 EDA 2024 

Appeal from the Judgment Entered September 23, 2024 
In the Court of Common Pleas of Philadelphia County Civil Division at 
No(s): 200501803 

BEFORE: KUNSELMAN, J., NICHOLS, J., and SULLIVAN, J. 
MEMORANDUM BY KUNSELMAN, J.: FILED OCTOBER 15, 2026 
I. Introduction 
In this negligence/product-defect-and-strict-liability case, Exxon Mobil 
Corp. appeals from the judgment entered in favor of Paul Gill for 
$725,000,000 and his wife, Diane, for $500,000.00. The jury found that Mobil 
Oil (an Exxon Mobil Corp. predecessor in interest)1 negligently manufactured 
and sold defective gasoline that contained a carcinogenic ingredient – i.e., 
benzene. Exxon neglected to preserve its sufficiency claim for appellate 
review. Furthermore, it fails to convince us that the trial court abused its 
discretion in any manner. Thus, we affirm. 
II. Factual & Procedural Background 
In 1974, Mr. Gill took a job at Cole’s Garage, a service station in Potter 
County, Pennsylvania. He pumped gas and repaired cars. Mr. Gill also lived 
____________________________________________ 
1 Exxon and Mobil were separate entities that merged in 1999 to form the 
combined entity Exxon Mobil Corp. We refer to Exxon Mobil Corp. as Exxon. 
J-A05005-26 
- 2 - 
in an apartment above the service station for a year. He worked at Cole’s 
Garage for the next five years, in nine-hour shifts, for five to six days per 
week. 
As part of his work, Mr. Gill used Mobil Oil’s gasoline to clean car parts. 
This was a common practice for mechanics, because manufacturers of 
gasoline, like Mobil Oil, never warned them that the benzene in gasoline was 
a carcinogen that became airborne when the gasoline was exposed to air. 
Mobil Oil failed to warn Mr. Gill of this dangerous and potentially lethal defect 
in its product, even though “the American Petroleum Institute advised its 
members[, including Mobil Oil, that] there was no safe level of benzene 
exposure [in] 1948.” N.T., 4/29/24, at 86. 
Benzene most typically enters the body by inhaling it or by absorption 
through the skin. See id. at 58. It infiltrates the blood stream and forms a 
compound, damaging the DNA of stem cells in the bone marrow. The marrow 
begins producing cancerous blood cells. Benzene is therefore a well-known 
and proven cause of leukemia. The World Health Organization, Environmental 
Protection Agency, and National Toxicology Program all agree “that benzene 
is a carcinogen . . . .” Id. at 55. 
When Mr. Gill pumped Mobil Oil’s gas and used it to wash car parts, he 
did not wear a respirator or gloves. Mr. Gill wore no protective equipment, 
because he did not know Mobil Oil’s gasoline was releasing carcinogenic 
benzene into his lungs and skin. 
J-A05005-26 
- 3 - 
Mr. Gill left Cole’s Garage in 1979. He became an EMT and instructor of 
other EMTs. In July of 2001, Mr. Gill married Diane, and the Gills merged their 
families from prior marriages. In 2018, Mr. Gill retired from his EMT career, 
and the Gills moved to a farm. They began raising show horses and had a 
family dog. 
Then, in 2019, Mr. Gill contracted acute myeloid leukemia (“AML”). His 
exposure to Mobil Oil’s gasoline 40 years prior at Cole’s Garage “was a 
substantial factor contributing to the cause of Mr. Gill’s AML.” N.T., 4/30/24, 
at 88. Other benzene-containing products to which he had repeated exposure 
were also substantial factors contributing to his AML. See id. at 88-89. 
Mr. Gill’s leukemia took a drastic toll on his standard of living and the 
Gills’ marriage. The first impact was when the accumulation of cancer in his 
blood caused a marked decline in Mr. Gill’s physical strength. He began to 
notice the effects in May of 2019, when cutting trees. Mr. Gill became fatigued 
and went to a hospital, where they diagnosed him with leukemia. After a six-
week stay and a battery of painful bone-marrow tests, physicians diagnosed 
him specifically with AML. 
This severely depressed Mr. Gill. Multiple rounds of chemotherapy at 
Rochester Hospital ensued. Doctors were able to bring his AML into remission. 
However, his weakened immune system permitted two cases of a food-
borne bacteria to infect his colon. Mr. Gill suffered severe cramps, diarrhea, 
nausea, and burning mouth sores. He had to have several blood transfusions 
due to his critically low blood-cell count. 
J-A05005-26 
- 4 - 
That July, Mr. Gill underwent a stem-cell transplant, which hospitalized 
him for a month. The transplant caused his immune system to attack his 
healthy organs: eyes, liver, and shoulders. Mr. Gill suffered loss of eye, liver, 
and skin function; chronic weakness; severe pain; and the stiffening of his 
joints. Physicians prescribed medications to stop his new white blood cells 
from attacking Mr. Gill’s body, but that, in turn, made him a diabetic and 
insulin-dependent. As a result, he has suffered from seizures and has gone 
into diabetic coma. 
In 2023, the immune-suppression medications gave Mr. Gill colorectal 
cancer. He underwent surgery to have a grapefruit-sized tumor and a foot of 
his colon removed. Two weeks later, Mr. Gill developed an infection from the 
surgery; he had extreme pain, could not sit down, and could not pass urine or 
waste. He had to receive five more rounds of chemo before the case went to 
a jury trial. The cancer has since spread to his liver, and he has two spots on 
his lungs that will require continued monitoring. 
Since his leukemia diagnosis, Mr. Gill has had to isolate himself from 
friends and family for fear that he will contract diseases from them. Similarly, 
the Gills have had to sell their horses and rehouse their dog, because Mr. Gill 
can no longer be around animals, due to his weakened immune system. He 
is not able to hunt and fish as much as he would like. The Gills cannot go to 
the movies, to the beach, or travel as much as they would like, because Mr. 
Gill might become sick, he gets tired easily, and the sun hurts his eyes. 
J-A05005-26 
- 5 - 
In addition, Mr. Gill’s diagnosis greatly impacted the Gills’ marriage. He 
cannot help his wife around the house or protect her the way he once did. 
Now, Mrs. Gill has to care for and protect him. Moreover, Mr. Gill will never 
be healed, as the cancer from his original leukemia keeps spreading to other 
parts of his body. He lives in constant pain and fear of losing his battle with 
cancer. Mr. Gill is worried that he will die and leave his family sooner than he 
otherwise would have, had he not contracted leukemia. 
In May of 2020, the Gills filed this suit against Exxon and several other 
defendants.2 They raised counts of negligence, gross negligence, breach of 
warranty, product-defect strict liability, battery, fraud, and loss of consortium. 
During discovery, the Gills produced two physicians to testify as experts 
on the medical cause of Mr. Gill’s leukemia. The first physician was Robert 
Laumbach, M.D., M.P.H., C.I.H., D.A.B.T. Dr. Laumbach, a professor at the 
Rutgers School of Public Health, with a master’s degree in public health, spent 
over 25 years analyzing the negative health impacts of occupational and 
environmental agents, including carcinogens, such as benzene. The Gills 
offered him as an “expert in occupational and environmental medicine, its core 
____________________________________________ 
2 The other defendants were United States Steel Corporation; Radiator 
Specialty Company; Atlantic Richfield Company; CRC Industries, Inc.; Sunoco, 
LLC; Safety-Kleen Systems, Inc.; Shell Oil Company; Berryman Products, 
Inc.; Univar Usa, Inc.; Ashland, LLC; Brenntag Southwest; Union Oil Company 
of California; The Blaster Corporation; Illinois Tool Works, Inc.; Henkel 
Corporation; and Root Oil Company, Inc. Some of the other defendants were 
dismissed at various stages below. Most of them eventually settled with the 
Gills, and none of them is a party to this appeal. 
J-A05005-26 
- 6 - 
disciplines of toxicology and epidemiology, and in industrial hygiene.” Dr. 
Laumbach’s Expert Report on Paul Gill, 3/7/22, at 3. 
The Gills’ second expert physician was Rory M. Shallis, M.D., a practicing 
hematologist-oncologist and assistant professor of medicine at Yale University 
School of Medicine. Dr. Shallis was a member of the Yale Cancer Outcomes, 
Public Policy and Effectiveness Research Center and board certified in internal 
medicine, hematology, and oncology. See Dr. Shallis’ Expert Report on Paul 
Gill, 3/7/22, at 1-2. He regularly researched the causes of cancer and worked 
with “experts in the Yale School of Public Health to accomplish epidemiological 
research as it relates to leukemogenic exposures and the risk of MDS and AML 
development.” Id. at 2. 
Exxon filed a motion in limine to exclude Drs. Laumbach and Shallis as 
expert witnesses. It claimed that “their opinions are not based on generally 
accepted methodologies and lack a reliable scientific foundation.” Motion in 
Limine to Exclude Medical Causation Experts at 2. It also filed a motion in 
limine to keep the doctors from telling the jury that there is no known amount 
of exposure to benzene at which it is not carcinogenic – what Exxon dubbed 
a “no safe threshold” theory. The trial court denied both motions, and the 
matter proceeded to a jury trial. 
At the close of the Gills’ case-in-chief, Exxon filed a motion for 
compulsory nonsuit on all counts in the Gills’ complaint. As to the element of 
causation to prove negligence and product-defect strict liability, Exxon argued 
the Gills offered no proof that gasoline caused Mr. Gill’s leukemia. According 
J-A05005-26 
- 7 - 
to Exxon, they only proved that the benzene in Mobil Oil’s gasoline caused Mr. 
Gill’s leukemia. See Exxon’s Memorandum of Law in Support of Motion for 
Nonsuit at 15 n.7 (quoting expert’s testimony as “there is definitive evidence, 
as we’ve seen, that benzene and benzene in gasoline cause leukemia,” N.T., 
4/30/24, at 39). 
The trial court partially dismissed the motion as moot, because the Gills 
had previously withdrawn their counts for battery and breach of warranty. 
See T.C.O., 5/7/24. The court granted the nonsuit as to the count for fraud 
and the Gills’ prayer for punitive damages, but it denied the nonsuit as to the 
counts for negligence and product-defect strict liability. See id. 
On May 9, 2024, the jury found in favor of the Gills on both counts. It 
awarded Mr. Gill a total of $725,000,000 for the pain and suffering, 
embarrassment and humiliation, loss of enjoyment of life, and disfigurement 
that the leukemia caused him. The jury also awarded Mrs. Gill $500,000 for 
loss of consortium. 
The following week, Exxon moved for post-trial relief and sought JNOV, 
a new trial, or remittitur of the verdict. 
It requested JNOV on five bases. First, it claimed that, under the one-
injury-one-recovery rule, a settlement agreement that the Gills reached with 
Root Oil prior to trial discharged any obligation of Exxon to compensate them. 
Second, the Gills offered insufficient evidence of product identification. Third, 
the Gills offered insufficient evidence of a causal link between Mobil Oil’s 
gasoline and Mr. Gill’s damages. Fourth, the Gills offered insufficient evidence 
J-A05005-26 
- 8 - 
that Mobil Oil failed to warn Mr. Gill of a design defect in its gasoline. And 
fifth, the Gills offered insufficient evidence of a design defect in Mobil Oil’s 
gasoline. 
Exxon also sought a new trial on eight bases. First, Exxon asserted that 
it deserved a new trial, because the trial court permitted Drs. Laumbach and 
Shallis to testify as medical-causation expert witnesses. Second, the trial 
court allowed the doctors to tell the jury that there is no safe level of exposure 
to benzene. Third, the trial court refuse

leads.caseName: Orchard BJK Co., LLC & Pocono Mountains Industries, Inc. v. Coolbaugh Twp. Bd. of Supers.
leads.court: Commonwealth Court of Pennsylvania
leads.text:
IN THE COMMONWEALTH COURT OF PENNSYLVANIA 

Orchard BJK Company, LLC and : 
Pocono Mountains Industries, Inc., : 
 Appellants : 
 : No. 959 C.D. 2025 
 v. : 
 : Submitted: September 14, 2026 
Coolbaugh Township Board of : 
Supervisors, Citizens for Pennsylvania’s : 
Future, Tobyhanna Creek/Tunkhannock : 
Creek Watershed Association and : 
Tobyhanna Conservation : 
Association, Inc. 

BEFORE: HONORABLE CHRISTINE FIZZANO CANNON, Judge 
HONORABLE LORI A. DUMAS, Judge 
HONORABLE BONNIE BRIGANCE LEADBETTER, Senior Judge 

OPINION NOT REPORTED 

MEMORANDUM OPINION BY 
JUDGE DUMAS FILED: October 15, 2026 

 Orchard BJK Company, LLC and Pocono Mountains Industries, Inc. 
(collectively Appellants) appeal from an order issued by the Court of Common Pleas 
of Monroe County (Common Pleas) and dated June 27, 2025. Through that order, 
Common Pleas sustained preliminary objections filed by Coolbaugh Township 
Board of Supervisors (Board) and dismissed Appellants’ Complaint, due to 
Common Pleas’ determination that the claims Appellants asserted therein are not yet 
ripe for adjudication. Upon review, we affirm. 
2 
I. BACKGROUND1 
 Appellants own a number of commercial ly and industrially zoned 
properties in Coolbaugh Township (Township). In April 2023, the Board approved 
Appellants’ application to subdivide one of those properties into two contiguous 
parcels: Lot 1, which covers 35.5 acres; and Lot 2, which covers 73.16 acres. The 
Board also contemporaneously and conditionally approved Appellants’ land 
development plan for Lot 1, which called for the construction of a n approximately 
333,000-square-foot warehouse thereon and complied with the version s of the 
Township’s Subdivision and Land Development Ordinance (SALDO) 2 and 
Stormwater Management and Earth Disturbance Ordinance (Stormwater 
Ordinance)3 that were in effect at the time. 
 Shortly thereafter, the Board embarked upon an effort to impose more 
stringent requirements upon stormwater management and warehouse construction in 
the Township . On August 2, 2023, the Board enacted amendments to the 
Stormwater Ordinance that increased the mandated minimum inner buffer distance 
for wetlands from 50 feet to 150 feet, and the mandated minimum outer buffer 
distance between buildings and wetlands from 100 feet to 150 feet. See Stormwater 
Ordinance § 344-21.E.-F. Notably, these amendments did not remove or alter the 
Stormwater Ordinance’s waiver provision, which allows the Board , upon 
application, to modify or waive water drainage and stormwater management 
requirements on a development-by-development basis. Id. § 344-9.C.; see id. § 344-

1 We draw this section’s substance largely from Common Pleas’ opinion for this matter. See 
generally Common Pleas Op., 6/27/25. 
2 Coolbaugh Township Subdivision and Land Development Ordinance, Monroe Cnty., Pa., as 
amended (2013). 
3 Coolbaugh Township Stormwater Management and Earth Disturbance Ordinance, Monroe 
Cnty., Pa., as amended (2014). 
3 
19.A. (requiring the submission of a Stormwater Ordinance -compliant stormwater 
management plan in instances where “[a] pplicants propos[e] regulated activities in 
Coolbaugh Township which do not fall under the exemption criteria included in § 
344-9”). 
 Appellants subsequently took two discrete steps in furtherance of their 
desire to develop Lot 2. First, on April 29, 2024, they submitted two documents to 
the Township: a preliminary land development plan application, through which they 
inter alia sought permission to construct an approximately 186,000 -square-foot 
warehouse on Lot 2; and a waiver petition, through which they requested that the 
Board modify the applicable wetlands buffer standards, so that Appellants would 
need only satisfy the pre -amendment requirements, rather than the more stringent 
ones enacted by the Board in August 2023. See generally Bd.’s Prelim. Objs., Exs. 
A-B (Appellants’ letter regarding preliminary land development plan application for 
Lot 2 and Appellants’ buffer requirement modification petition; see also Compl., 
Exs. G-H (sketch plans for proposed Lot 2 warehouse development). 
 Second, while the plan application and waiver petition were both still 
pending before the Board, Appellants filed suit against the Board in Common Pleas 
on May 3, 2024. Therein, Appellants alleged that the Board, by enacting the buffer 
requirement amendments, had violated Appellants’ constitutional right to enjoy their 
property and had passed invalid special legislation. Compl., ¶¶60-87. Accordingly, 
Appellants requested that Common Pleas issue a declaratory judgment that deemed 
those amendments unconstitutional and void ab initio. Id., Wherefore Clause. 
 The Board responded to Appellants’ Complaint by filing preliminary 
objections, in which it specifically asserted that Common Pleas should dis miss the 
complaint because (a) Common Pleas lacked jurisdiction over the matter ; (b) the 
4 
Complaint failed to conform to law or rule, contained references to scandalous or 
impertinent matters, was insufficiently specific, and contained claims upon which 
no legal relief could be granted; and (c) Appellants had a pending prior action and 
had faile d to exhaust or pursue adequate statutory and non -statutory remedies. 
Prelim. Objs., ¶¶10 -90. Common Pleas construed several of these pre liminary 
objections as, in essence, assertions that Appellants’ claims lacked ripeness, 
sustained those preliminary objections, and dismissed the C omplaint. This appeal 
to our Court followed shortly thereafter. 
II. DISCUSSION4 
 Appellants present two arguments for our consideration, which we 
summarize as follows. First, Appellants assert that Common Pleas committed an 
error of law by sua sponte raising and addressing the ripeness of their claims . 

4 In ruling on preliminary objections, [the trial c]ourt must “accept as 
true all well-pleaded material allegations in the [complaint] and any 
reasonable inferences that [it] may draw from the averments.” 
Highley v . Dep’t of Transp. , 195 A.3d 1078, 1082 (Pa. Cmwlth. 
2018). However, [the trial court is] “not bound by legal conclusions, 
unwarranted inferences from facts, argumentative allegations, or 
expressions of opinion encompassed in the [complaint].” Id.. . . 
 “[W]here any doubt exists as to whether the preliminary objections 
should be sustained, the doubt must be resolved in favor of 
overruling the preliminary objections.” Pa. State Lodge, Fraternal 
Ord. of Police v. Dep’t of Conservation & Nat. Res., 909 A.2d 413, 
416 (Pa. Cmwlth. 2006). 
M.T. v. Pa. State Police, 298 A.3d 466, 469 n.5 (Pa. Cmwlth. 2023) (cleaned up). “Importantly, 
documents attached as exhibits, documents referenced in the complaint, as well as facts already of 
record may also be considered” by the trial court when adjudicating a party’s preli minary 
objections. Fraternal Ord. of Police Lodge No. 5 by McNesby v. City of Phila., 267 A.3d 531, 542 
(Pa. Cmwlth. 2021). Furthermore, “[i]t is well established that in reviewing a trial court’s grant 
of preliminary objections, this Court must determine whether the trial court committed an error of 
law, and in doing so, must apply the same standard as the trial court.” Id. at 541 (cleaned up). 

5 
Second, Appellants maintain that Common Pleas also erred on the merits because 
their claims are currently ripe for judicial disposition. Appellants’ Br. at 23-42. 
 Appellants’ first argument is rather mystifying, considering that the 
Board did raise the issue of ripeness when this matter was before Common Pleas . 
Specifically, the Board demurred to both of the complaint’s counts and argued in 
relevant part: 
41. Count I of [Appellants’] Complaint contains a 
declaratory judgment action asking [Common Pleas] to 
find the Township’s Stormwater Ordinance, as amended, 
unlawful special legislation. 
. . . . 
43. [Appellants] have no clear legal right for [their] 
declaratory judgment action of an unlawful special 
legislation claim in this case. 
44. [Appellants] have failed to allege any facts in the 
Complaint to support a claim for declaratory judgment. 
. . . . 
56. There is no actual case or controversy and the 
subject matter alleged in the Complaint is not yet ripe 
for judicial determination, nor will it be until the 
Board issues its decision on [Appellants’] Waiver 
Request. 
57. There will be no actual case or controversy ripe for 
judicial determination until after the . . . Board . . . has 
an opportunity to hear, consider[,] and issue a decision 
on [Appellants’] above-referenced Waiver Request. 
. . . . 
59. Therefore, the instant declaratory judgment action set 
forth within Count I of the Complaint should be dismissed. 
. . . . 
61. Count II of [Appellants’] Complaint also contains a 
declaratory judgment action asking [Common Pleas] to 
find the Township’s Stormwater Ordinance, as amended, 
constitutionally invalid. 
6 
62. As more specifically set forth above, [Appellants] 
have no clear legal right for [their] declaratory judgment 
action set forth in Count II of the Complaint. 
63. [Appellants] have failed to allege any facts in the 
Complaint to support a claim for declaratory 
judgment, and in particular have failed to adequately 
allege the existence of an actual case or controversy 
that is ripe for judicial determination. 
. . . . 
71. Therefore, Count II of the Complaint should similarly 
be dismissed for legal insufficiency. 
Prelim. Objs., ¶¶41, 43-44, 56-57, 59, 61-63, 71 (emphasis added); see Br. in Support 
of Prelim. Objs. at 10-11, 13 (demurring to Counts I and II, on the basis that those 
claims are not ripe for adjudication). Appellants’ assertion that Common Pleas 
raised the issue of ripeness sua sponte is thus plainly incorrect.5 
 We are similarly unpersuaded by Appellants’ second argument. 
Generally speaking, “[t] he doctrine of ripeness concerns the timing of a court’ s 
intervention in litigation. The basic rationale underlying the ripeness doctrine is to 
prevent the courts, through avoidance of premature adjudication, from entangling 
themselves in abstract disagreements.” Phantom Fireworks Showrooms, LLC v. 
Wolf, 198 A.3d 1205, 1217 (Pa. C mwlth. 2018) (cleaned up). The standard for 
determining whether a declaratory judgment action is ripe is subject to “a relatively 
lenient standard[.]” Id. at 1217-18. “An action is ripe for adjudication under the 
Declaratory Judgments Act where it presents the ripening seeds of a controversy.” 
Id. at 1218 (cleaned up). Even so, “[o]nly where there is a real controversy may a 

5 It is true that Common Pleas only determined that the Board had effectively raised the issue 
of ripeness through a number of its other, non-demurrer objections to the Complaint. See Common 
Pleas Op., 6/27/25, at 3-6. This was harmless error at most, given that the Board did specifically 
demur to the Complaint on ripeness grounds and also incorporated its ripeness averments by 
reference into its insufficient specificity and prior pending action objections. See Prelim. Objs., 
¶¶41, 43-44, 56-57, 59, 61-63, 71-72, 80. 
7 
party obtain a declaratory judgment. A declaratory judgment must not be employed 
to determine rights in anticipation of events which may never occur or for 
consideration of moot cases or as a medium for the rendition of an advisory opinion 
which may prove to be purely academic.” Gulnac by Gulnac v. S. Butler Cnty. Sch. 
Dist., 587 A.2d 699, 701 (Pa. 1991). 
 With these precepts in mind, we conclude that Appellants’ lawsuit was 
premature, as the aforementioned buffer requirements have yet to actually harm 
them and, in fact, may never do so. Appellants asserted in their Complaint that the 
Stormwater Ordinance amendments effectively prevent the erection of warehouses 
on Lot 2 and have caused many of its other properties to decrease in value . See 
Compl., ¶¶40-64. Additionally, Appellants maintained that those amendments were 
designed “to prevent or restrict” the d

revision until final publication in the Michigan Appeals Reports. 

-1- 
S T A T E O F M I C H I G A N 

C O U R T O F A P P E A L S 

ZECORRA ENTERPRISES, LLC, 

 Petitioner-Appellant, 

UNPUBLISHED 
October 14, 2026 
9:40 AM 
v No. 376030 
Tax Tribunal 
REDFORD TOWNSHIP, 

LC No. 23-001305 
 Respondent-Appellee. 

Before: BORRELLO, P.J., and BAZZI and LIEVENSE, JJ. 

PER CURIAM. 
 In this action contesting the tax assessment of real property, petitioner, Zecorra Enterprises, 
LLC, appeals by right the Michigan Tax Tribunal’s opinion and judgment determining the true 
cash value of petitioner’s commercial property for the 2023 tax year. In making this determination, 
the tribunal adopted and applied a renovation deduction proposed by respondent, Redford 
Township. Finding no errors warranting reversal, we affirm. 
I. BASIC FACTS AND PROCEDURAL HISTORY 
 This case involves the parties’ dispute over the valuation of petitioner’s commercial 
property, located in Redford Township, Michigan. The building on the property previously 
operated as a bowling alley, which closed in 2019 and fell into disrepair. Petitioner executed a 
purchase agreement to buy the property in June 2022, and thereafter signed a contract with Mann 
Construction to renovate the “ vacant retail premises building into a Turn Key Box location for a 
proposed Dollar General store” in September 2022. 
 The sale of the property closed in October 2022, and petitioner paid a total acquisition cost 
of $450,000. The cost breakdown included $200,000 as the “[c]ontract sales price,” plus $250,000 
in “[o]ther [c]onsideration[.]” Petitioner’s appraiser, Michael Collins, characterized the sale of the 
property as “an arm’s length transaction .” However, respondent’s appraiser, John Widmer, 
claimed the $200,000 sale price was a “significant outlier” from the market rate because the 
property had been listed at a price of $525,000 in June 2021, signifying a 62% discount to 
petitioner’s purchase price. According to Collins, the “other consideration” in the acquisition cost 
included personal property, fixtures, and furniture associated with the bowling alley. Photographs 
-2- 
indicate that the bowling -alley fixtures were removed in October 2022 , after the property was 
purchased. 
 In December 2022, petitioner agreed to lease the property to Dolgencorp, LLC (Dollar 
General). The lease obligated petitioner to perform construction on the premises, to be completed 
by April 1, 2023, after which Dollar General would take possession of the property. The timing 
and extent of the construction performed on the property is disputed. Collins represented that 
petitioner did not make any renovation payments in 2022, the renovations occurred in 2023, and 
the cost of construction totaled $797,783.70. Petitioner’s owner told Collins the property was 
“cleaned up and secured” in 2022, but “no significant work had occurred.” Conversely, while 
Widmer could not identify what specific work was performed in 2022, he claimed that based on 
his review of the documentation, “roughly $80,300” of construction work was performed in 2022.1 
Dollar General took possession of the property in May 2023. 
 In May 2023, petitioner initiated the instant action by filing a petition in the Tax Tribunal 
to contest respondent’s 2023 tax assessment, alleging that respondent erroneously determined the 
property’s true cash value . Accordingly, petitioner requested the tribunal reduce the property’s 
assessed and taxable value. 
 Collins and Widmer filed appraisal reports with the Tax Tribunal. They agreed regarding 
the highest and best use of the property , with Collins concluding it was “commercial 
repurpose/use,” and Widmer concluding it was the property’s “current retail use . . . .” However, 
their determinations of the property’s true cash value as of the December 31, 2022 valuation date 
differed significantly.2 To determine the property’s true cash value, both appraisers relied on the 
sales-comparison and income-capitalization valuation approaches.3 

1 Collins’s testimony was based on a general ledger dated January 1, 2023 to August 31, 2023, that 
petitioner provided to him. Widmer’s analysis relied on a general ledger dated January 1, 2022 to 
July 12, 2023, which respondent purportedly received from petitioner through discovery. At the 
time of his appraisal, Collins had not seen the ledger produced in discovery . In contrast to the 
general ledger Collins relied on , the one Widmer relied on listed four nominal payments made 
from November 10, 2022 to December 15, 2022 . Both general ledgers listed a $78,983.78 
payment made on January 12, 2023. Widmer attributed th ose costs to work performed in 2022 
because, in his experience, construction work “is paid when it’s done.” 
2 The tribunal’s property -tax assessment for the 2023 tax year depended on the value of the 
property as of the December 31, 2022 tax day. See MCL 211.2(2) (providing that “[t]he taxable 
status of persons and real and personal property for a tax year shall be determined as of each 
December 31 of the immediately preceding year, which is considered the tax day”). 
3 “The three valuation methodologies that have been found acceptable and reliable by the Tax 
Tribunal and the courts are the cost -less-depreciation approach, the sales -comparison or market 
approach, and the capitalization -of-income approach.” Menard, Inc v Escanaba , 315 Mich App 
512, 523; 891 NW2d 1 (2016) (quotation marks and citation omitted). As summarized in Collins’s 
report, the sales -comparison approach “ utilizes sales of comparable properties in areas that are 

-3- 
 Under the sales-comparison approach, Collins identified the property’s true cash value as 
$214,000. For the income -capitalization approach, Collins estimated the property’s value as 
$212,000. Noting that the property required remodeling, Collins then deducted a “Build -
Out/Repair Allowance” of $57,000 to reach a true cash value of $155,000. This deduction 
reflected the amount needed to renovate the property “to attract the interest of a prospective 
tenant.” Reconciling the two approaches, Collins determined the property’s true cash value was 
$180,000. 
 Widmer identified the property’s true cash value under both the sales -comparison and 
income-capitalization approaches as $570,000. Notably, under the income -capitalization 
approach, Widmer identified a “Stabilized True Cash Value” of $1,095,931. Widmer next made 
adjustments “to address the non -stabilized occupancy status of the property,” deducting 
petitioner’s monthly renovation cost by $121,464 per month for the four month “holding period” 
between the valuation date and the date the property was completed and occupied. After adjusting 
for loss of rent and the amount for present value, Widmer identified a total “[n]on-stabilized 
adjustment” of $525,000, which he deducted from the Stabilized True Cash Value for a true cash 
value of $570,000. 
 The Tax Tribunal held a three -day hearing to determine the proper valuation of the 
property. The parties presented documentary evidence and testimony from Collins and Widmer 
in support of their true -cash-value determinations . The tribunal issued its final opinion and 
judgment on May 27, 2025, determining that the true cash value of the property was $525,000. It 
found “that Petitioner’s witness and evidence were not more persuasive than Respondent’s 
valuation evidence and cogent analysis.” 
 Regarding the highest and best use of the property, the tribunal noted the parties’ agreement 
and found “no dispute that the subject’s highest and best use is for a repurposed commercial use 
permissible under current zoning.” The tribunal also considered evidence regarding the condition 
of the property on the valuation date, providing: 
 The Tribunal does not accept Petitioner’s premise that the subject property 
condition was the singular driving force for the value of the subject as of December 
31, 2022. In this regard, Petitioner’s photographic evidence of the subject building 
is unpers uasive. The appraiser’s analysis of the subject’s condition as well as 
renovation costs was unclear given the inconsistent and incomplete photographs. 
There are no photographs as of December 31, 2022, from either appraiser. 
Likewise, Petitioner’s appraiser did not have any interior photographs of the subject 
as of January 2023. Petitioner’s appraisal report included subject photographs 
which were taken in October 2022 by someone other than Petitioner’s appraiser. 
Again, the October 2022 photographs of dismantled bowling lanes and equipment 
indicated initial renovation work prior to tax day. Yet, Petitioner’s appraiser 
asserted that there were no renovations to the subject property as of December 31, 

considered to be competitive to the subject,” while the income-capitalization approach evaluates a 
property’s earning capability based on either its market-derived capitalization rate or discounted 
annual cash flow. 
-4- 
2022. Petitioner’s workfile also included subject photographs which were undated 
and unauthored. The gaps in the photographic evidence are unpersuasive to the 
condition of the subject property as of tax day. Therefore, the condition of the 
subject property is not a determinative element for the subject property’s market 
value for December 31, 2022. 
 The tribunal weighed the documentary evidence presented, finding that “Petitioner’s bank 
financing, Petitioner’s purchase date of the subject, Petitioner’s lease agreement with Dollar 
General, and Petitioner’s agreement with Mann Construction for renovations played a significant 
part in the market value of the subject property.” It noted that “the sale price was not proven to be 
commensurate with the market,” and was therefore “not presumptive market value for the subject 
property.” Further, while it recognized that “the renovation costs of $800,000 are also an important 
element to the analysis of the subject property,” those costs did not “necessarily equate to value.” 
 The Tax Tribunal then made independent determinations of the property’s true cash value. 
Under the sales -comparison approach, it concluded the property’s market value was $529,000. 
Under the income -capitalization approach, it determined the property’s Stabilized True Cash 
Value was $1,046,250. The tribunal then considered the parties’ arguments regarding the correct 
amount of nonstabilized deductions for renovations. It gave petitioner’s proposed renovation 
deduction of $57,184 “no weight or credibility in the income analysis,” reasoning that the 
adjustment was unsupported and Collins’s “testimony was too vague and broad to be applied to 
the subject or comparable data.” Accordingly, it adopted respondent’s proposed deduction of 
$525,000, explaining: 
 Respondent’s appraiser considered the subject’s overall renovation cost 
from October 2022 to April 2023. Respondent’s analysis stemmed from 
Petitioner’s general ledger which denoted the total renovation cost of the subject 
property. Respondent developed a 4 -month discounted cash flow (DCF) with 
application and market support. Contrary to the opposing party’s challenges, 
Respondent’s appraiser adjusted the subject’s stabilized value by rent loss, 
renovation costs, and an appropriate discount rate. The analysis was well reasoned 
and supported by market analysis. 
Applying respondent’s deduction under the income -capitalization approach produced a true cash 
value of $521,000. Reconciling the two approaches, the Tax Tribunal’s final determination of the 
property’s true cash value was $525,000. This appeal ensued. 
II. TRUE CASH VALUE 
 On appeal, petitioner argues the Tax Tribunal erred in its true-cash-value determination by 
relying on Widmer’s renovation deduction, which only accounted for a portion of petitioner’s 
actual renovation costs. In

CFS Enters., Inc. v CG & J Realty, LLC 
 2026 NY Slip Op 05929 
 October 14, 2026 
 Appellate Division, Second Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 CFS Enterprises, Inc., respondent, 
 v 
 CG & J Realty, LLC, appellant, et al., defendants. 

 Supreme Court of the State of New York, Appellate Division, Second Judicial Department 
 Decided on October 14, 2026 
 2024-13568, (Index No. 703051/23) 
 Francesca E. Connolly, J.P. 
 Valerie Brathwaite Nelson 
 Barry E. Warhit 
 James P. McCormack, JJ. 

 Redmond Law PLLC, New York, NY (Jennifer Redmond of counsel), for appellant. 
 Chan Vitanza LLP, New York, NY (Henry C. Chan, Virginie Brizon, George Paliogiannis, and Deema Hassan of counsel), for respondent. 

 [*1] 
 DECISION & ORDER 
 In an action, inter alia, to foreclose a mechanic's lien, the defendant CG & J Realty, LLC, appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Queens County (Cassandra A. Johnson, J.), dated October 24, 2024. The order, insofar as appealed from, denied the motion of the defendant CG & J Realty, LLC, to vacate and cancel a bond and to dismiss the cause of action to foreclose the mechanic's lien insofar as asserted against it. 
 ORDERED that the order is affirmed insofar as appealed from, with costs. 
 On November 7, 2022, the plaintiff filed a notice under the Lien Law, claiming that it had a lien on certain real property located in Queens (hereinafter the premises) that was owned by the defendant CG & J Realty, LLC (hereinafter the defendant). In February 2023, the plaintiff commenced this action against, among others, the defendant, asserting, inter alia, a cause of action to foreclose the mechanic's lien. In April 2023, the defendant filed a notice of discharge of public improvements lien bond and posted a bond pursuant to Lien Law § 19 to discharge the lien (hereinafter the Section 19 bond). In July 2023, Century Construction Group Corp. filed a bond pursuant to Lien Law § 37 (hereinafter the Section 37 bond) and moved to discharge "all liens and claims that may be filed against [the premises]." In an order dated October 10, 2023, the Supreme Court discharged all liens and claims against the premises, setting forth that the Section 37 bond "shall supersede all prior bonds that discharged any liens and claims" against the premises. 
 Subsequently, by order to show cause, the defendant moved pursuant to Lien Law § 59 to vacate and cancel the Section 19 bond and to dismiss the cause of action to foreclose the mechanic's lien insofar as asserted against it. The plaintiff opposed the defendant's motion. In an order dated October 24, 2024, the Supreme Court, among other things, denied the defendant's motion. The defendant appeals. 
 "Mechanic's liens have their derivation entirely in statutory law, existing neither in common law nor in equity" ( Umbaugh Bldrs. v Parr Co. of Suffolk , 86 Misc 2d 1036 , 1037 [Sup Ct, Suffolk County]). As such, "[s]trict compliance with the statutory requirements is mandated and the court does not have discretion to excuse noncompliance" ( Matter of EK Mt Kisco, LLC v Arcon Constr. Group, Inc. , 138 AD3d 1118 , 1118-1119 [internal quotation marks omitted]; see Matter of [*2] HMB Acquisition Corp. v F & K Supply , 209 AD2d 412, 412 ). 
 Lien Law § 59 provides, in pertinent part, that "[a] mechanic's lien notice of which has been filed on real property or a bond given to discharge the same may be vacated . . . by an order of a court of record. Before such order shall be granted, a notice shall be served upon the lienor, either personally or by leaving it [at] his [or her] last known place of residence, with a person of suitable age, with directions to deliver it to the lienor." 
 Here, the defendant failed to satisfy the requirements of Lien Law § 59, as the defendant merely filed on NYSCEF the order to show cause informing the plaintiff of the defendant's intention to vacate the bond and did not personally serve it on the plaintiff or leave it with a person of suitable age and discretion at the plaintiff's last known place of residence ( see Matter of Eastchester Church Inc. , 44 Misc 3d 653, 654 [Sup Ct, Bronx County]). 
 Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly denied the defendant's motion to vacate the bond and to dismiss the cause of action to foreclose the mechanic's lien insofar as asserted against it. 
 The plaintiff seeks costs in the form of reimbursement of reasonable attorneys' fees and expenses incurred in defending this appeal pursuant to 22 NYCRR 130-1.1(c), alleging that the defendant's conduct in taking this appeal was frivolous. 
 "A court, in its discretion, may award to any party or attorney in any civil action or proceeding before the court . . . costs in the form of reimbursement for actual expenses reasonably incurred and reasonable attorney's fees, resulting from frivolous conduct" ( U.S. Bank N.A. v Tait , 234 AD3d 889 , 891 [internal quotation marks omitted]; see Curet v DeKalb Realty, LLC , 127 AD3d 914, 916 ). "Although the advancement of a meritless position may serve as the basis for a finding of frivolity, the standard for such a showing is high: the rule provides that a position will be deemed frivolous only where it is completely without merit in law and cannot be supported by a reasonable argument for an extension, modification or reversal of existing law" ( Hossain v Hossain , 243 AD3d 894 , 896 [internal quotation marks omitted]; see West Hempstead Water Dist. v Buckeye Pipeline Co., L.P. , 152 AD3d 558, 558-559 ). "A party seeking . . . an award of an attorney's fee pursuant to 22 NYCRR 130.1.1[ ] has the burden of demonstrating that the conduct of the opposing party was frivolous within the meaning of" 22 NYCRR 130-1.1(c) ( Matter of Miller v Miller , 96 AD3d 943, 944 ). 
 Here, the plaintiff failed to establish that the defendant's conduct was frivolous within the meaning of 22 NYCRR 130-1.1(c) ( see Zhuoya Luo v Wensheng Wang , 176 AD3d 1016 , 1018). 
 The parties' remaining contentions either are without merit or need not be reached in light of our determination. 
 CONNOLLY, J.P., BRATHWAITE NELSON, WARHIT and MCCORMACK, JJ., concur.

 Darrell M. Joseph 
 Clerk of the Court

leads.caseName: Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v. Hall
leads.court: Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of the State of New York
leads.text:
Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v Hall 
 2026 NY Slip Op 05932 
 October 14, 2026 
 Appellate Division, Second Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 Deutsche Bank National Trust Company, etc., respondent, 
 v 
 Roy Hall, appellant, et al., defendants. 

 Supreme Court of the State of New York, Appellate Division, Second Judicial Department 
 Decided on October 14, 2026 
 2025-01573, (Index No. 610529/15) 
 Betsy Barros, J.P. 
 Lillian Wan 
 Donna-Marie E. Golia 
 Elena Goldberg Velazquez, JJ. 

 Andrea S. Gross, St. Albans, NY, for appellant. 
 Atlas Solomon LLP, New York, NY (Jordan M.Smith of counsel), for respondent. 

 [*1] 
 DECISION & ORDER 
 In an action to foreclose a mortgage, the defendant Roy Hall appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Suffolk County (Joseph Farneti, J.), dated January 2, 2025. The order, insofar as appealed from, granted the plaintiff's motion pursuant to CPLR 306-b to extend the time to serve the summons and complaint upon that defendant, and denied those branches of that defendant's cross-motion which were pursuant to CPLR 306-b and 3211(a) to dismiss the complaint insofar as asserted against him. 
 ORDERED that the order is affirmed insofar as appealed from, with costs. 
 In July 2005, the defendant Roy Hall (hereinafter the defendant) executed a note that was secured by a mortgage on certain real property located in Amityville. In August 2010, the plaintiff commenced an action against the defendant, among others, to foreclose the subject mortgage (hereinafter the 2010 action). However, by order dated March 18, 2015, the Supreme Court directed dismissal of the 2010 action pursuant to CPLR 3215(c). 
 In October 2015, the plaintiff commenced this action against the defendant, among others, to foreclose the mortgage. On October 10, 2015, the plaintiff served copies of the summons, complaint, certificate of merit, and RPAPL 1303 notice upon an individual believed to be the defendant at the subject property. The defendant interposed an answer asserting various affirmative defenses, including lack of personal jurisdiction. In December 2015, the defendant moved, inter alia, pursuant to CPLR 3211(a)(8) to dismiss the complaint insofar as asserted against him. The plaintiff opposed the motion. In January 2018, the plaintiff moved, among other things, for summary judgment on the complaint insofar as asserted against the defendant, to strike the defendant's answer, and for an order of reference. In an order dated September 9, 2019, the Supreme Court granted the defendant's motion to the extent of scheduling a hearing to determine, inter alia, whether the defendant had been properly served with the summons and compliant, and denied the plaintiff's motion without prejudice. 
 In December 2019, after a hearing, the Supreme Court determined that the person served on October 10, 2015, was not the defendant and directed the plaintiff to move for an extension of time to serve the defendant. The plaintiff moved pursuant to CPLR 306-b to extend the time to serve the summons and complaint upon the defendant. The defendant opposed the motion [*2] and cross-moved, among other things, pursuant to CPLR 306-b and 3211(a) to dismiss the complaint insofar as asserted against him, based on the plaintiff's failure to serve him with the summons and complaint and its failure to comply with the notice requirement of RPAPL 1303. In an order dated January 2, 2025, the court, inter alia, granted the plaintiff's motion and denied those branches of the defendant's cross-motion. The defendant appeals. 
 Generally, service of a summons and complaint must be made within 120 days after the commencement of the action ( see CPLR 306-b). "Pursuant to CPLR 306-b, a court may, in the exercise of discretion, grant an extension of time within which to effect service for good cause shown or in the interest of justice" ( Bhatara v Kolaj , 222 AD3d 926, 930 [internal quotation marks omitted]). "The more flexible interest of justice standard accommodates late service that might be due to mistake, confusion, or oversight, so long as there is no prejudice to the defendant" ( id. ; see U.S. Bank N.A. v Bindra , 217 AD3d at 720). "In considering the interest of justice standard, the court may consider diligence, or lack thereof, along with any other relevant factor in making its determination, including expiration of the Statute of Limitations, the meritorious nature of the cause of action, the length of delay in service, the promptness of a plaintiff's request for the extension of time, and prejudice to the defendant" ( Bhatara v Kolaj , 222 AD3d at 930 [internal quotation marks omitted]; see U.S. Bank N.A. v Bindra , 217 AD3d at 720). "The determination of whether to grant an extension of time in the interest of justice is within the discretion of the motion court" ( Bhatara v Kolaj , 222 AD3d at 930; see U.S. Bank N.A. v Bindra , 217 AD3d at 720). 
 Here, the Supreme Court providently exercised its discretion in granting the plaintiff's motion in the interest of justice, and properly determined that dismissal of complaint insofar as asserted against the defendant pursuant to CPLR 306-b and 3211(a)(8) on the ground of the plaintiff's failure to serve the defendant with the summons and complaint was not warranted. The plaintiff demonstrated, among other things, that the action was timely commenced, that service was timely attempted and was believed by the plaintiff to have been made within 120 days after the commencement of the action, but was subsequently found to be defective, and that the extension of time would not prejudice the defendant ( see Hall v L & A Operational, LLC , 228 AD3d 846, 847; Bhatara v Kolaj , 222 AD3d at 931; U.S. Bank N.A. v Bindra , 217 AD3d at 720; Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. v Boakye-Yiadom , 213 AD3d 976, 977; HSBC Bank, USA v Gibatov , 183 AD3d 555, 556-557; JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. v Kothary , 178 AD3d 791, 793). Additionally, the plaintiff demonstrated a potentially meritorious cause of action ( see Hall v L & A Operational, LLC , 228 AD3d at 847; Bhatara v Kolaj , 222 AD3d at 931; U.S. Bank N.A. v Bindra , 217 AD3d at 721; see generally Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v Kingsbury , 171 AD3d 871, 871). 
 The defendant's contention that dismissal of the complaint insofar as asserted against him was warranted on the ground that the plaintiff failed to comply with RPAPL 1303 is without merit, as RPAPL 1303 only requires that an RPAPL 1303 notice be given to a mortgagor if the action relates to an owner-occupied one-to-four family dwelling, and here the subject property was not owner-occupied ( see RPAPL 1303[1][a]; Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. v Paulsen , 237 AD3d 1348). 
 Accordingly, the Supreme Court providently exercised its discretion in granting the plaintiff's motion pursuant to CPLR 306-b to extend the time to serve the summons and complaint upon the defendant, and properly denied those branches of the defendant's cross-motion which were pursuant to CPLR 306-b and 3211(a) to dismiss the complaint insofar as asserted against him. 
 BARROS, J.P., WAN, GOLIA and GOLDBERG VELAZQUEZ, JJ., concur. 
 ENTER:

leads.caseName: Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v. Merrill
leads.court: Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of the State of New York
leads.text:
Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v Merrill 
 2026 NY Slip Op 05933 
 October 14, 2026 
 Appellate Division, Second Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 Deutsche Bank National Trust Company, etc., appellant, 
 v 
 Pamela Merrill, respondent, et al., defendants. 

 Supreme Court of the State of New York, Appellate Division, Second Judicial Department 
 Decided on October 14, 2026 
 2025-01447, (Index No. 711920/23) 
 Lara J. Genovesi, J.P. 
 William G. Ford 
 Helen Voutsinas 
 Donna-Marie E. Golia, JJ. 

 McCarter & English, LLP, New York, NY (Adam M. Swanson and Jessie D. Bonaros of counsel), for appellant. 
 Mobilization for Justice, Inc., New York, NY (Tiffany Liston and Liana Goff of counsel), for respondent. 

 [*1] 
 DECISION & ORDER 
 In an action to foreclose a mortgage, the plaintiff appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Queens County (Tracy Catapano-Fox, J.), entered December 30, 2024. The order, insofar as appealed from, denied the plaintiff's motion, inter alia, for summary judgment on the complaint insofar as asserted against the defendant Pamela Merrill and for an order of reference, and granted those branches of that defendant's cross-motion which were for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against her and on her counterclaim pursuant to RPAPL 1501(4) to cancel and discharge of record the mortgage. 
 ORDERED that the order is affirmed insofar as appealed from, with costs. 
 On March 30, 2005, the defendant Pamela Merrill executed a note in the sum of $164,800 in favor of GreenPoint Mortgage Funding, Inc. The note was secured by a mortgage on certain real property located in Laurelton. Merrill allegedly defaulted on her payment obligations under the note in July 2009. By assignment of mortgage dated October 29, 2009, the mortgage was assigned to the plaintiff. 
 On November 19, 2009, the plaintiff commenced an action against Merrill, among others, to foreclose the mortgage (hereinafter the 2009 action). The plaintiff elected in the complaint "to call due the entire amount secured by the mortgage." Merrill interposed an answer to the complaint. In November 2015, the plaintiff moved to discontinue the 2009 action and to cancel the notice of pendency. In an order dated March 23, 2016, and entered April 11, 2016, the Supreme Court granted the plaintiff's motion. 
 On April 5, 2016, the plaintiff commenced a second action to foreclose the mortgage against Merrill, among others (hereinafter the 2016 action). In an order dated January 6, 2023, the Supreme Court, inter alia, directed dismissal of the complaint in the 2016 action for failure to comply with RPAPL 1304. 
 On June 8, 2023, the plaintiff commenced this action to foreclose the mortgage [*2] against Merrill, among others. Merrill interposed an answer in which she asserted, among other things, an affirmative defense alleging that the action was barred by the statute of limitations and a counterclaim pursuant to RPAPL 1501(4) to cancel and discharge of record the mortgage. The plaintiff moved, inter alia, for summary judgment on the complaint insofar as asserted against Merrill and for an order of reference. Merrill cross-moved, among other things, for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against her as time-barred and on her counterclaim pursuant to RPAPL 1501(4) to cancel and discharge of record the mortgage in light of the enactment of the Foreclosure Abuse Prevention Act (FAPA) (L 2022, ch 821 [eff Dec. 30, 2022]). In an order entered December 30, 2024, the Supreme Court, inter alia, denied the plaintiff's motion and granted those branches of Merrill's cross-motion which were for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against her and on her counterclaim pursuant to RPAPL 1501(4) to cancel and discharge of record the mortgage. The plaintiff appeals. 
 "An action to foreclose a mortgage is governed by a six-year statute of limitations" ( U.S. Bank N.A. v Santos , 218 AD3d 827, 828 ; see CPLR 213[4]; Lubonty v U.S. Bank N.A. , 34 NY3d 250 , 261; U.S. Bank N.A. v Singh , 247 AD3d 816 , 818; FV-1, Inc. v Palaguachi , 234 AD3d 818 , 820). "[E]ven if a mortgage is payable in installments, once a mortgage debt is accelerated, the entire amount is due and the statute of limitations begins to run on the entire debt" ( Bank of N.Y. Mellon v Mor , 201 AD3d 691, 694 ; see U.S. Bank N.A. v Singh , 247 AD3d at 818; U.S. Bank Trust, N.A. v Boreshesky , 241 AD3d 1385 , 1386; Citimortgage, Inc. v Gunn , 234 AD3d 922 ). "The entire mortgage debt will be deemed to have been accelerated by, as relevant here, the commencement of a mortgage foreclosure action in which the complaint seeks payment of the full outstanding loan balance" ( U.S. Bank N.A. v Connor , 204 AD3d 861, 863 ; see U.S. Bank N.A. v Singh , 247 AD3d at 818; U.S. Bank Trust, N.A. v Boreshesky , 241 AD3d at 1386-1387). 
 CPLR 203(h), as amended by FAPA, provides, in relevant part, that once a cause of action to foreclose a mortgage has accrued, no party may, in form or effect, unilaterally revive or reset the accrual thereof, or otherwise purport to effect a unilateral extension of the statute of limitations ( see U.S. Bank N.A. v Singh , 247 AD3d at 818; U.S. Bank Trust, N.A. v Horowitz , 238 AD3d 1093 ; FV-1, Inc. v Palaguachi , 234 AD3d at 821). Moreover, FAPA amended CPLR 3217(e) to provide, in relevant part, that the voluntary discontinuance of a foreclosure action shall not toll, extend, revive, or reset the statute of limitations, unless expressly prescribed by statute ( see U.S. Bank N.A. v Singh , 247 AD3d at 818; FV-1, Inc. v Palaguachi , 234 AD3d at 821). 
 Pursuant to RPAPL 1501(4), a person having an estate or interest in real property subject to a mortgage may maintain an action to secure the cancellation and discharge of record of the mortgage and to adjudge the estate or interest free of it, if the applicable statute of limitations for commencing a foreclosure action has expired ( see U.S. Bank N.A. v Singh , 247 AD3d at 818; U.S. Bank N.A. v Medianik , 223 AD3d 935 , 938; Ditmid Holdings, LLC v JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. , 180 AD3d 1002, 1003 ). 
 Here, Merrill established, prima facie, that the six-year statute of limitations began to run in November 2009 when the plaintiff commenced the 2009 action and elected in the complaint to call due the entire amount secured by the mortgage ( see U.S. Bank N.A. v Singh , 247 AD3d at 818; HSBC Bank USA, N.A. v Corrales , 224 AD3d 816 , 818). Merrill further demonstrated that this action was commenced in June 2023, more than six years later ( see CPLR 213[4]; U.S. Bank N.A. v Singh , 247 AD3d at 818; U.S. Bank Trust, N.A. v Boreshesky , 241 AD3d at 1388; Citimortgage, Inc. v Gunn , 234 AD3d at 923; U.S. Bank N.A. v Doura , 204 AD3d 721, 723 ). 
 In opposition, the plaintiff failed to raise a triable issue of fact. Contrary to the plaintiff's contention, applying FAPA, its voluntary discontinuance of the 2009 action did not revive or reset the statute of limitations ( see CPLR 203[h]; 3217[e]; IPA Asset Mgt., LLC v HSBC Bank USA, N.A. , 234 AD3d 948 , 950; Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. v Edwards , 231 AD3d 1189 , 1193). Moreover, since the 2016 action was untimely commenced, the plaintiff's contention that it could avail itself of the savings provision contained in CPLR 205-a to render this action timely is without merit. 
 Furthermore, there is no merit to the plaintiff's contention that FAPA does not apply retroactively ( see Van Dyke v U.S. Bank, N.A. , 45 NY3d 461 , 474; Article 13 LLC v Ponce De Leon Fed. Bank , 45 NY3d 441 , 451-453). The plaintiff's arguments challenging FAPA's constitutionality are without merit ( see Van Dyke v U.S. Bank, N.A. , 45 NY3d 461 ; Article 13 LLC v Ponce De Leon Fed. Bank , 45 NY3d 441 ; Wilmington Sav. Fund Socy., FSB v Lozowski , 245 AD3d 986 ; Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v Dagrin , 233 AD3d 1065 , 1069-1071). 
 Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly granted those branches of Merrill's cross-motion which were for summary judgment dismissing the complaint insofar as asserted against her and on her counterclaim pursuant to RPAPL 1501(4) to cancel and discharge of record the mortgage, and properly denied the plaintiff's motion, among other things, for summary judgment on the complaint insofar as asserted against Merrill and for an order of reference. 
 GENOVESI, J.P., FORD, VOUTSINAS and GOLIA, JJ., concur.
