leads.caseName: Matter of Hunter v. Zoning Bd. of Appeals of the Town of Islip
leads.court: Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of the State of New York
leads.text:
Matter of Hunter v Zoning Bd. of Appeals of the Town of Islip 
 2026 NY Slip Op 05953 
 October 14, 2026 
 Appellate Division, Second Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 In the Matter of Michael L. Hunter III, et al., appellants, 
 v 
 Zoning Board of Appeals of the Town of Islip, respondent. 

 Supreme Court of the State of New York, Appellate Division, Second Judicial Department 
 Decided on October 14, 2026 
 2024-10955, (Index No. 604535/24) 
 Lara J. Genovesi, J.P. 
 William G. Ford 
 Helen Voutsinas 
 Donna-Marie E. Golia, JJ. 

 Sahn Ward Braff Coschignano PLLC, Uniondale, NY (Michael H. Sahn, Joseph R. Bjarnson, and Ralph Branciforte of counsel), for appellants. 
 William F. Garbarino, Town Attorney, Islip, NY (Jordan L. Lite and Joseph V. DeMaggio of counsel), for respondent. 

 [*1] 
 DECISION & ORDER 
 In a proceeding pursuant to CPLR article 78 to review so much of a determination of the Zoning Board of Appeals of the Town of Islip dated January 23, 2024, as, after a hearing, denied so much of the petitioners' application as was for certain area variances, the petitioners appeal from a judgment of the Supreme Court, Suffolk County (Christopher Modelewski, J.), dated September 6, 2024. The judgment denied the petition and dismissed the proceeding. 
 ORDERED that the judgment is affirmed, with costs. 
 In January 2021, the Zoning Board of Appeals of the Town of Islip (hereinafter the ZBA) granted the petitioners' application for a permit to renovate their existing detached garage, which had been constructed prior to the enactment of the zoning laws. Thereafter, the petitioners demolished the detached garage and constructed a new structure. In a letter dated October 6, 2022, the Town of Islip Building Division, Zoning Department, informed the petitioners that their detached garage had been reviewed and that the newly constructed garage did not conform with the previously granted permit. In November 2022, the petitioners applied to the ZBA, inter alia, for area variances related to their newly constructed garage. 
 After a hearing, the ZBA denied so much of the petitioners' application as was for area variances related to their newly constructed garage. The petitioners commenced this proceeding pursuant to CPLR article 78 to review that portion of the ZBA's determination. By judgment dated September 6, 2024, the Supreme Court denied the petition and dismissed the proceeding. The petitioners appeal. 
 Local zoning boards have broad discretion in considering applications for variances, and judicial review is limited to determining whether the action taken by the board was illegal, arbitrary, or an abuse of discretion ( see Matter of Kami Holding Corp. v Zoning Bd. of Appeals of the Vil. of Westbury , 223 AD3d 811 , 812; Matter of Carnelian Farms, LLC v Leventhal , 151 AD3d 844, 845 ). The determination of a local zoning board is entitled to great deference, and will be set aside only if it is illegal, arbitrary and capricious, or irrational ( see Matter of Carella v Zoning Bd. [*2] of Appeals of the Town of Ramapo , 235 AD3d 974 , 975; Matter of Gabriele v Zoning Bd. of Appeals of the Town of Eastchester , 228 AD3d 659 , 660). 
 The determination of the ZBA was not arbitrary and capricious. When a zoning board of appeals makes a determination of whether to grant an area variance to an applicant, the zoning board is required to engage in a balancing test, weighing the benefit of the grant to the applicant against the detriment to the health, safety, and welfare of the neighborhood or community if the variance is granted ( see Matter of Massian v Board of Zoning Appeals of the Town of Brookhaven , 210 AD3d 984, 985 ; Matter of Morris Motel, LLC v DeChance , 199 AD3d 687, 688 ). The zoning board must consider the following factors when making its determination: "whether (1) an undesirable change will be produced in the character of the neighborhood or a detriment to nearby properties will be created by the granting of the area variance; (2) the benefit sought by the applicant can be achieved by some method, feasible for the applicant to pursue, other than an area variance; (3) the requested area variance is substantial; (4) the proposed variance will have an adverse effect or impact on the physical or environmental conditions in the neighborhood or district; and (5) the alleged difficulty was self-created" ( Matter of Bernstein v Putnam Val. Zoning Bd. of Appeals , 191 AD3d 779, 781 ; see Matter of D.P.R. Scrap Metal, Inc. v Board of Zoning Appeals of Town of N. Hempstead , 187 AD3d 748, 749 ). 
 Here, the record demonstrates that the ZBA engaged in the required balancing test and considered the relevant statutory factors. The area variances sought by the petitioners were substantial in nature ( see Matter of Pecoraro v Board of Appeals of Town of Hempstead , 2 NY3d 608, 614 ; Matter of Bonadonna v Board of Zoning Appeals of the Inc. Vil. of Upper Brookville , 220 AD3d 855, 858 ). The evidence before the ZBA also supported its conclusions that granting the requested area variances would produce an undesirable change in the character of the neighborhood ( see Matter of Seaview Assn. of Fire Is., NY, Inc. v Town of Islip Zoning Bd. of Appeals , 221 AD3d 717, 719 ; Matter of Nataro v DeChance , 149 AD3d 1081, 1082 ). Further, as the ZBA determined that no similar variances had been granted, it was permitted to consider the possibility that granting the requested variances could set a negative precedent within the area ( see Matter of Seaview Assn. of Fire Is., NY, Inc. v Town of Islip Zoning Bd. of Appeals , 221 AD3d at 719 ). Moreover, the ZBA properly found that any hardship was self-created ( see Matter of Kami Holding Corp. v Zoning Bd. of Appeals of the Vil. of Westbury , 223 AD3d at 813; Matter of Latuga v Giannadeo , 140 AD3d 771, 772 ). 
 Finally, the petitioners' contention that so much of the ZBA's determination as denied so much of their application as was for area variances related to their newly constructed garage was arbitrary and capricious because the ZBA had previously granted their application in 2021 regarding their original garage is without merit, as they failed to establish that the ZBA reached a different result on essentially the same facts ( see Matter of Harris v Zoning Bd. of Appeals of Town of Carmel , 137 AD3d 1130, 1132 ; Matter of Christian Airmen, Inc. v Town of Newstead Zoning Bd. of Appeals , 115 AD3d 1319 , 1322). Therefore, so much of the ZBA's determination as denied so much of the petitioners' application as was for area variances related to their newly constructed garage was rational and not arbitrary and capricious ( see Matter of Kami Holding Corp. v Zoning Bd. of Appeals of the Vil. of Westbury , 223 AD3d at 813; Matter of Seaview Assn. of Fire Is., NY, Inc. v Town of Islip Zoning Bd. of Appeals , 221 AD3d at 718-719 ). 
 GENOVESI, J.P., FORD, VOUTSINAS and GOLIA, JJ., concur.

Matter of VN Prop., Inc. v Byrne 
 2026 NY Slip Op 05961 
 October 14, 2026 
 Appellate Division, Second Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 In the Matter of VN Property, Inc., appellant, 
 v 
 Rita Byrne, etc., et al., respondents. 

 Supreme Court of the State of New York, Appellate Division, Second Judicial Department 
 Decided on October 14, 2026 
 2024-08064, (Index No. 615288/23) 
 Mark C. Dillon, J.P. 
 Paul Wooten 
 Lourdes M. Ventura 
 Lisa S. Ottley, JJ. 

 Andrew J. Levitt, P.C., Melville, NY, for appellant. 
 Kendric Law Group P.C., Cold Spring Harbor, NY (Christopher Kendric of counsel), for respondents. 

 [*1] 
 DECISION & ORDER 
 In a proceeding pursuant to CPLR article 78 to review a determination of the Zoning Board of Appeals of the Town of Oyster Bay dated July 20, 2023, which, after a hearing, denied the petitioner's application for certain area variances, the petitioner appeals from an order and judgment (one paper) of the Supreme Court, Nassau County (Conrad D. Singer, J.), dated April 29, 2024. The order and judgment, inter alia, denied the petition and, in effect, dismissed the proceeding. 
 ORDERED that the order and judgment is affirmed, with costs. 
 The petitioner, the owner of a residential property located in Hicksville, applied to the Zoning Board of Appeals of the Town of Oyster Bay (hereinafter the ZBA) for area variances, inter alia, for certain extensions to the second floor. Specifically, the petitioner sought variances, among other things, for gross floor area, minimum and total side yard setbacks, and roof pitch. After a hearing, the ZBA denied the application, and the petitioner commenced this proceeding pursuant to CPLR article 78 to review the ZBA's determination. By order and judgment dated April 29, 2024, the Supreme Court, inter alia, denied the petition and, in effect, dismissed the proceeding. The petitioner appeals. 
 Local zoning boards have broad discretion in considering variance applications, and judicial review is limited to determining whether the action taken by the board was affected by an error of law, arbitrary and capricious, or an abuse of discretion ( see id. § 7803[3]; Matter of Bonadonna v Board of Zoning Appeals of the Inc. Vil. of Upper Brookville , 220 AD3d 855, 856-857 ; Matter of White Birch Circle Realty Corp. v DeChance , 212 AD3d 729, 730 ). Where, as here, a zoning board's determination is made after a public hearing, its determination should be upheld if it has a rational basis and is supported by evidence in the record ( see Matter of Bonadonna v Board of Zoning Appeals of the Inc. Vil. of Upper Brookville , 220 AD3d at 857 ; Matter of Ogden Land Dev., LLC v Zoning Bd. of Appeals of Vil. of Scarsdale , 121 AD3d 695, 696 ). 
 In considering an application for area variances, Town Law § 267-b(3)(b) requires a zoning board to engage in a balancing test, weighing the benefit to the petitioner against the detriment to the health, safety, and welfare of the neighborhood or community if the area variances are granted ( see Matter of White Birch Circle Realty Corp. v DeChance , 212 AD3d at 730 ). In particular, a zoning board must consider: "(1) whether an undesirable change will be produced in the character of the neighborhood or a detriment to nearby properties will be created by the granting [*2] of the area variance; (2) whether the benefit sought by the applicant can be achieved by some method, feasible for the applicant to pursue, other than an area variance; (3) whether the requested area variance is substantial; (4) whether the proposed variance will have an adverse effect or impact on the physical or environmental conditions in the neighborhood or district; and (5) whether the alleged difficulty was self-created, which consideration shall be relevant to the decision of the board of appeals, but shall not necessarily preclude the granting of the area variance" (Town Law § 267-b[3][b]). The zoning board, in applying the balancing test, is not required to justify its determination with supporting evidence for each of the five statutory factors as long as its determination balancing the relevant considerations is rational ( see Matter of Humphreys v Somers Zoning Bd. of Appeals , 206 AD3d 1000 , 1002). 
 Here, contrary to the petitioner's contention, the record reflects that the ZBA engaged in the requisite balancing of interests and considered the appropriate factors pursuant to Town Law § 267-b(3)(b) in determining the petitioner's application, and the ZBA's determination had a rational basis and was supported by the record ( see Matter of Maldonado v Board of Appeals of the Inc. Vil. of Val. Stream , 244 AD3d 1210 , 1211-1212; Matter of White Birch Circle Realty Corp. v DeChance , 212 AD3d at 731 ). The ZBA rationally concluded, inter alia, that the requested variances were substantial, that granting the variances would produce an undesirable change in the character of the neighborhood, and that the petitioner's alleged hardship was self-created. 
 Thus, the ZBA's determination was not affected by an error of law, arbitrary and capricious, or an abuse of discretion. Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly denied the petition and, in effect, dismissed the proceeding. 
 The petitioner's remaining contention is without merit. 
 DILLON, J.P., WOOTEN, VENTURA and OTTLEY, JJ., concur.

 Darrell M. Joseph 
 Clerk of the Court

leads.caseName: Pennymac Corp. v. New York City Envtl. Control Bd.
leads.court: Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of the State of New York
leads.text:
Pennymac Corp. v New York City Envtl. Control Bd. 
 2026 NY Slip Op 05965 
 October 14, 2026 
 Appellate Division, Second Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 Pennymac Corp., respondent, 
 v 
 New York City Environmental Control Board, et al., defendants; 194 Grant Corp., nonparty-appellant. 

 Supreme Court of the State of New York, Appellate Division, Second Judicial Department 
 Decided on October 14, 2026 
 2023-07960, (Index No. 21870/08) 
 Colleen D. Duffy, J.P. 
 Linda Christopher 
 Carl J. Landicino 
 Susan Quirk, JJ. 

 Michael Kennedy Karlson, New York, NY, for nonparty-appellant. 
 Friedman Vartolo LLP, New York, NY (Ronald P. Labeck of counsel), for respondent. 

 [*1] 
 DECISION & ORDER 
 In an action to foreclose a mortgage, nonparty 194 Grant Corp. appeals from an order of the Supreme Court, Kings County (Larry D. Martin, J.), dated May 18, 2023. The order denied that nonparty's motion pursuant to CPLR 1012 and 1013 for leave to intervene in this action and, thereupon, inter alia, pursuant to CPLR 5015(a)(3) and in the interests of substantial justice to vacate an amended judgment of foreclosure and sale of the same court (Mark I. Partnow, J.) dated August 13, 2019. 
 ORDERED that the order is affirmed, with costs. 
 In July 2008, the plaintiff's predecessor in interest commenced this action against Beverly Anthony, among others, to foreclose a mortgage on certain real property located in Brooklyn (hereinafter the property). At the time of the commencement of the action, the plaintiff's predecessor in interest filed a notice of pendency against the property. In March 2017, the Supreme Court granted the plaintiff's unopposed motion for leave to enter a default judgment against all non-answering defendants, including Anthony, to substitute the plaintiff for its predecessor in interest in this action, and for an order of reference. In August 2019, the court issued an amended judgment of foreclosure and sale, directing the sale of the property (hereinafter the 2019 amended judgment of foreclosure and sale). 
 In August 2022, nonparty 194 Grant Corp. (hereinafter 194 Grant) moved pursuant to CPLR 1012 and 1013 for leave to intervene in this action, alleging, among other things, that on August 19, 2008, it purchased the property from Anthony and, thereupon, inter alia, pursuant to CPLR 5015(a)(3) and in the interests of substantial justice to vacate the 2019 amended judgment of foreclosure and sale. The plaintiff opposed. In an order dated May 18, 2023, the Supreme Court denied 194 Grant's motion as untimely. 194 Grant appeals. 
 "Intervention under CPLR 1012 or 1013 requires a timely motion" ( Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. v Gray , 238 AD3d 1098, 1099 [internal quotation marks omitted]; see Castle Peak 2012-1 Loan Trust v Sattar , 140 AD3d 1107, 1108). In determining the timeliness of a motion for leave to intervene, courts consider, among other things, "the extent of the time lag between the [*2] making of the motion and the proposed intervenor's acquisition of knowledge of the circumstances upon which the motion for leave to intervene is based" ( Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. v Gray , 238 AD3d at 1099-1100 [internal quotation marks omitted]; see U.S. Bank, N.A. v Tsimbalisty , 181 AD3d 749, 750). 
 Here, as the Supreme Court properly determined, the filing of a notice of pendency at the time of the commencement of the action provided constructive notice of the action ( see CPLR 6501). Since 194 Grant's title to the property was recorded after the filing of the notice of pendency, 194 Grant is bound by all proceedings taken in the action after that filing to the same extent as if it were a party to the action ( see Bank of Am., N.A. v Burton , 233 AD3d 644, 645; Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. v Lance , 196 AD3d 535, 536). 194 Grant did not move for leave to intervene in this action until August 2022—approximately 14 years after it allegedly took title to the property—and failed to offer any reason for the delay in moving for that relief. Accordingly, the court providently exercised its discretion in denying, as untimely, those branches of 194 Grant's motion which were pursuant to CPLR 1012 and 1013 for leave to intervene in this action ( see Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. v Gray , 238 AD3d at 1099). 
 Moreover, although there is no specific time limit within which to move for vacatur under CPLR 5015(a)(3), the motion must be made within a reasonable time ( see Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. v Olivo , 241 AD3d 763, 765; Empire State Conglomerates v Mahbur , 105 AD3d 898, 899). Here, since the 2019 amended judgment of foreclosure and sale was issued in August 2019 and 194 Grant did not move to vacate it until August 2022, three years later, the Supreme Court also providently exercised its discretion in denying, as untimely, that branch of 194 Grant's motion which was pursuant to CPLR 5015(a)(3) to vacate the 2019 amended judgment of foreclosure and sale ( see Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. v Olivo , 241 AD3d at 765). 
 Although a court has the inherent discretionary authority to vacate its own judgment in the interests of substantial justice when unique or unusual circumstances warrant such relief ( see Brown-Wilks v Vornado Realty Trust , 247 AD3d 706, 708), no such circumstances are present here. Accordingly, the Supreme Court properly denied that branch of 194 Grant's motion which was to vacate the 2019 amended judgment of foreclosure and sale in the interests of substantial justice. 
 The parties' remaining contentions either are without merit or need not be reached in light of our determination. 
 DUFFY, J.P., CHRISTOPHER, LANDICINO and QUIRK, JJ., concur. 
 ENTER: 
 Darrell M. Joseph 
 Clerk of the Court

leads.caseName: US Bank N.A. v. Vento
leads.court: Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of the State of New York
leads.text:
US Bank N.A. v Vento 
 2026 NY Slip Op 05991 
 October 14, 2026 
 Appellate Division, Second Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 US Bank National Association, etc., respondent, 
 v 
 Jason Vento, appellant, et al., defendants. 

 Supreme Court of the State of New York, Appellate Division, Second Judicial Department 
 Decided on October 14, 2026 
 2025-04269, (Index No. 710479/21) 
 Valerie Brathwaite Nelson, J.P. 
 Linda Christopher 
 Lourdes M. Ventura 
 Donna-Marie E. Golia, JJ. 

 Binakis Law, P.C., Astoria, NY (Patrick Binakis of counsel), for appellant. 
 Atlas Solomon LLP, New York, NY (Eric M. Levine of counsel), for respondent. 

 [*1] 
 DECISION & ORDER 
 In an action to foreclose a mortgage, the defendant Jason Vento appeals from an order and judgment of foreclosure and sale (one paper) of the Supreme Court, Queens County (Scott Dunn, J.), entered February 26, 2025. The order and judgment of foreclosure and sale, insofar as appealed from, granted those branches of the plaintiff's motion which were to confirm a referee's report and for a judgment of foreclosure and sale, confirmed the referee's report, and directed the sale of the subject property. 
 ORDERED that the order and judgment of foreclosure and sale is reversed insofar as appealed from, on the law, with costs, those branches of the plaintiff's motion which were to confirm the referee's report and for a judgment of foreclosure and sale are denied, so much of the referee's report as determined that the mortgaged premises should be sold in one parcel is rejected, and the matter is remitted to the Supreme Court, Queens County, for further proceedings in accordance herewith. 
 In August 2009, the plaintiff commenced this action against, among others, the defendant Jason Vento (hereinafter the defendant) to foreclose a mortgage on certain real property located in Queens. The plaintiff moved, inter alia, for an order of reference. By order dated May 16, 2017, the Supreme Court granted the plaintiff's motion and appointed a referee to compute the amount due to the plaintiff. Subsequently, in an order dated February 6, 2024, the court appointed a substitute referee. 
 Thereafter, the plaintiff moved, among other things, to confirm the referee's report and for a judgment of foreclosure and sale. The defendant opposed the motion. By order and judgment of foreclosure and sale entered February 26, 2025, the Supreme Court, inter alia, granted those branches of the plaintiff's motion, confirmed the referee's report, and directed the sale of the subject property. The defendant appeals. 
 Contrary to the defendant's contention, the referee's failure to provide notice or hold a hearing on the issues addressed in the referee's report did not warrant denial of that branch of the plaintiff's motion which was to confirm the referee's report. "[A]s long as a defendant is not prejudiced by the inability to submit evidence directly to the referee, a referee's failure to notify a defendant and hold a hearing is not, by itself, a basis to reverse a judgment of foreclosure and sale and remit the matter for a hearing and a new determination of amounts owed" ( Bank of N.Y. Mellon [*2] v Viola , 181 AD3d 767, 770; see Excel Capital Group Corp. v 225 Ross St. Realty, Inc. , 165 AD3d 1233, 1236). "Where, as here, a defendant had an opportunity to raise questions and submit evidence directly to the Supreme Court, which evidence could be considered by the court in determining whether to confirm the referee's report, the defendant is not prejudiced by any error in failing to hold a hearing" ( Bank of N.Y. Mellon v Viola , 181 AD3d at 770; see Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. v O'Brien , 234 AD3d 730, 732). 
 Nevertheless, the Supreme Court should not have confirmed the referee's report. "The report of a referee should be confirmed whenever the findings are substantially supported by the record, and the referee has clearly defined the issues and resolved matters of credibility" ( U.S. Bank N.A. v Winnie Realty Group, LLC , 237 AD3d 871, 873 [internal quotation marks omitted]). "The referee's findings and recommendations are advisory only and have no binding effect on the court, which remains the ultimate arbiter of the dispute" ( id. [internal quotation marks omitted]). However, "[a] referee's findings should not be deemed substantially supported by the record when those findings are based upon inadmissible evidence" ( id. ). 
 Here, contrary to the defendant's contention, the referee's computation of the amount due to the plaintiff was not based upon inadmissible evidence, and the referee's findings in that regard were substantially supported by the record ( cf. Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. v Laronga , 219 AD3d 1559, 1561). However, because the referee failed to identify any documents or other sources upon which he based his finding that the mortgaged premises should be sold in one parcel, that finding is unsupported by the record ( see Ridgewood Sav. Bank v Kapoor , 222 AD3d 797, 799). 
 Accordingly, the Supreme Court should have denied those branches of the plaintiff's motion which were to confirm the referee's report and for a judgment of foreclosure and sale, and we remit the matter to the Supreme Court, Queens County, for a new determination as to whether the mortgaged premises can be sold in parcels. 
 BRATHWAITE NELSON, J.P., CHRISTOPHER, VENTURA and GOLIA, JJ., concur.

 Darrell M. Joseph

Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. v Begum 
 2026 NY Slip Op 05996 
 October 14, 2026 
 Appellate Division, Second Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 Wells Fargo Bank, National Association, etc., respondent, 
 v 
 Resma Begum, etc., appellant, et al., defendants. 

 Supreme Court of the State of New York, Appellate Division, Second Judicial Department 
 Decided on October 14, 2026 
 2024-09027, (Index No. 706362/15) 
 Betsy Barros, J.P. 
 Helen Voutsinas 
 Donna-Marie E. Golia 
 Phillip Hom, JJ. 

 PM Law P.C., New York, NY (Pankaj Malik of counsel), for appellant. 
 McCalla Raymer Leibert Pierce, LLP, New York, NY (Adam D. Weiss of counsel), for respondent. 

 [*1] 
 DECISION & ORDER 
 In an action, inter alia, to foreclose a mortgage, the defendant Resma Begum appeals from a judgment of foreclosure and sale of the Supreme Court, Queens County (Scott Dunn, J.), entered May 29, 2024. The judgment of foreclosure and sale, insofar as appealed from, upon an order of the same court (Thomas D. Raffaele, J.) entered December 6, 2018, among other things, granting that branch of the plaintiff's motion which was for summary judgment on the complaint insofar as asserted against the defendant Resma Begum, and upon an order of the same court (Scott Dunn, J.) entered April 3, 2024, inter alia, granting those branches of the plaintiff's motion which were to confirm a referee's report and for a judgment of foreclosure and sale, confirmed the referee's report and directed the sale of the subject property. 
 ORDERED that the judgment of foreclosure and sale is affirmed insofar as appealed from, with costs. 
 In March 2007, Mohamed Adam Ali Mian (hereinafter the decedent) executed a note and mortgage encumbering certain real property located in Woodside. The decedent allegedly defaulted on his obligations under the note in December 2009. He died in November 2014. The mortgage ultimately was assigned to the plaintiff in October 2016. 
 This mortgage foreclosure action was commenced in June 2015. The defendant Resma Begum (hereinafter the appellant), who is the decedent's widow and the administrator of and heir to his estate, interposed an answer. 
 In December 2017, the plaintiff moved, inter alia, for summary judgment on the complaint insofar as asserted against the appellant. The appellant opposed the motion and cross-moved to dismiss the complaint. In an order entered December 6, 2018, the Supreme Court, among other things, granted that branch of the plaintiff's motion and referred the matter to a referee to compute the amount due on the note. 
 In a report dated January 23, 2019, the referee concluded that the amount due on the note was $1,440,895.67. On March 9, 2022, the plaintiff moved, inter alia, to confirm the referee's [*2] report and for a judgment of foreclosure and sale. On June 9, 2022, the appellant opposed the plaintiff's motion and cross-moved for certain relief. 
 In an order entered April 3, 2024, the Supreme Court, inter alia, granted those branches of the plaintiff's motion. A judgment of foreclosure and sale was then entered on May 29, 2024. This appeal ensued. 
 Here, the plaintiff established, prima facie, that its predecessor in interest had standing to commence this action by submitting, inter alia, an affidavit of an employee of the plaintiff's loan servicer, a document execution associate, which established, prima facie, that the plaintiff's predecessor in interest had possession of the note, endorsed in blank, at the time of commencement of the action ( see Aurora Loan Servs., LLC v Taylor , 25 NY3d 355, 361 ; Bank of Am., N.A. v Nicolosi , 200 AD3d 1018, 1022 ). In opposition, the appellant failed to raise a triable issue of fact. 
 In support of the plaintiff's motion, among other things, for summary judgment on the complaint insofar as asserted against the appellant, the plaintiff submitted an affidavit of service in which the process server attested that he had served the appellant with, inter alia, the summons and complaint and an RPAPL 1303 notice in bold 14-point type, printed on colored paper, which color differed from that of the color of the summons and complaint, with the title printed in 20-point type. The process server attested that the notice served complied with all the requirements of RPAPL 1303. This affidavit of service was sufficient to establish, prima facie, that the plaintiff's predecessor in interest provided notice in compliance with RPAPL 1303 ( see Tri-State III, LLC v Litkowski , 239 AD3d 911 , 914). In opposition, the appellant failed to raise a triable issue of fact. 
 Further, the appellant, who was not a borrower, was not entitled to notice pursuant to RPAPL 1304 and could not raise that defense on the decedent's behalf ( see HSBC Bank USA, N.A. v Congregation Khal Chasidei Skwera, Inc. , 213 AD3d 814, 815 ; U.S. Bank N.A. v Lloyd-Lewis , 205 AD3d 838, 839 ). 
 Moreover, the appellant failed to timely object to the referee's report. "CPLR 4403 requires a motion to reject a referee's report to be made within 15 days of the filing of the report, while 22 NYCRR 202.44(a) requires the defendant to move to confirm or reject the report within 30 days after notice of the filing of the report" ( Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v Gopaul , 229 AD3d 443 , 445; see HSBC Bank USA, N.A. v Sewell , 198 AD3d 953, 955 ). Here, the referee's report was filed on March 9, 2022, when the plaintiff moved, inter alia, to confirm the referee's report. The appellant did not raise any objections to the report until she made her cross-motion on June 9, 2022, more than 30 days later. "Therefore, that branch of the [appellant's] cross-motion which was, in effect, to reject the referee's report was untimely" ( Deutsche Bank Natl. Trust Co. v Gopaul , 229 AD3d at 445). 
 The appellant's contention that the document execution associate improperly relied upon unproduced business records is improperly raised for the first time on appeal ( see U.S. Bank N.A. v Moschetta , 216 AD3d 848 , 849). 
 The appellant's remaining contention is without merit. 
 Accordingly, we affirm the judgment of foreclosure and sale insofar as appealed from. 
 BARROS, J.P., VOUTSINAS, GOLIA and HOM, JJ., concur.

 Darrell M. Joseph

*** FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST’S HAWAIʻI REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER ***

 Electronically Filed
 Supreme Court
 SCWC-XX-XXXXXXX
 14-OCT-2026
 07:55 AM
 Dkt. 12 OP
 IN THE SUPREME COURT OF THE STATE OF HAWAIʻI

 ---o0o---
________________________________________________________________

 STEWART NORRIE,
 individually and as Trustee of the Stewart Norrie Trust,
 Respondent/Appellant-Appellant,

 vs.

 MAUI COUNTY BOARD OF VARIANCES AND APPEALS;
 JACKY TAKAKURA, in her official capacity as Director of the
 Department of Planning for the County of Maui;
 DEPARTMENT OF PLANNING, COUNTY OF MAUI,
 Petitioners/Appellees-Appellees.
________________________________________________________________

 SCWC-XX-XXXXXXX

 CERTIORARI TO THE INTERMEDIATE COURT OF APPEALS
 (CAAP-XX-XXXXXXX; CASE NO. 2CCV-XX-XXXXXXX)

 OCTOBER 14, 2026

 DEVENS, C.J., McKENNA, EDDINS, AND GINOZA, JJ., AND CIRCUIT
 JUDGE CASTAGNETTI, ASSIGNED BY REASON OF VACANCY

 OPINION OF THE COURT BY McKENNA, J.

 I. Introduction

 This is a secondary agency appeal. The Intermediate Court

of Appeals (“ICA”) reversed a Maui County Board of Variances and
  *** FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST’S HAWAIʻI REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER ***

Appeals’ (“BVA”)1 decision and order based on the violation of a

procedural rule stating that a decision and order, accompanied

by findings of fact and conclusions of law, must be rendered

within forty-five days of a triggering date.

 We hold that the deadline in the rule is directory, not

mandatory, and that there was no actual prejudice to appellant’s

substantial rights. We therefore vacate the ICA’s judgment on

appeal and reinstate the decisions of the Circuit Court of the

Second Circuit (“circuit court”).2

 The Department of Planning, County of Maui (“Department”)

revoked Stewart Norrie (“Norrie”)’s bed and breakfast (“B&B”)

permit and imposed a two-year ban on future B&B applications.

This decision was sustained by the BVA. At its November 24,

2021 meeting, the BVA stated on the record that it was upholding

the Department’s decision. The BVA did not vote to adopt the

draft findings of fact and conclusions of law (“FOF/COL”) until

its January 13, 2022 meeting. The actual FOF/COL were not filed

until January 31, 2022.

1 The BVA “[h]ears and determines applications for variances from the
strict application of any general plan, zoning, subdivision or building
ordinances. Holds public hearing prior to ruling on a variance application
and issues findings of fact and conclusions of law on decisions granting or
denying variance applications.” Board of Variances & Appeals, Cnty. of Maui,
https://www.mauicounty.gov/172/Board-of-Variances-Appeals
[https://perma.cc/HZB4-ETHL].

2 The Honorable Kelsey T. Kawano presided.

 2
 *** FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST’S HAWAIʻI REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER ***

 Norrie appealed to the circuit court, arguing in part that

BVA Rules of Practice and Procedure (“RPP”) § 12-801-60 (eff.

1999) (the “45-day rule”) required the BVA to file its FOF/COL

within forty-five days of oral argument and that, therefore, the

BVA decision and order had to be reversed. RPP § 12-801-60

provides:

 A proceeding shall stand submitted for decision by the
 board after the taking of evidence, the submission of a
 report by the hearing officer, and the filing of such
 briefs or the presentation of such oral argument as may
 have been allowed. A party to the proceeding may submit a
 proposed decision and order which shall include proposed
 findings of fact. Said proposals shall be mailed to each
 party to the proceeding and an opportunity given to each
 party to comment thereon.

 Every decision and order adverse to a party to the
 proceeding, rendered by the board in a contested case,
 shall be in writing or stated in the record and shall be
 accompanied by separate findings of fact and conclusions of
 law. If any party to the proceeding has filed proposed
 findings of fact, the board shall incorporate in its
 decision a ruling which addresses such findings. Such
 decisions and orders in contested cases shall be rendered
 within forty-five days from the presentation of oral
 argument by the parties.

 The circuit court affirmed the BVA’s decision. On Norrie’s

appeal to the ICA, the parties repeated the arguments they had

made below. In supplemental briefing ordered by the ICA,

however, the BVA conceded that RPP § 12-801-60 is “mandatory.”

 The ICA reversed the circuit court and BVA decisions. See

Norrie v. Maui Cnty. Bd. of Variances & Appeals, No. CAAP-23-

0000668, 2026 WL 1266063 (Haw. App. May 8, 2026) (SDO). It held

that the BVA’s violation of its own 45-day rule required

reversal of the two-year ban because the FOF/COL were rendered

 3
 *** FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST’S HAWAIʻI REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER ***

more than forty-five days after the November 24, 2021 hearing.

The ICA also concluded that reversal of the BVA’s decision was

required due to prejudice to Norrie’s substantial right to

operate a B&B.

 On certiorari, the BVA argues that the ICA erred because it

satisfied RPP § 12-801-60 when it orally stated its decision in

the record on November 24, 2021. It also argues abrogating an

entire administrative proceeding and denying appellate review on

the merits because of a short delay in the FOF/COL is unjust.

 We are not bound by the BVA’s apparent concession of law

before the ICA that the 45-day deadline is mandatory. Umberger

v. Dep’t of Land & Nat. Res., 140 Hawaiʻi 500, 520 n.38, 403 P.3d

277, 297 n.38 (2017). Under our precedent, administrative rule

deadlines are directory, not mandatory, unless a consequence is

provided for failure to meet the deadline.

 We hold that because there is no consequence provided in

RPP § 12-801-60, the 45-day rule is directory, not mandatory.

We also hold that to the extent the ICA based its reversal on

Hawaiʻi Revised Statutes (“HRS”) § 91-14(g)(3) (2012 & Supp.

2022), which authorizes reversal for agency decisions made upon

unlawful procedure, it also erred. There was no prejudice to

Norrie’s substantial rights based on the short delay in the

BVAʻs issuance of its FOF/COL.

 4
 *** FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST’S HAWAIʻI REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER ***

 We therefore vacate the ICA’s June 12, 2026 judgment on

appeal and affirm the circuit court’s September 21, 2023

findings of fact, conclusions of law, and decision and order, as

well as its October 6, 2023 final judgment.

 II. Background

A. Factual Background

 Norrie ran a B&B on Maui since 2015. He last renewed his

permit in 2018 with a 2023 expiration date. The B&B permit

required the owner to stay on property with guests and to comply

with agency and government regulations.

 In February 2020, Norrie’s neighbor complained to the

Department that Norrie was violating his B&B permit by not

residing on the property while guests were present and by having

guests who did not comply with quiet hour requirements. In

March 2020, a neighbor contacted the Maui Police Department

(“MPD”) to complain about excessive noise from Norrie’s B&B.

 Norrie responded that the B&B stopped operating in March

2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic. But on April 6, 2020, a

neighbor contacted the MPD regarding a party that was occurring

at the B&B in violation of COVID-19 Public Health Emergency

Rules. Norrie admitted to police to having “several friends

over to his residence for a social gathering.”

 During its investigation, the Department saw an Expedia.com

advertisement and Norrie’s comment on his website. In that

 5
 *** FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST’S HAWAIʻI REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER ***

comment, Norrie said he owned two homes on Maui and sometimes

lived at his second home instead of at the B&B. Norrie did not

deny that he made this statement.

 On May 8, 2020, the Department issued a notice of warning

for violations of Norrie’s B&B permit, including the requirement

to comply with agency and government regulations. Yet, in June

and July of 2020, neighbors continued to contact the MPD to

complain about loud music from the B&B.

 Hence, on August 5, 2020, the Department issued a “Two-Year

Owner Ban and Revocation of a Bed and Breakfast (B&B) Home

Permit” (“ban”). The Department concluded that Norrie had

violated the following provisions of the Maui County Code

(“MCC”):

 MCC, Section 19.64.065(A)(1)(c): Evidence of non-responsive
 management;
 MCC, Section 19.64.065(A)(1)(d): Police reports of noise or
 other disturbances on the property;
 MCC, Section 19.64.065(A)(1)(e): Warnings or violations
 resulting from requests for service;
 MCC, Section 19.64.065(A)(1)(t): Neighbor complaints of
 noise and other disturbances relating to bed and breakfast
 home operations; provided that the department has received
 at least three complaints about the bed and breakfast home
 within a twelve-month period. Complaints must be from
 property owners or lessees of record located on two or more
 different lots within a five-hundred-foot radius of the bed
 and breakfast home;
 MCC, Section 19.64.065(A)(1)(g): Noncompliance with permit
 conditions; and
 MCC, Section l9.64.065(A)(1)(h): Noncompliance with this
 chapter.

MCC § 19.64.065(A)(1) (2018).

 6
  *** FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST’S HAWAIʻI REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER ***

 On September 3, 2020, Norrie filed an appeal to the BVA.3

The BVA was initially scheduled to hold a hearing on March 11,

2021, but the hearing was rescheduled multiple times at Norrie’s

request. Then, on August 9, 2021, Norrie filed a motion for

automatic reversal based on HRS § 91-13.5 (2012), discussed in

Section II.B.2.b below.

 On August 12, 2021, the BVA deferred the matter to

September 23, 2021, to allow for additional briefing.

 On September 23, 2021, the BVA held a contested case

hearing. BVA’s counsel told the BVA it “would need to render

[a] decision within 45 days of the close of oral argument” and

stated that the “deadline is important — important to follow,

obviously.”

 Norrie testified that he lived on his property and the

majority of the noise complaints occurred after he had stopped

operating a B&B due to COVID-19 restrictions. He said he

instead began offering the property as a long-term rental.4 A

3 Under RPP § 12-801-8 (eff. 1999), the BVA is composed of “nine members,
appointed by the mayor and approved by the council.” RPP § 12-801-22(a)
(eff. 2005) regulates voting of the BVA and requires “an affirmative vote of
a majority of the membership to which the board is entitled.” RPP § 12-801-
11 (eff. 1999) provides that the quorum necessary to transact business is a
majority of all members to which the board is entitled; it also provides that
the concurrence of a majority of all members to which the board is entitled
shall be necessary to take any action. Therefore, five members are required
for a quorum and five votes are needed to reach a decision.

4 The circuit court later found Norrie’s testimony unreliable,
particularly as it was contradicted by his written statements about often not
being at the B&B.

 7
  *** FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST’S HAWAIʻI REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER ***

neighbor testified that he had complained to Norrie several

times about the noise and regularly saw large gatherings of

people at the B&B.

 All five BVA members present voted to deny Norrie’s motion

for automatic approval based on HRS § 91-13.5, but two of the

five voted to grant his appeal. The BVA therefore failed to

reach the required five-vote threshold for a decision. The BVA

deferred the matter.

 On October 28, 2021, the BVA reconvened with six of its

nine members, but was again unable to reach a five-vote majority

decision. BVA October 28, 2021 Meeting,

https://archive.org/details/211028-bc-bva

[https://perma.cc/GM2G-99BQ].5 The final vote was 4-2 to deny

the appeal. BVA October 28, 2021 Meeting Minutes Summary,

https://www.mauicounty.gov/AgendaCenter/ViewFile/Minutes/_102820

21-804 [https://perma.cc/4A7R-PFPP].

Filed 10/14/26

 CERTIFIED FOR PUBLICATION

 IN THE COURT OF APPEAL OF THE STATE OF CALIFORNIA

 FOURTH APPELLATE DISTRICT

 DIVISION THREE

 SCOTTSDALE INSURANCE
 COMPANY,
 G065564
 Plaintiff and Respondent,
 (Super. Ct. No. 30-2024-01411000)
 v.
 OPINION
 CALIFORNIA MILITARY
 DEPARTMENT,

 Defendant and Appellant.

 Appeal from a judgment of the Superior Court of Orange County,
William D. Claster, Judge. Affirmed.
 Rob Bonta, Attorney General, Tamar Pachter, Senior Assistant
Attorney General, Brian D. Wesley and Jarrad L. Wood, Deputy Attorneys
General, for Defendant and Appellant.
 Selman Leichenger Edson Hsu Newman & Moore, Sheryl W.
Leichenger and Elisabeth M. D’Agostino for Plaintiff and Respondent.
  This appeal arises from a summary judgment in favor of
Scottsdale Insurance Company (Scottsdale) declaring that two policies issued
to nonparty TL Veterans Construction, Inc. (TL Veterans) had been
rescinded. The present appeal is by the California Military Department
(CMD), who sought compensation under the policies as an additional insured.
 CMD hired TL Veterans to renovate two buildings at the Joint
Forces Training Base in Los Alamitos (the Los Alamitos Base project). During
the construction, TL Veterans negligently caused a fire, resulting in a total
loss of one of the buildings. TL Veterans and CMD made claims on the
insurance policies issued by Scottsdale, but Scottsdale’s subsequent
investigation revealed that TL Veterans had made material
misrepresentations on its application for insurance. Scottsdale rescinded the
policies and filed the underlying lawsuit seeking a judicial declaration that
they had been effectively rescinded, which the trial court granted. CMD
appealed and raises essentially two arguments.
 First, CMD contends Scottsdale waived its statutory right of
rescission by failing to adequately investigate a prior claim TL Veterans had
submitted. We conclude, as did the trial court, that the prior claim would not
have revealed one of Scottsdale’s primary bases for rescission, which was TL
Veterans’ misrepresentation that it was not working with asbestos. In fact,
the Los Alamitos project involved asbestos abatement. This was an
independent ground for rescission that was not waived.
 Second, CMD contends that once a third party has taken an
economic position based on an insurance policy—here, CMD relying on the
policy to award the contract to TL Veterans—the insurer loses the right of
rescission. However, CMD cites no precedent for applying such a rule in the
context of a misrepresentation on an insurance application. The authorities

 2
 CMD relies on apply general principles of equity and are inconsistent with
Insurance Code section 6501, which permits the insurer to rescind “any time”
before a lawsuit is filed to enforce the policy. Accordingly, we affirm.
 UNDISPUTED FACTS
 On or about August 24, 2020, TL Veterans entered into a contract
with the California Department of General Services for ‘“replacement of roof
[sic] of the Skilled Nursing Facilities of the Department of State Hospitals in
the City of Norwalk, County of Los Angeles, California . . . .”’ (Norwalk
project). In carrying out the Norwalk project, TL Veterans entered into a
subcontract with JNH Roofing on or about December 22, 2020, which valued
the subcontract at approximately $1 million. The Department of General
Services publicly posted a notice of its award of the Norwalk project to TL
Veterans on California’s procurement website. The notice stated the amount
awarded under the contract was approximately $2.2 million.
 In January 2021, TL Veterans submitted an insurance
application (2021 application) to respondent Scottsdale through its
underwriter. The 2021 application identified TL Veterans’ ‘“Exposures”’ as
follows: “a. Gross Receipts for the next 12 months? $300,000 [¶] b. What are
the Gross Receipts for the last 12 months? $300,000 [¶] c. What are your
subcontractor costs for the next 12 months? $90,000.” The 2021 application
requested that TL Veterans ‘“Describe in detail your largest project in the
last 5 years along with the receipts $$$. (DETAIL REQUIRED FOR
CARRIER APPROVAL).”’ TL Veterans responded with ‘“county office
remodeling $105,869.”’ The 2021 application did not mention the Norwalk
project or reflect the value of its contract.

 1 Further statutory references will be to the Insurance Code

except as otherwise specified.

 3
  The 2021 application asked TL Veterans if it had ‘“been involved
or do you subcontract any work involving blasting operations, hazardous
waste, asbestos, mold, PCB’s or medical and/or industrial life?”’ TL Veterans
answered ‘“No.”’ In fact, the Norwalk project involved a skilled nursing
facility.
 Based on the representations contained in the 2021 application,
Scottsdale issued primary and excess insurance policies, Policy Nos.
RBS0072806 and XLS0115910, effective January 23, 2021, through January
23, 2022, to TL Veterans as the named insured (2021-2022 policies). The
primary policy had a limit of $1 million, and the excess policy had a limit of
$4 million.
 Less than a month later, on February 16, 2021, CMD posted a
notice of an award of a new contract to TL Veterans for approximately $3
million for the Los Alamitos Base project. The contract included asbestos
abatement. TL Veterans provided the CMD with a certificate of liability
insurance reflecting the insurance policies it had obtained from Scottsdale.
 On or about September 8, 2021, Scottsdale received notice of a
claim pertaining to alleged water intrusion at a building involved in the
Norwalk project (the Norwalk claim). The Norwalk claim described the
incident as follows: ‘“TL Veterans Construction, Inc. hired a subcontractor,
project [sic]. Demolition of the roof of the building was completed, and the
roof was covered by plastic covers while waiting for the new roof materials to
be installed by JNH Roofing (subcontractor). When it rained early in the
morning on July 26, 2021, water seep [sic] through those plastic covers and
flowed down inside the building. Patients from 3 out of 4 units inside the
building had to evacuate and were relocated to a different building.
Restoration company was immediately hired. Their work includes removing

 4
 ceiling, removing water, drying wet parts of the building, etc.”’ The Norwalk
claim did not state the contract price or subcontractor costs involved in the
underlying project. Pursuant to the 2021-2022 policies’ terms, Scottsdale
denied coverage for the water intrusion claim under the policies’ open roof
and open building exclusion, among other provisions, and TL Veterans did
not challenge the denial.
 On or about January 21, 2022, TL Veterans submitted an
application to Scottsdale to renew the insurance policies (2022 application).
On the 2022 application, TL Veterans once again misrepresented its gross
receipts from the previous 12 months and anticipated receipts for the
upcoming 12 months as $300,000. And it similarly misrepresented its largest
project over the previous five years as a school remodel in the amount of
$135,000. TL Veterans misrepresented that it had not been involved in
asbestos or medical work. In fact, the Los Alamitos Base project included
asbestos abatement. Based on TL Veterans’ representations, Scottsdale once
again issued primary and excess policies in the same amounts.
 On May 27, 2022, TL Veterans notified Scottsdale of a fire that
occurred at the Los Alamitos Base project, seeking coverage under the
policies. The fire completely destroyed one of the buildings being renovated,
requiring a complete demolition and rebuild. A subsequent investigation
revealed that the fire was caused by construction crews leaving a powered
light fixture on top of flammable roofing materials that eventually ignited
due to the heat from the light fixture. TL Veterans accepted responsibility for
causing the fire.
 After conducting an investigation and discovering TL Veterans’
misrepresentations, on November 7, 2022, Scottsdale sent TL Veterans a
letter through counsel demanding that TL Veterans agree to rescind the

 5
 insurance policies. Scottsdale cited as bases for the rescission that TL
Veterans had omitted information in its 2022 application concerning the size
of the contracts and the fact that the Los Alamitos project involved asbestos
removal. Scottsdale’s letter included a draft complaint that it threatened to
file if TL Veterans did not agree to the rescission. After some back and forth,
Scottsdale and TL Veterans agreed to rescind the insurance policies on
January 19, 2023.
 PROCEDURAL HISTORY
 On July 2, 2024, Scottsdale filed the underlying complaint
seeking declaratory relief confirming its rescission of the insurance policies.
CMD filed a cross-complaint asserting causes of action for promissory
estoppel and declaratory relief against Scottsdale. CMD filed a separate
lawsuit against TL Veterans and obtained a default judgment in the amount
of $9,787,124.
 The parties agreed to a case management order in which the case
would be tried in two phases. The first phase included Scottsdale’s causes of
action and CMD’s declaratory relief claim. The second phase included any
remaining claims by CMD.2
 Scottsdale and CMD filed competing motions for summary
judgment/adjudication as to phase one issues. The trial court granted
Scottsdale’s motion, declaring the insurance policies rescinded and deemed
void ab initio. Afterward, CMD voluntarily dismissed its remaining claims
without prejudice, leaving no claims to be resolved. The court thus entered
judgment in favor of Scottsdale. CMD timely appealed.

 2 There was, at that time, a pending motion to amend CMD’s

cross-complaint to add additional causes of action.

 6
  DISCUSSION
 CMD does not dispute that TL Veterans, the insured, made
material misrepresentations in its 2022 application. In particular, TL
Veterans grossly misrepresented the size of the projects it was taking on, and
it misrepresented the fact that it was performing asbestos abatement. CMD
recognizes this would ordinarily give the insurer a right to rescind the
contract. However, it argues the right to rescind was lost for two reasons.
First, Scottsdale waived the right by failing to adequately investigate the
Norwalk claim, which would have revealed TL Veterans’ misrepresentations.
Second, Scottsdale was prevented from rescinding the contract due to CMD’s
economic reliance on the policies. We address each argument in turn under a
de novo standard of review. (Hamburg v. Wal-Mart Stores, Inc. (2004) 116
Cal.App.4th 497, 502 [“Summary judgments are reviewed de novo”].)
 I.
 SCOTTSDALE DID NOT WAIVE THE RIGHT TO RESCIND
A. Legal Principles
 An insurer is entitled to material information bearing on the
insured’s risk. Section 332 provides, “Each party to a contract of insurance
shall communicate to the other, in good faith, all facts within his knowledge
which are or which he believes to be material to the contract and as to which
he makes no warranty, and which the other has not the means of
ascertaining.” Section 330 states, “Neglect to communicate that which a party
knows, and ought to communicate, is concealment.” “[A]n insurer does not
have the duty to investigate the insured’s statements made in an insurance
application and to verify the accuracy of the representations. [Citation.]
Rather, it is the insured’s duty to divulge fully all he or she knows.”
(American Way Cellular, Inc. v. Travelers Property Casualty Co. of America

 7
 (2013) 216 Cal.App.4th 1040, 1051 (American Way); Mitchell v. United
National Ins. Co. (2005) 127 Cal.App.4th 457, 477 (Mitchell) [“an insurer has
the right to rely on the insured’s answers to questions in the insurance
application without verifying their accuracy”].) The obligation to accurately
communicate material information is fundamental to an insurer’s ability to
exercise judgment concerning whether to take on the risk of the insured. (Old
Line Life Ins. Co. v. Superior Court (1991)

leads.caseName: WILLIAM FRANK JENNINGS v. ROMULUS INVESTMENTS, LLC
leads.court: Court of Appeals of Georgia
leads.text:
THIRD DIVISION
DILLARD, P. J.,
GOBEIL and PIPKIN, JJ.
NOTICE: Motions for reconsideration must be
received no later than 4:30 pm on the 10th day after
the decision was issued to be deemed timely filed. 
https://www.gaappeals.gov/rules
October 14, 2026
In the Court of Appeals of Georgia
A26A1018. JENNINGS v. ROMULUS INVESTMENTS, LLC et al.
DILLARD, Presiding Judge.
William Jennings suffered serious, permanent injuries when a massive tree on
his next door neighbor’s property fell and crushed the house he was leasing from
Romulus Investments while he was still inside. Jennings filed suit against Romulus and
its two owners, Christopher Alvey and Wendell Rhodes,1 claiming the lease and
statutory law imposed duties on Romulus to protect him against the hazard posed by
the tree—even though it did not sit on the leased property. Romulus moved for
summary judgment, which the trial court granted. Jennings contends the court erred
1 For the sake of clarity, we refer to Romulus Investments, Christopher Alvey,
and Wendell Rhodes collectively as “Romulus” throughout this opinion.
in doing so, arguing that genuine issues of material fact remain as to whether (1)
Romulus owed a duty under the lease; (2) it owed a duty under OCGA § 51-3-1; (3) it
owed a duty under OCGA § 44-7-14; and (4) attorney fees and punitive damages were
warranted. For the following reasons, we reverse.2
Viewed in the light most favorable to Jennings (i.e., the nonmoving party),3 the
record shows that Alvey and Rhodes formed Romulus to buy residential properties and
lease them. Toward that end, on April 2, 2021, Romulus purchased the property
located at 10 Circle Drive in Lindale, Georgia. And on April 5, 2021, Romulus entered
into a lease with Jennings for that property. Under the lease, Jennings paid $650 in
monthly rent (in person) to Romulus’s office in Rome. Significantly, the lease provided
that the “[l]andlord shall maintain the property at all times ... . Tenant must call
landlord and notify him of any problems immediately and the Landlord will have the
problem repaired as soon as possible.” The lease also added that “[s]ubject to
Tenant’s consent (within a reasonable time period), the Landlord shall have the right
2 Oral argument was held on May 5, 2026, and is archived on the Court’s
website. See Court of Appeals of the State of Georgia, Oral Argument, Case No.
A26A1018 (May 5, 2026), available at https://vimeo.com/1191278959.
3 See, e.g., Swanson v. Tackling, 335 Ga. App. 810, 810 (783 SE2d 167) (2016).
2
to inspect the premises for suspected damage or poor housekeeping habits, to show
property to perspective buyers or any other person for business purposes.”
Additionally, in a paragraph titled “Hazards,” the lease provided that “[a]ny known
safety hazards are to be made known to Landlord ASAP.” 
Right next door to the leased property—10 Circle Drive—is 8 Circle Drive, an
empty lot. This lot is owned by Jennings’s neighbor, Misty Carroll, who purchased the
property from another neighbor, David Jordan, who resided across the street from
Jennings at 9 Circle Drive. Near the boundary between 10 Circle Drive and 8 Circle
Drive was a massive oak tree estimated to be over 80 years old. And while the tree’s
trunk sat on 8 Circle Drive, some of its large limbs and branches extended well over the
10 Circle Drive property line—even over the house Jennings rented from Romulus.
Unfortunately, at least two times after Jennings began renting 10 Circle Drive, large
branches from the tree on 8 Circle Drive fell on the house. And sometime in the spring
of 2022, lightning struck the tree, causing a large limb to fall on Jennings’s truck and
damage it. Jennings notified Romulus—via Alvey—about the tree’s limbs falling on
the property and his truck. In doing so, Jennings told Alvey that he believed the tree
3
was decaying and dangerous and someone “needed to come out and look at it.”
Jennings also shared his concerns with others in Romulus’s office when he dropped off
his rent check on the first of each month. 
Despite these warnings, neither Romulus nor Carroll—the owner of 8 Circle
Drive—ever inspected the tree to assess its health or undertook any measures to
remove the tree or its limbs that were overhanging on to the 10 Circle Drive property
(where Jennings resided). Moreover, Romulus and Carroll apparently never
communicated with each other about removing the tree or the overhanging limbs.
Tragically, around noon on July 14, 2022, the tree fell on the 10 Circle Drive house,
crashing through the roof and pinning Jennings underneath a large part of the trunk and
debris. Fire department and emergency medical personnel quickly arrived on the
scene, but it took nearly two hours before Jennings was rescued from the destroyed
home. And because of the accident, Jennings suffered a serious injury to his spinal
cord, which rendered him permanently paralyzed from the chest down. 
Later on, Jennings filed suit in the Superior Court of Floyd County against
Alvey, Rhodes, and Romulus, alleging claims for breach of the lease agreement,
4
premises liability, failure to keep the premises in good repair and fit for habitation, and
common-law negligence. And along with compensatory damages, Jennings sought
attorney fees and punitive damages. Romulus filed answers, and discovery ensued. At
the end of discovery, Romulus moved for summary judgment as to all of Jennings’s
claims, which the trial court granted after a hearing. 
Jennings appealed, and in an unpublished opinion, we vacated the trial court’s
ruling—without addressing the merits of Jennings’s arguments—and remanded the
case with direction that the court clarify the basis for granting summary judgment as
to the breach-of-lease claim because it had not been mentioned in the order.4 After
remand, the court again granted Romulus’s motion for summary judgment, issuing an
identical order but with an added section addressing Jennings’s breach-of-lease claim.
This appeal follows.
Summary judgment is proper if “the pleadings, depositions, answers to
interrogatories, and admissions on file, together with the affidavits, if any, show that
there is no genuine issue as to any material fact and that the moving party is entitled
4 See Jennings v. Romulus Investments, LLC et al., Case No. A25A1111 (decided
November 3, 2025) (unpublished opinion).
5
to a judgment as a matter of law.”5 Importantly, if the movant meets this burden, the
nonmovant “cannot rest on its pleadings, but rather must point to specific evidence
giving rise to a triable issue.”6 And speculation which “raises merely a conjecture or
possibility is not sufficient to create even an inference of fact for consideration on
summary judgment.”7 Moreover, if summary judgment is granted, it enjoys no
presumption of correctness on appeal, and an appellate court must satisfy itself that the
requirements of OCGA § 9-11-56(c) have been met.8 Importantly, in conducting this
de novo review, we are charged with “viewing the evidence, and all reasonable
conclusions and inferences drawn from the evidence, in the light most favorable to the
5 OCGA § 9-11-56(c). See Swanson, 335 Ga. App. at 811 (explaining that
summary judgment is appropriate when “the moving party can show that there is no
genuine issue of material fact and that the movant is entitled to judgment as a matter
of law” (punctuation omitted)).
6 Handberry v. Manning Forestry Servs., LLC, 353 Ga. App. 150, 151–52 (836
SE2d 545) (2019) (punctuation omitted).
7 Id. at 152 (punctuation omitted).
8 See Cowart v. Widener, 287 Ga. 622, 624(1)(a) (697 SE2d 779) (2010)
(“Summary judgments enjoy no presumption of correctness on appeal, and an
appellate court must satisfy itself de novo that the requirements of OCGA § 9-11-56(c)
have been met.”).
6
nonmovant.”9 With these guiding principles in mind, we turn now to Jennings’s claims
of error.
1. Jennings first contends the trial court erred in granting summary judgment as
to his claims that Romulus owed a duty under the lease and an implied warranty of
habitability to protect against the hazard posed by the oak tree. We agree.
The construction of a lease—or any other contract—is “a question of law for
the court,”10 involving the following three analytical steps:
The first step is to decide whether the language of the contract is clear
and unambiguous. If so, the contract is enforced according to its plain
terms, and the contract alone is looked to for meaning. Second, if the
language of the contract is ambiguous in some respect, the rules of
contract construction must be applied by the court to resolve the
ambiguity. And finally, if ambiguity remains after applying the rules of
9 Benefield v. Tominich, 308 Ga. App. 605, 607(1) (708 SE2d 563) (2011)
(punctuation omitted). Accord Swanson, 335 Ga. App. at 810.
10 Shields v. RDM, LLC, 355 Ga. App. 409, 413(1) (844 SE2d 297) (2020)
(punctuation omitted). See Gleaton & Assocs., Inc. v. Cornelius, 366 Ga. App. 712,
715(1) (884 SE2d 103) (2023) (“The construction of the provisions of a lease is
generally a question for the court to determine as a matter of law.” (punctuation
omitted)).
7
construction, the issue of what the ambiguous language means and what
the parties intended must be resolved by a jury.11
The cardinal rule of contract construction is, of course, “to ascertain the intention of
the parties, as set out in the language of the contract.”12 And when the language of a
contract is plain and unambiguous, “judicial construction is not only unnecessary but
forbidden.”13
Here, the lease agreement provides that the “[l]andlord shall maintain the
property at all times ... [and the] [t]enant must call landlord and notify him of any
problems immediately and the [l]andlord will have the problem repaired as soon as
possible.” Importantly, the term “maintain” in this context is defined as “[t]o keep
11 Shields, 355 Ga. App. at 413(1) (punctuation omitted). Accord Bd. of Cmm’rs
of Crisp Cty. v. City Cmm’rs of the City of Cordele, 315 Ga. App. 696, 699 (727 SE2d
524) (2012).
12 Shields, 355 Ga. App. at 413(1) (punctuation omitted). Accord Stanley v. Gov’t
Emps. Ins. Co., 344 Ga. App. 342, 344(1) (810 SE2d 179) (2018).
13 SPI Holdco, LLC v. Mookerji, 361 Ga. App. 449, 453(1) (864 SE2d 633) (2021)
(punctuation omitted).
8
up, preserve, cause to continue in being (a state of things, a condition, an activity, etc.);
to keep vigorous, effective, or unimpaired; to guard from loss or deterioration.”14
In addition to the language of the lease, the Supreme Court of Georgia has held
that
[a] landlord is subject to liability for physical harm caused ... by a
dangerous condition existing before or arising after the tenant has taken
possession, if he has failed to exercise reasonable care to repair the
condition and the existence of the condition is in violation of ... an implied
warranty of habitability ... or a duty created by statute or administrative
regulation.15
Indeed, far from being a recent development, our Supreme Court has explained that
the General Assembly long ago rejected traditional property law conceptions of
landlord-tenant law, in which a lessor grants and a lessee acquires an estate in
14 Oxford English Dictionary Online, Maintain (verb) (II.7.a),
https://doi.org/10.1093/OED/3208186595 (last visited October 13, 2026).
15 Thompson v. Crownover, 259 Ga. 126, 129(3) (381 SE2d 283) (1989)
(punctuation omitted). Accord Bastien v. Metro. Park Lake Assocs., L.P., 209 Ga. App.
881, 882 (434 SE2d 736) (1993); Restatement of Law (Second) of Property, Land. &
Ten. § 17.6 (1977). See also OCGA § 44-7-13(b) (“Any contract, lease, license, or
similar agreement, oral or written, for the use or rental of real property as a dwelling
place is deemed to include a provision that the premises is fit for human habitation.”).
9
land—instead championing a unique-at-the-time requirement that a “landlord must
keep the premises in repair and is liable for all substantial improvements placed upon
them by his consent.”16
Here

leads.caseName: Lisa Debar v. FirstEnergy Corp
leads.court: Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit
leads.text:
UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS FOR THE 
THIRD CIRCUIT 
No. 25-2006 
LISA DEBAR, Individually and as personal representative of 
the Estate of Cody Hatt, 
Appellant 

v. 

FIRSTENERGY CORP.; FIRSTENERGY GENERATION LLC; 
FIRSTENERGY SOLUTIONS CORP.; FIRSTENERGY 
PENNSYLV ANIA ELECTRIC CO.; FIRSTENERGY SERVICE CO.; ET 
AL. 

AMENDED PURSUANT TO CLERKS ORDER DA TED 7/14/25 
_____________________________ 
On Appeal from the U.S. District Court, E.D. Pa. 
Chief Judge Wendy Beetlestone, No. 2:24-cv-05164 

Before: RESTREPO, BIBAS, and FISHER, Circuit Judges 
Argued: Apr. 20, 2026; Filed: Oct. 14, 2026 
_____________________________ 
OPINION OF THE COURT 
FISHER, Circuit Judge. 

2 
Cody Hatt suffered fatal injuries while working for a 
demolition contractor that was tearing down a power plant in 
Pennsylvania known as Hatfield’s Ferry . His mother, as his 
survivor and on behalf of his estate, sued the owner and 
operators of the plant for negligence . T he District Court 
dismissed the complaint. 
Two Pennsylvania tort law doctrines govern this appeal. 
First, when a property owner hires an independent contractor 
to work on the property, the owner does not owe a duty to 
employees of the contractor. There is an exception when the 
owner hires a contractor but retains detailed control over the 
job—over not only what is to be done, but how and by whom. 
The retained-control exception is difficult to show ; an owner 
does not retain control by imposing safety requirements or 
contract specifications for the work. Here, the plaintiff has not 
alleged facts that, if true, would demonstrate that the 
defendants retained sufficient control . The second applicable 
tort law doctrine is that a landowner has no duty to protect 
those invited onto its land from dangers that are open and 
obvious. The risks of demolishing the long-disused Hatfield’s 
Ferry Power Station were indeed obvious, and the complaint 
fails to allege otherwise. We will therefore affirm. 
I. 
A. Which documents we consider 
At the outset, we confront the question of what parts of 
the record to consider on appeal . When ruling on a motion to 
dismiss, “courts may consider documents integral to or 
explicitly relied upon in the complaint, or any undisputedly 

3 
authentic document that a defendant attaches . . . to a motion 
to dismiss if the plaintiff’s claims are based on the document.” 
In re Asbestos Prod. Liab. Litig. (No. VI) , 822 F.3d 125, 133 
n.7 (3d Cir. 2016) (citation modified). The parties attached five 
documents to the complaint and the motion to dismiss. All of 
them are within bounds for us to consider, but we rely primarily 
on the two about which DeBar has expressed no objection: the 
demolition contract and the Specification. 
The demolition contract. DeBar attached to her 
complaint a document titled “Purchase Order,” which was the 
demolition contract between North American Dismantling and 
FirstEnergy Service. The District Court took this document 
into account, and correctly so: the demolition contract is 
“integral to or explicitly relied upon in the complaint.” In re 
Asbestos Prod., 822 F.3d at 133 n.7. 
The Specification. DeBar alleged that FirstEnergy 
Service created the “Generation Specification of the Hatfield 
Power Plant . . . , which set forth detailed specifications for 
how the demolition work was to be performed .” App. 965 . 
FirstEnergy Service attached to its motion to dismiss a 
document title d “FIRSTENERGY GENERATION, LLC 
SPECIFICATION FLT -SPEC-XX-XXXX FOR 
DEMOLITION OF HATFIELD POWER PLANT,” App. 
1052. The District Court did not consider this document 
because its title does not exactly match the references in the 
complaint. But i f the mismatch created doubt, DeBar has 
cleared it up on appeal : in her brief, she cites FirstEnergy’s 
Specification document, treating it as a source of information 
about the parties’ contract. In other words, she does not dispute 

4 
the Specification’s authenticity. Additionally, DeBar’s claims 
are based on this document , which outlines FirstEnergy’s 
requirements for the demolition project . So we will consider 
the Specification. 
The remaining documents. DeBar referenced two other 
documents in the complaint but did not attach them: the “FE 
Generation Personal Safety Manual” and the FirstEnergy 
Service “Code of Conduct.” App. 966. It is unclear whether 
either of these documents is among the three FirstEnergy 
attached to its motion to dismiss : the “Preliminary Work Plan 
for FirstEnergy – Demolition, Hatfield Power Plant,” App. 
1137; North American Dismantling’s “Environmental, Health, 
Safety and Security Plan and Manual for FirstEnergy Hatfield 
Power Plant,” id. at 1169; and the “North American 
Dismantling Corp. Safety Program,” id. at 1194. Even if these 
attachments are not the documents DeBar referenced in the 
complaint, we still may consider them if they are “undisputedly 
authentic” and DeBar’s “claims are based on [them].” In re 
Asbestos Prod., 822 F.3d at 133 n.7. 
DeBar has not question ed the authenticity of the 
documents. And her claims are based on the documents, 
because—like the demolition contract and Specification—they 
lay out the duties of FirstEnergy Service and North American 
Dismantling with regard to the Hatfield ’s Ferry demolition 
project. So we may take these attachments into account as well. 
In the District Court, DeBar complained that 
FirstEnergy Service “carefully controlled the documents . . . 
that it wishe [d] for the Court to consider, ” providing some 
“while holding back others .” App. 1668 n.2. Even without 

5 
considering the “Preliminary Work Plan,” the “Environmental, 
Health, Safety and Security Plan, ” and the “North American 
Dismantling Corp. Safety Program” —the documents 
FirstEnergy Service “wishe[d] for the Court to consider,” id.—
the complaint fails to state a claim.1 
B. Factual and procedural history 
1. The plant and the contract 
Allegheny Energy Supply owned a coal -fired power 
plant, the Hatfield’s Ferry Power Station, in Carmichaels, 
Pennsylvania. The plant was operated by FirstEnergy Corp. 
and FirstEnergy Service. In 2013, FirstEnergy Corp. and 
FirstEnergy Service , under pressure from the Environmental 
Protection Agency, decided to shut down coal generation at 
Hatfield’s Ferry . In 2022, demolition of the plant began —
including its two cooling towers, which were around 500 feet 
high, and its three emissions stacks, which ranged from 540 to 
700-plus feet. 
FirstEnergy Service contracted with North American 
Dismantling to complete more than $4 million worth of 
demolition work at the plant. FirstEnergy Service entered into 
the contract, titled a “Purchase Order,” “on its own behalf and 
on behalf of its affiliates,” who were not named. App. 1009. 
FirstEnergy assigned a buyer and a project manager to the 
project who used e-mail addresses with the domain 
“@firstenergycorp.com.” Id. at 1010. The Specification called 

1 Defendants argue persuasively that these documents 
further show that the District Court correctly dismissed the 
complaint. See Appellee’s Br. 9–13, 40–41. 

6 
for a “Purchaser’s Engineer” to serve as “the designated 
Engineering Representative from the Project Engineering 
Department, FirstEnergy Corp.” Id. at 1056. North American 
Dismantling was to submit invoices “electronically at the 
FirstEnergy Supplier Portal,” which had a 
“firstenergycorp.com” web address, and to direct payment 
questions to an e-mail address with the 
“@firstenergycorp.com” domain. Id. at 1010. 
The contract provided that the demolition work was to 
be performed “in accordance with [FirstEnergy’s] Generation 
Specification of Hatfield Power Plant.” Id. at 1010. 
FirstEnergy Service had “unobstructed access to Contractor’s 
or any of its Subcontractors’ Work, facilities, procedures and 
records for the purpose of observing and reviewing Work 
completion and quality.” Id. at 1014. The work was “subject to 
[FirstEnergy Service’s] inspection, tests, and count at any time 
or place at [FirstEnergy Service’s] discretion.” Id. North 
American Dismantling’s employees working at Hatfield were 
“subject to [FirstEnergy Service’s] continuing approval,” and 
FirstEnergy Service retained the right to “object to any [North 
American Dismantling] employee who, in [FirstEnergy 
Service’s] opinion, did not meet” the contract criteria “or 
whose performance [was] unsatisfactory.” Id. at 1015. If 
FirstEnergy Service objected to a North American Dismantling 
employee, North American Dismantling was required to 
“immediately replace or remove such individual.” Id. 
For its part, North American Dismantling agreed that it 
would be “considered an independent contractor . . . 
responsible for all acts and omissions (negligent or otherwise) 

7 
of its agents, employees and subcontractors.” Id. at 1013. North 
American Dismantling was “alone . . . liable and responsible 
for the manner and methods by which the Work [was] 
performed and for materials, work force and equipment.” Id. 
North American Dismantling “assume[d] full responsibility for 
[its] employees’ acts and omissions (negligent or otherwise)” 
and was required to “enforce all . . . worker health and safety 
and similar requirements.” Id. at 1015. 
With regard to safety, North American Dismantling 
agreed it was “solely responsible for the safety and health of 
its employees” and would “conduct the Work in a manner to 
avoid risk of bodily harm to persons or damage to property.” 
Id. at 1016. North American Dismantling further committed to 
“take all necessary safety and health precautions, and . . . do 
everything necessary to prevent accidents or injury to persons 
on . . . the premises.” Id. In addition, it would “not require any 
employee . . . to work in surroundings or under working 
conditions that [were] . . . hazardous, or dangerous to safety or 
health.” Id. 
North American Dismantling also agreed that it had 
“examined the site in all ways pertinent to performance 
required by the Specification, and that it [had] informed itself 
concerning the physical and geological conditions to be 
encountered . . . [and] the character of the Work to be 
performed.” Id. at 1027. The Specification further provided 
that FirstEnergy Service “assume[d] no responsibility for 
buildings and structures to be Demolished. Conditions existing 
at time of inspection for bidding purpose [would] be 
maintained by [FirstEnergy Service] as far as practical.” Id. at 

8 
1082. 
Drawing on the contract documents, DeBar alleged that 
FirstEnergy Service “exerted actual control over the 
[demolition] work by instructing and/or directing [North 
American Dismantling]” where, when, by what means, and 
with what equipment to do the work and by “giving 
instructions and/or directi ons to [North American 
Dismantling] personnel as to the manner of doing the actual 
demolition work.” Id. at 965. DeBar also alleged that 
FirstEnergy Service required North American Dismantling to 
comply with a “Code of Conduct” and with the Specification 
document, which “set forth detailed specifications for how the 
demolition work was to be performed.” Id. 
To further support her allegations that FirstEnergy 
Service actually controlled the work, DeBar invoked the “FE 
Generation Personal Safety Manual.” Id. at 966. And she noted 
the assignment to the project of the FirstEnergy Service project 
manager and purchaser representative, who oversaw 
“contracted personnel to assure compliance with the contract 
documents . . . , field construction work and continuous 
monitoring of project safety.” Id. at 966, 967. She alleged that 
when North American Dismantling “elected to or intended to 
do the work in a manner inconsistent with how [FirstEnergy 
Service] dictated” in the Specification, Personal Safety 
Manual, and Code of Conduct, FirstEnergy Service “ forced 
strict compliance with [those] documents, thereby exerting 
actual control.” Id. at 967.
