leads.court: Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit
leads.text:
NOT FOR PUBLICATION 

In the 
United States Court of Appeals 
For the Eleventh Circuit 
____________________ 
No. 25-12814 
____________________ 

ATTORNEY GENERAL, STATE OF FLORIDA, 
DEPARTMENT OF LEGAL AFFAIRS, 
Plaintiﬀ-Appellant, 
versus 

SNAP INC., 
Defendant-Appellee. 
 ____________________ 
Appeal from the United States District Court 
for the Northern District of Florida 
D.C. Docket No. 3:25-cv-00676-MW-HTC 
____________________ 

Before NEWSOM, LUCK, and TJOFLAT, Circuit Judges. 
PER CURIAM: 
With the rise of social media usage comes concern about its 
impact on the mental health of its users, particularly adolescents. 
In response to this growing concern, Florida’s legislature enacted a 
USCA11 Case: 25-12814 Document: 64-1 Date Filed: 10/14/2026 Page: 1 of 23 
2 Opinion of the Court 25-12814 
law to regulate social media platforms that use addictive features. 
This case arises from the State’s attempt to enforce that law. While 
the law raises serious constitutional questions, we do not reach 
them because the District Court lacked subject matter jurisdiction 
over this case. 
I. BACKGROUND 
The Florida legislature enacted House Bill 3 (“HB3”) in 2024. 
H.B. 3, 2024 Leg., Reg. Sess. (Fla. 2024) (codified in relevant part in 
Fla. Stat. § 501.1736). HB3 requires qualifying social media plat-
forms to prohibit minors from entering contracts to become ac-
count holders.1 Id. § 501.1736(2)(1). A social media platform quali-
fies under the statute if it meets certain criteria and employs one of 
five “addictive” features.2 

1 The law requires platforms to prohibit minors younger than 14 from becom-
ing account holders. Fla. Stat. § 501.1736(2)(a)–(b)(1). It allows minors aged 14 
or 15 to become account holders with consent from the minor’s parent or 
guardian. Id. § 501.1736(3)(a)–(b)(1). 
2 Section 501.1736 states, in relevant part: 
(e) “Social media platform” means an online forum, website, 
or application that satisfies each of the following criteria: 
1. Allows users to upload content or view the content or activ-
ity of other users; 
2. Ten percent or more of the daily users who are younger 
than 16 years of age spend on average 2 hours per day or longer 
on the online forum, website, or application on the days when 
using the online forum, website or application during the pre-
vious 12 months or, if the online forum, website, or application 
USCA11 Case: 25-12814 Document: 64-1 Date Filed: 10/14/2026 Page: 2 of 23 
25-12814 Opinion of the Court 3 
 The statute went into effect on January 1, 2025, authorizing 
the Office of the Attorney General’s Department of Legal Affairs 
(the “Department”) to bring civil actions to enforce HB3 against 
qualifying platforms and impose monetary sanctions “of up to 

did not exist during the previous 12 months, during the previ-
ous month; 
3. Employs algorithms that analyze user data or information 
on users to select content for users; and 
4. Has any of the following addictive features: 
a. Infinite scrolling, which means either: 
(I) Continuously loading content, or content that loads as the 
user scrolls down the page without the need to open a separate 
page; or 
(II) Seamless content, or the use of pages with no visible or 
apparent end or page breaks. 
b. Push notifications or alerts sent by the online forum, web-
site, or application to inform a user about specific activities or 
events related to the user’s account. 
c. Displays personal interactive metrics that indicate the num-
ber of times other users have clicked a button to indicate their 
reaction to content or have shared or reposted the content. 
d. Auto-play video or video that begins to play without the 
user first clicking on the video or on a play button for that 
video. 
e. Live-streaming or a function that allows a user or advertiser 
to broadcast live video content in real-time. 
Fla. Stat. § 501.1736(1)(e) 
USCA11 Case: 25-12814 Document: 64-1 Date Filed: 10/14/2026 Page: 3 of 23 
4 Opinion of the Court 25-12814 
$50,000 per violation” and, in some cases, punitive damages. 
Fla. Stat. § 501.1736(5). 
 In April 2025, the Department brought such an enforcement 
action against Snap Inc., the operator of the popular social media 
platform known as Snapchat. The complaint alleged Snap, a quali-
fying platform under the statute, was “openly defying” HB3 by 
contracting with minors under the age of 14. The Department sued 
Snap in Florida state court for violating HB3 and the Florida De-
ceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act (“FDUTPA”) . It sought, 
among other things, injunctive relief, civil penalties, and punitive 
damages. 
A. Removal to Federal Court 
 Snap filed a notice of removal in the Northern District of 
Florida, arguing the Court had subject matter jurisdiction pursuant 
to 28 U.S.C. § 1332(a) and the federal officer removal statute, which 
allows removal of actions against any person “acting under [a fed-
eral] officer . . . for or relating to any act under color of such office.” 
28 U.S.C. § 1442(a)(1). The Department moved for remand. 
1. Federal Officer Removal 
 Snap argued the Department’s claims were removable un-
der the federal officer removal statute because Snap provided ad-
vertising services to two federal agencies: the Department of 
Homeland Security (“DHS”) and the Food and Drug Administra-
tion (“FDA”). It asserted the Department’s claims “interfere with 
Snap’s ability to carry out its responsibilities” under DHS and FDA 
USCA11 Case: 25-12814 Document: 64-1 Date Filed: 10/14/2026 Page: 4 of 23 
25-12814 Opinion of the Court 5 
officers, and it argued HB3 “would penalize Snap for its work as-
sisting the federal government in accomplishing its goals of reach-
ing teenage audiences” with the advertisements. 
 Snap purportedly entered into memorandums of under-
standing (“MOUs”) with DHS’s Cyber Crimes Center and Child 
Exploitation Investigations Unit to help DHS develop its 
“Know2Protect” campaign —a public safety initiative directed at 
educating teenagers and adults about online safety and preventing 
child sexual exploitation and abuse.3 DHS purportedly handpicked 
Snap to help carry out the campaign because of the platform’s abil-
ity to reach “one of the campaign’s key audiences: teens.” Under 
the MOUs, Snap conducted research on young adults’ awareness 
of child exploitation risks and devel oped advertising features to 
“bring important online safety information to [the teen] commu-
nity directly.” 
 Similarly, Snap contends that it assist ed with public health 
campaigns for the FDA’s Center for Tobacco Products. The cam-
paigns targeted audiences of 13 to 17 with messages about the risks 
of vaping and cigarette use.4 The FDA contracted with a third-party 
media agency to create advertising campaigns with SNAP. Specifi-
cally, in the lead up to the FDA’s 2025 campaigns, the marketing 
agency provided Snap with briefs explaining the FDA’s goals for 

3 Snap states that DHS carries out the Know2Protect campaign in furtherance 
of its child exploitation prevention responsibilities under 6 U.S.C. § 473. 
4 Snap alleged that the FDA carried out this advertisement campaign pursuant 
to its duties under 21 U.S.C. §§ 393(d)(2)(D) and 387a(e). 
USCA11 Case: 25-12814 Document: 64-1 Date Filed: 10/14/2026 Page: 5 of 23 
6 Opinion of the Court 25-12814 
the campaigns. Snap then submitted proposals for the campaigns 
and explained how its proprietary algorithms could help the FDA 
reach their intended audience. After receiving FDA approval, the 
marketing agency purchased advertising from Snap for one of the 
campaigns. 
 The Department moved to remand, arguing (1) Snap’s 
“brief partnership[s]” with DHS, the FDA, and their contractors 
came “nowhere near the deep and enduring ties, control, and su-
pervision” required to establish Snap “act[ed] under” a federal of-
ficer, (2) Snap failed to provide any evidence to support its allega-
tions of federal officer jurisdiction, and (3) Snap failed to show that 
the conduct for which it was being sued was performed under color 
of federal law. 
2. Diversity Jurisdiction 
 Snap also argued the Department’s claims were removable 
under diversity jurisdiction. Because the relief the Department 
sought was “allegedly for the direct benefit of identifiable, individ-
ual Florida citizens,” Snap argued “the citizenship of those individ-
uals control[led] for the purposes of diversity.” 
 In its motion for remand, the Department responded that it 
brought the suit pursuant to its statutory mandate to enforce the 
laws at issue. It also pointed out that it sought injunctive and puni-
tive relief, making clear the aim of the suit was to bring a benefit to 
the State by “deterring future violations by Snap or other wrong-
doers.” The Department contended that this meant the interested 
party was the State of Florida. 
USCA11 Case: 25-12814 Document: 64-1 Date Filed: 10/14/2026 Page: 6 of 23 
25-12814 Opinion of the Court 7 
B. The Department’s Motion for Temporary Injunction 
 The Department also asked the District Court to temporar-
ily enjoin Snap from violating HB3. It argued the Attorney General 
had a legal right to an injunction because Snap was openly violating 
HB3 and the enforcement of HB3 does not violate the First Amend-
ment. 
 Snap responded that the Department’s injunction argument 
was foreclosed by the District Court ’s recent order in Comput. & 
Commc’ns Indus. Ass’n v. Uthmeier , 826 F.Supp.3d 1358 (N.D. Fla. 
2025) (“CCIA”). In that case, which was filed prior to the instant 
suit, two nonprofit associations representing internet and technol-
ogy companies sued for a declaration that HB3 violates the First 
Amendment and sought preliminary and permanent injunctions 
barring the Florida Attorney General from enforcing it. Id. The Dis-
trict Court found HB3 is likely unconstitutional and preliminary 
enjoined its enforcement.
5 Id. at 1390. 
 Snap also argued the Department failed to show a likelihood 
of success on the merits because HB3 violates the First Amend-
ment and the Commerce Clause and is preempted by the Chil-
dren’s Online Privacy Protection Act. 

5 That decision is currently on appeal before this Court. 
USCA11 Case: 25-12814 Document: 64-1 Date Filed: 10/14/2026 Page: 7 of 23 
8 Opinion of the Court 25-12814 
* * * 
 The District Court sided with Snap on both motions. It de-
nied the Department’s motion to remand, finding that Snap estab-
lished the three elements required for federal officer removal based 
on its relationships with DHS and the FDA. It also denied the De-
partment’s motion for temporary injunction, relying on its finding 
in CCIA that HB3 was likely unconstitutional. The Department 
timely appeals both denials. 
II. DISCUSSION 
 This case requires us to answer three questions: (1) Do we 
have jurisdiction to hear this appeal? (2) Was the case properly re-
moved to federal court under the federal officer removal statute? 
(3) And, if not, is additional fact-finding required to determine if the 
case was properly removed to federal court under diversity juris-
diction? We answer each question in turn. 
A. Appellate Jurisdiction 
 We are obligated to inquire sua sponte into our own juris-
diction to hear an appeal. Thomas v. Blue Cross & Blue Shield Ass’n , 
594 F.3d 814, 818 (11th Cir. 2010). Appellate courts have jurisdic-
tion over appeals of final orders of the district courts and certain 
nonfinal orders, including those denying injunctions. 28 U.S.C. 
§§ 1291, 1292(a)(1). Congress specifically vested appellate courts 
with jurisdiction over appeals of orders remanding cases to state 
court pursuant to the federal officer removal statute. Id. §§ 1447(d), 
1442. However, Congress is silent as to whether we have jurisdic-
tion over appeals of orders denying such remands. While “such an 
USCA11 Case: 25-12814 Document: 64-1 Date Filed: 10/14/2026 Page: 8 of 23 
25-12814 Opinion of the Court 9 
order is not final and appealable if standing

leads.caseName: Bank of New York Mellon v. Layne
leads.court: Court of Appeals of Oregon
leads.text:
776 October 14, 2026 No. 993
This is a nonprecedential memorandum opinion 
pursuant to ORAP 10.30 and may not be cited 
except as provided in ORAP 10.30(1).
IN THE COURT OF APPEALS OF THE 
STATE OF OREGON
THE BANK OF NEW YORK MELLON, 
 fka The Bank of New York, as Trustee for the 
Certificateholders of the CWMBS Inc., CHL Mortgage 
Passthrough Trust 2006-HYB4, Mortgage Pass Through 
Certificates, Series 2006-HYB4,
Plaintiff-Respondent,
v.
Linton Cecil LAYNE; 
Lillie Mae Brunell as Trustee of Be Incredible Holding 
Trust, dated January 1, 2012; Citibank South Dakota NA; 
and All Other Unknown Parties Claiming Any Right, Title, 
Lien or Interest in Real Property Commonly Known as 
2186 East Main Street, Hillsboro, OR 97123,
Defendants,
and
Nancy Kay LAYNE,
Defendant-Appellant.
Washington County Circuit Court
23CV23393; A188585
Andrew Erwin, Judge.
Argued and submitted September 22, 2026.
Nancy Kay Layne argued the cause and filed the briefs 
pro se.
Vanessa L. Moore argued the cause for respondent. Also 
on the brief were Gregor A. Hensrude and Klinedinst PC.
Before Aoyagi, Presiding Judge, Kamins, Judge, and 
Pagán, Judge.
KAMINS, J.
Affirmed.
Nonprecedential Memo Op: 353 Or App 776 (2026) 777
 KAMINS, J.
 Defendant, appearing pro se, appeals from a general 
judgment of foreclosure, which the trial court entered after 
granting the motion for summary judgment that plaintiff, 
the Bank of New York Mellon’s, filed. On appeal, defendant 
argues (1) that the bank did not put forward the necessary 
proof to prevail, (2) that the court applied the wrong statute 
of limitations, and (3) that the court abused its discretion 
by awarding attorney fees and costs.1 For the following rea-
sons, we affirm.
 Defendant originally executed a promissory note, 
secured by a deed of trust, with Sierra Pacific Mortgage 
Company. Through a series of endorsements and assign -
ments, plaintiff became the holder of the promissory note and 
deed of trust. There is no dispute that defendant defaulted 
on her mortgage payments. However, defendant argues that 
plaintiff did not meet its burden to establish that it was a 
party properly entitled to enforce the note.
 In reviewing a ruling on summary judgment, we 
view the record in the light most favorable to defendant, as 
the nonmoving party, to determine whether there are any 
genuine issues of material fact and whether plaintiff was 
entitled to judgment as a matter of law. ORCP 47 C; Jones v. 
General Motors Corp., 325 Or 404, 420, 939 P2d 608 (1997).
 In the context of judicial foreclosure on a negotiable 
instrument, such as a promissory note secured by a deed of 
trust, a party has the power to enforce the underlying note 
if they are “the holder of the instrument, a nonholder in pos-
session of the instrument who has the rights of a holder, or a 
person not in possession of the instrument who is entitled to 
enforce the instrument * * *.” ORS 73.0301. A “holder” means 
“[t]he person in possession of a negotiable instrument that is 
 1 Defendant first assigns error to the summary judgment ruling, arguing 
that the plaintiff did not meet its burden to establish that plaintiff was a person 
entitled to enforce the note. In her second assignment of error, defendant chal -
lenges the general judgment of foreclosure, contending that the underlying sum-
mary judgment and fee rulings were erroneous. In her third assignment of error, 
defendant challenges the summary judgment ruling, contending that plaintiff’s 
claim was time-barred. In her fourth assignment of error, defendant challenges 
the trial court’s denial of her motion to vacate/set aside the judgment. In her fifth 
assignment of error, defendant challenges the fee award.
778 Bank of New York Mellon v. Layne
payable either to bearer or to an identified person that is the 
person in possession.” ORS 71.2010(2)(v)(A). “Thus, to be enti-
tled to enforce a negotiable instrument as a holder, a party 
must simply demonstrate that it is in possession of the instru-
ment and that the instrument is payable either to the bearer 
or to the party itself.” Deutsche Bank Trust Co. Americas v. 
Walmsley, 277 Or App 690, 696, 374 P3d 937 (2016).
 In this case, plaintiff established that it was the 
holder of the note through an allonge on the note and recorded 
assignments of the deed of trust. See Nationstar Mortgage, 
LLC v. Hinkle , 321 Or App 300, 308, 516 P3d 718 (2022) 
(“[A] plaintiff’s right to enforce the note through foreclosure 
survives a transfer of interest because it vests in the party 
to whom the note is transferred.”). On appeal, defendant con-
tends that the evidence plaintiff introduced showing that it 
possessed the note was inadmissible. To support her posi -
tion, defendant relies on U.S. Bank National Assn. v. McCoy, 
290 Or App 525, 415 P3d 1116 (2018), where we held that a 
loan servicer’s declaration that the assignee held the prom-
issory note at the relevant time was inadmissible hearsay 
and, without it, the evidence in the record was insufficient 
to establish that the plaintiff was entitled to judgment as a 
matter of law. However, there, the defendant had challenged 
the admissibility of the loan servicer’s declaration in the 
court below, moving to strike it because it was not based on 
the declarant’s personal knowledge. Id. at 530. In contrast, 
here, defendant did not raise the admissibility challenges 
below that she now argues on appeal. Therefore, defendant’s 
argument is unpreserved, and we decline to review her first 
assignment of error for plain error. See ORAP 5.45(4)(a) 
(“Each assignment of error must demonstrate that the ques-
tion or issue presented by the assignment of error timely 
and properly was raised and preserved in the lower court.”); 
John Hyland Const., Inc. v. Williamsen & Bleid, Inc. , 287 
Or App 466, 471, 402 P3d 719, 724 (2017) (“In our system of 
justice, the purpose of an appeal is not to give the appellant 
an opportunity to pursue a new theory that it did not rely on 
below.”); State v. Atwood, 332 Or App 495, 498 n 2, 549 P3d 
51 (2024) (“[W]e normally will not exercise [our] discretion 
in the absence of an explicit request for plain-error review 
and concomitant plain-error arguments.”).
Nonprecedential Memo Op: 353 Or App 776 (2026) 779
 Defendant also argues that plaintiff’s claim was 
time-barred. Defendant first raised her statute of limita -
tions argument in her motion to vacate/set aside the judg -
ment.2 Even assuming that was the proper vehicle to raise 
the motion, the time period to bring a foreclosure suit is 
10 years from the date of maturity or expiration of the mort-
gage debt, unless the parties agree to extend it. ORS 88.110. 
The date of maturity of defendant’s mortgage debt was 
April 1, 2036. There was therefore no genuine dispute as 
to whether plaintiff’s judicial foreclosure action was timely.
 Finally, defendant assigns error to the award of 
attorney fees and costs, arguing that the billing records 
plaintiff submitted were insufficient to support the award. 
“Whether a party is entitled to attorney fees presents a 
question of law, but whether fees are reasonable is a fac -
tual determination that we review for abuse of discretion.” 
Makarios-Oregon, LLC v. Ross Dress-for-Less, Inc ., 293 Or 
App 732, 739, 430 P3d 142, adh’d to as modified on recons, 
295 Or App 449, 430 P3d 1125 (2018).
 The trial court rightly determined that plaintiff 
was entitled to attorney fees and costs under the parties’ 
contract and pursuant to ORS 20.096(1) because plaintiff 
was the prevailing party. And plaintiff’s itemized cost bill 
provided adequate detail about the services rendered to 
allow the trial court to conclude that plaintiff’s requested 
fees and costs were reasonable.
 Affirmed.
 2 Defendant also assigns error to the trial court’s denial of her motion to 
vacate/set aside, referring this court to her motion below, where she advanced 
essentially the same arguments as above regarding plaintiff’s entitlement to 
enforce, along with the statute of limitations challenge. Although we recognize 
the challenges inherent in representing oneself pro se in an appellate court, we 
cannot step out of our role as neutral arbiter to “make or develop a party’s argu -
ment.” Beall Transport Equipment Co. v. Southern Pacific , 186 Or App 696, 700 
n 2, 64 P3d 1193, adh’d to as clarified on recons , 187 Or App 472, 68 P3d 259 
(2003); see also JGB Enterprises, LLC v. OLCC, 325 Or App 326, 340, 529 P3d 262 
(2023) (rejecting minimally developed arguments incorporating argument below 
by reference); Johnson v. Mullen, 331 Or App 112, 118, 545 P3d 1261, rev den, 372 
Or 361 (2024) (rejecting an argument that was raised but not sufficiently devel -
oped in appellant’s brief). We therefore reject defendant’s assignment of error 
pertaining to the motion to vacate/set aside.

leads.caseName: Paxton v. Clackams County
leads.court: Court of Appeals of Oregon
leads.text:
No. 980 October 14, 2026 699
IN THE COURT OF APPEALS OF THE 
STATE OF OREGON
Michael PAXTON 
and Tyler McDonald,
Petitioners,
v.
CLACKAMAS COUNTY,
Respondent.
Land Use Board of Appeals
2026018; 
A191348
Submitted September 9, 2026.
Michael Paxton and Tyler McDonald filed the brief pro 
se.
Caleb Huegel and Billy J. Williams filed the brief for 
respondent.
Before Joyce, Presiding Judge, O’Connor, Judge, and 
DeVore, Senior Judge.
JOYCE, P. J.
Affirmed.
700 Paxton v. Clackams County
 JOYCE, P. J.
 In this petition for judicial review from a Land Use 
Board of Appeals (LUBA) order, we are asked to interpret 
the Clackamas County Zoning and Development Ordinance 
(ZDO) 1206.05, which sets out how an applicant can verify 
a nonconforming use. Under ZDO 1206.05(B), an applicant 
can obtain a rebuttable presumption that a nonconforming 
use was lawfully established and has continued uninter -
rupted since the adoption of restrictive zoning, if the appli -
cant proves “[t]he existence, continuity, nature and extent of 
the nonconforming use for the 10-year period immediately 
preceding the date of the application.” The county hear -
ings officer, which LUBA affirmed, determined that peti -
tioners were required to prove that the use had not been 
discontinued for any 24-month period during that 10-year 
period, based on the definition of discontinuation in ZDO 
1206.04(A). On review, petitioners assert that that interpre-
tation is legally incorrect. As explained below, we conclude 
that proving continuity in ZDO 1206.05(B) does require 
proof that the nonconforming used has not been discontin -
ued, as provided in ZDO 1206.04(A). Accordingly, LUBA’s 
order was not “unlawful in substance,” ORS 197.850(9)(a), 
and we affirm.
 We take the following facts from the county hear -
ings officer’s decision and LUBA’s order. Petitioner Paxton 
owns a two-story building on a .92-acre property near 
Sandy, Oregon. Prior to any zoning restrictions, the build -
ing was used as a restaurant and bar. The county estab -
lished restrictive zoning starting in 1967 that precluded 
the restaurant and bar use. In 1974, the county verified the 
restaurant as a legally established nonconforming use. In 
2005, the county again verified the nonconforming use of a 
restaurant and approved an alteration of the nonconforming 
use to office use. On March 4, 2024, the building was signifi-
cantly damaged in a fire. In November 2024, Paxton pur -
chased the property, and on March 4, 2025, Paxton applied 
to the county to verify the nonconforming use of office use 
and to obtain an alteration to repair the fire damage.
 The county planning director denied Paxton’s appli-
cation, and the hearings officer affirmed that denial after 
Cite as 353 Or App 699 (2026) 701
a de novo hearing. The hearings officer determined that 
Paxton failed to demonstrate that “[t]he previously approved 
nonconforming office use of the site continued without inter-
ruptions of more than 24 consecutive months,” and thus 
could not be verified under ZDO 1206.05. 1 The hearings 
officer identified several gaps in Paxton’s evidence that did 
not meet that burden, including no evidence demonstrat -
ing actual use of the site as an office by Parkland Property 
Management Inc. or Rockport Crain LLC, and no evidence 
that Hood Alternative Medical Center LLC used the site as 
an office from 2014 to 2020, as opposed to a medical clinic, 
for retail sales of alternative medicines, or other non-office 
use. There was also evidence that the office use was dis -
placed by illegal residential use, including that the lower 
floor of the building was gutted and remodeled for residen -
tial use in 2014, the second story and the rear of the lower 
floor of the building was used as a residence from May 2015 
to January 2020, and the entire lower floor was used as a 
residence before the fire in March 2024.
 LUBA affirmed the county’s denial. LUBA’s deci -
sion was largely based on rejecting petitioner’s reading of the 
hearings officer’s decision and determining that the hear -
ings officer correctly applied the two-step, burden-shifting 
approach for the rebuttable presumption in ZDO 1206.05, 
because the hearings officer determined that petitioners had 
not met their initial burden. LUBA stated, “The hearings 
officer correctly determined that petitioners bore the burden 
of establishing the continuity of the nonconforming use for 
the ten-year period preceding the application. The hearings 
officer reviewed the evidence submitted by petitioners and 
determined that they had not met that burden.”
 On judicial review of LUBA’s order, petitioner 
argues that LUBA misconstrued ZDO 1206.05(B) when 
it held petitioners were required to prove as part of their 
threshold showing that the nonconforming use was not 
discontinued for any 24-month period during the 10-year 
 1 The hearings officer also denied the application because Paxton did not 
demonstrate that “[t]he nonconforming office use was ‘lawfully resumed’ within 
one year of the fire that damaged the structure,” as required by ZDO 1206.06. 
That basis of denial is not at issue on judicial review because LUBA did not 
address it after concluding the first basis for denial was sufficient.
702 Paxton v. Clackams County
period preceding the application. The county asserts that 
petitioner did not preserve that argument before LUBA. We 
reject the county’s preservation argument. Although peti -
tioners framed their argument differently before LUBA, in 
our view, petitioners’ essential argument about what ZDO 
1206.05(B) requires has remained the same. We thus turn 
to the merits of that argument.
 Because the county’s decision came from the hear -
ings officer and not the county’s governing body, the hear -
ings officer’s interpretation of the county ordinance is not 
due any deference. Gage v. City of Portland, 319 Or 308, 317, 
877 P2d 1187 (1994). Thus, the proper construction of the 
county’s ordinance “is a question of law, which we resolve 
using the same rules of construction that we use to interpret 
statutes.” City of Eugene v. Comcast of Oregon II, Inc. , 359 
Or 528, 540, 375 P3d 446 (2016). In this case, we start and 
end with the text and context. See State v. Gaines, 346 Or 
160, 171, 206 P3d 1042 (2009) (“[T]here is no more persua -
sive evidence of the intent of the legislature than the words 
by which the legislature undertook to give expression to its 
wishes.” (Internal quotation marks omitted.)).
 We start with the text of the ordinance that governs 
verifying nonconforming uses, ZDO 1206.05, which provides 
in full:2
“Verification of nonconforming use status requires 
review as a Type II application pursuant to Section 1307, 
Procedures, and shall be subject to the following standards 
and criteria:
 “A. The nonconforming use lawfully existed at the 
time of the adoption of zoning regulations, or a change 
in zoning regulations, which prohibited or restricted the 
use, and the nonconforming use has not been subsequently 
abandoned or discontinued. Once an applicant has verified 
that a nonconforming use was lawfully established, an 
applicant need not prove the existence, continuity, nature 
and extent of the nonconforming use for a period exceeding 
20 years immediately preceding the date of application for 
verification; or
 2 We note that the county’s ordinances for nonconforming uses implements 
ORS 215.130.
Cite as 353 Or App 699 (2026) 703
 “B. The existence, continuity, nature and extent of 
the nonconforming use for the 10-year period immediately 
preceding the date of the application is proven. Such evi -
dence shall create a rebuttable presumption that the non -
conforming use, as proven, lawfully existed at the time of, 
and has continued uninterrupted since, the adoption of 
restrictive zoning regulations, or a change in the zoning 
or zoning regulations, that have the effect of prohibiting 
the nonconforming use under the current provisions of this 
Ordinance.”
 ZDO 1206.05 provides two pathways for verifica -
tion. Under subparagraph (A), an applicant can verify a non-
conforming use by proving that the use was lawfully estab -
lished and not subsequently abandoned or discontinued for 
a period not to exceed 20 years immediately preceding the 
application. Through the second sentence in subparagraph 
(A), whether a use has not been abandoned or discontinued 
is linked to proving “the existence, continuity, nature and 
extent of the nonconforming use.”
 Under the second pathway in subparagraph (B), 
which is the pathway petitioners sought to use, an appli -
cant can verify a nonconforming use by relying on a rebut -
table presumption that the use was lawfully established and 
continued uninterrupted. That presumption is obtained by 
proving “[t]he existence, continuity, nature and extent of the 
nonconforming use for the 10-year period immediately pre -
ceding the date of the application.” Thus, subparagraph (B) 
uses the exact same phrase as used in subparagraph (A) 
as the means for proving a use has not been abandoned or 
discontinued. That context suggests that “existence, conti -
nuity, nature and extent of the nonconforming use” means, 
at least in part, not abandoned or discontinued. Petitioners’ 
argument that only the first pathway requires the appli -
cant to show that a use has not been discontinued or aban -
doned does not address the full text or context of those two 
provisions.
 Further, the context of the entire nonconforming 
use section of the ZDO supports our reading that proving 
continuity of use means proving the use has not been dis -
continued. Several provisions in the nonconforming use 
section refer to “continuity” and “continued,” but those 
704 Paxton v. Clackams County
terms are not defined or given a standard. See ZDO 1206.01 
(“Section 1206 is adopted to provide standards, criteria, and 
procedures under which a nonconforming use may be con -
tinued, maintained, verified, restored, replaced, and altered 
and under which a vested right may be determined.”); ZDO 
1206.02 (“A nonconforming use may be continued although 
not in conformity with the regulations for the zoning dis -
trict in which the use is located.”); ZDO 1206.05 (verification 
requires proving “continuity”). However, ZDO 1206.04(A), 
which is titled “discontinuation,” provides, “[i]f a noncon -
forming use is discontinued for a period of more than 24 
consecutive months, the use shall not be resumed unless the 
resumed use conforms to the requirements of this Ordinance 
and other regulations applicable at the time of the proposed 
resumption.”
 The juxtaposition of not providing standards for 
showing continuity but instead providing a standard for 
discontinuation in ZDO 1206.04, strongly suggests that 
the county intended that applying ZDO 1206.04 was how 
continuity would be determined. Reading the provisions as 
whole, we conclude that whether a nonconforming use has 
continuity requires confronting whether it has been discon-
tinued for long enough that the use cannot be resumed as 
provided in the county code; otherwise, showing continuity 
would not be tethered to the time frame the county has set 
for when a use is considered discontinued.
 We thus conclude that LUBA’s order is not unlaw -
ful in substance, because, under ZDO 1206.05(B) petitioners 
bore the burden of establishing the continuity of the noncon-
forming use for the 10-year period preceding the application, 
which required showing that the use was not discontinued 
for a period of more than 24 consecutive months, as provided 
in ZDO 1206.04(A), during that 10-year period.
 Affirmed.

leads.caseName: CRG Acquisition, LLC v. Planning Board of Appeals of Holliston
leads.court: Massachusetts Appeals Court
leads.text:
NOTICE: All slip opinions and orders are subject to formal
revision and are superseded by the advance sheets and bound
volumes of the Official Reports. If you find a typographical
error or other formal error, please notify the Reporter of
Decisions, Supreme Judicial Court, John Adams Courthouse, 1
Pemberton Square, Suite 2500, Boston, MA, 02108-1750; (617) 557-
1030; SJCReporter@sjc.state.ma.us

25-P-915 Appeals Court

 CRG ACQUISITION, LLC, & another1 vs. PLANNING BOARD OF
 HOLLISTON & another.2

 No. 25-P-915.

 Suffolk. February 13, 2026. - October 14, 2026.

 Present: Sacks, Singh, & Toone, JJ.

Zoning, Site plan approval, Special permit, Permitted use, By-
 law, Judicial review. Municipal Corporations, By-laws and
 ordinances, Planning board. Planning Board. Practice,
 Civil, Summary judgment, Zoning appeal, Declaratory
 proceeding. Declaratory Relief.

 Civil action commenced in the Land Court Department on
August 27, 2021.

 The case was heard by Howard P. Speicher, J., on a motion
for summary judgment, and the entry of judgment was ordered by
Lauren E. Reznick, J.

 Jason R. Talerman (Stephen J. Chaplin also present) for the
defendant.
 Donald R. Pinto, Jr., for the plaintiff.

 1 Jon Delli Priscoli, as trustee of the New Hopping Brook
Realty Trust.
 2 Town of Holliston.
  2

 TOONE, J. Plaintiff CRG Acquisition, LLC (CRG), seeks to

develop a large warehouse in the town of Holliston (town).

After the town's planning board denied CRG's application for a

special permit and modified site plan approval, CRG and

coplaintiff New Hopping Brook Realty Trust (trust)3 sought

judicial review in the Land Court under G. L. c. 40A, § 17, and

also sought, under G. L. c. 240, § 14A, a declaration that its

proposed warehouse does not need a special permit because it is

a use permitted as of right under § III.G.1 of the town's zoning

bylaw, which applies to a "[w]holesale office or showroom,

including warehouse facilities."4 After a judge of the Land

Court granted summary judgment for CRG on its c. 240, § 14A

claim, a judgment entered declaring that CRG needed no special

permit and remanding its application for modified site plan

approval to the planning board. This appeal followed. We

conclude that, even though (1) neither the town nor the planning

board is entitled to deference for their interpretation of the

use tables in the zoning bylaw, (2) the town's position that

CRG's proposed warehouse is not covered by § III.G.1 is correct.

Accordingly, we reverse the judgment in favor of CRG on the

 3 We refer to the plaintiffs collectively as CRG.

 4 The town amended its bylaw in 2022, while this case was
pending in the Land Court. We refer herein to the town's bylaw,
as amended in 2016, that applied at the time CRG filed its
complaint.
  3

c. 240, § 14A claim and direct that judgment enter for the town

and planning board and that a declaration in accordance with

this opinion be entered.

 Background. The pertinent facts in this case are

undisputed. CRG is the buyer in a pending purchase and sale

agreement to buy seventy-two acres of land from the trust. The

site is in the town's industrial zoning district. In 2019, CRG

applied to the planning board for site plan approval for the

development of an approximately 800,000 square foot warehouse

and distribution facility. The proposed project would have 423

trailer truck spaces, 170 loading docks, and 129 passenger

vehicle parking spaces.

 In March 2020, after several public hearings, the planning

board approved CRG's site plan with thirty-one general and

special conditions. The planning board found that the

application for site review was consistent with its regulations

governing special permit and site plan submissions, and that the

project met the general conditions for approval of site plans as

specified in § VII.5 of the zoning bylaw. The planning board

noted in its site plan decision that the town's building

inspector "has expressed concern that ultimately the use may

require a Special Permit under the provisions of Section
  4

[III.G.3] General industrial uses,"5 and one of the special

conditions of approval provided that, "[s]hould the Inspector of

Buildings find that the proposed use requires additional relief

under Zoning By-Laws Section III - Use Regulations, further

review by the Planning Board is required as is an amendment of

the record plan set."

 In June 2020, CRG applied to the planning board for a

special permit, while maintaining that no special permit was

required. CRG also applied for amended site plan approval,

proposing to modify the previously approved site plan by

reducing the number of tractor trailer spaces and loading docks.

In July 2021, after holding eleven public hearings, the planning

board denied CRG's application for a special permit based on

concerns about traffic, noise, and negative impacts on the

town's historical and agricultural character and the character

of surrounding neighborhoods. The planning board also denied

CRG's application for modified site plan approval, reiterating

the same concerns and concluding that the application failed to

satisfy the general conditions for approval set forth in

§ VII.5.a-g of the bylaw.

 5 As the planning board notes in its brief, its reference in
the decision to § III.G.2 was "an apparent scrivener's error."
It is, instead, § III.G.3 that applies to proposed general
industrial uses of this size (occupying more than 15,000 square
feet of floor area).
  5

 CRG filed this action in August 2021. The first two counts

of the complaint challenged, pursuant to G. L. c. 40A, § 17, the

planning board's denial of the special permit and its denial of

CRG's application for modified site plan approval. The third

count of the complaint sought a declaration under G. L. c. 240,

§ 14A, that CRG's proposed warehouse is a use allowed by right

under § III.G.1 of the bylaw and does not require a special

permit.

 After CRG moved for summary judgment, a judge (motion

judge) allowed CRG's motion as to the third count of the

complaint. The motion judge found that the bylaw defined

"warehouse" for a reason and "that reason must include an intent

to define the use as listed in the By-Law's Table of Uses." The

presence of that term in § III.G.1 "and in no other place in the

Table of Uses" showed, in the judge's view, that "the principal

use of a property as a warehouse, as defined in Section I-E of

the By-Law, is allowed as an independent, principal use of

property as of right in the Industrial District."

 The motion judge then dismissed the first count of the

complaint as moot and denied summary judgment on the second

count "because there is insufficient evidence on the record that

would allow the court to conclude as a matter of law that the

Planning Board acted arbitrarily or unreasonably in its denial

of CRG's application for modified site plan review." After the
  6

parties jointly moved for entry of a final judgment, a second

judge allowed the motion and ordered entry of a judgment that

provided the declaration requested by CRG; dismissed the first

count as moot; and, with respect to the second count, remanded

CRG's application for modified site plan approval to the

planning board for further proceedings, "thereupon dismissing

Count II without prejudice."6

 Discussion. We review the judge's summary judgment

decision de novo. Nunez v. Syncsort Inc., 496 Mass. 706, 709

(2025). We similarly review the judge's determinations of law,

including his interpretation of the zoning bylaw, de novo.

Shirley Wayside Ltd. Partnership v. Board of Appeals of Shirley,

461 Mass. 469, 475 (2012) (Shirley Wayside).

 1. Deference. Before turning to the merits, we must

determine whether the interpretation of the bylaw advanced by

the planning board and town in this case is entitled to

 6 The judgment further states that the planning board
"shall, on remand, keep open and hold in abeyance its
consideration of the Application pending final disposition of
the appeal of . . . so much of the Summary Judgment Decision as
concerns Count III of the complaint. . . . Should the Town's
Appeal fail and so much of the Summary Judgment Decision as
concerns Count III of the complaint become a final judgment, the
Planning Board shall" reopen proceedings and perform a
substantive review of CRG's modified application. If, on the
other hand, the town's appeal succeeds and "so much of the
Summary Judgment Decision as concerns Count III is reversed,"
"the plaintiffs will not further pursue the project that is the
subject of the Application."
  7

deference. Although the judge ultimately concluded that the

defendants' interpretation is unreasonable, he acknowledged that

courts generally "give[] deference to a local board's reasonable

construction of its own [zoning] bylaw." The defendants contend

that deference applies and the judge erred by "impermissibly

substitut[ing] [his] own preferred interpretation of the Town's

Zoning Bylaw for the [planning board's] reasonable

interpretation." For its part, CRG argues that deference may

apply when a party challenges a local board's decision under

G. L. c. 40A, § 17, but not when it proceeds under G. L. c. 240,

§ 14A, and "there is no underlying zoning decision adopting an

interpretation of the local bylaw to which the court must (or

can) defer."

 We conclude that, with respect to CRG's claim under

G. L. c. 240, § 14A -- the only one before us -- we owe no

deference to the defendants' position. We defer to a local

board's legal conclusions on matters within its authority,

including its reasonable construction of bylaws it is charged

with implementing. See Shirley Wayside, 461 Mass. at 474,

citing Wendy's Old Fashioned Hamburgers of N.Y., Inc. v. Board

of Appeal of Billerica, 454 Mass. 374, 381 (2009) (Wendy's);

Doherty v. Planning Bd. of Scituate, 467 Mass. 560, 566-567

(2014). CRG's first two claims, brought under c. 40A, § 17,

involved decisions within the planning board's authority: its
  8

denial of the special permit and modified site plan approval.

By contrast, CRG's claim under c. 240, § 14A, seeks a

determination of a question which the planning board did not

have authority to decide: whether the proposed warehouse is a

use permitted as of right under the bylaw's use tables.

 The bylaw provides that it is enforced by the building

inspector, and persons aggrieved by the building inspector's

decisions may appeal to the zoning board of appeals. See G. L.

c. 40A, §§ 7, 8; Stevens v. Zoning Bd. of Appeals of Bourne, 97

Mass. App. Ct. 713, 715 n.6 (2020).7 Although the planning board

serves as the special permit granting authority "for any Site

Plan approval application that also requires a Special Permit"

under the use tables,8 neither the bylaw nor the planning board's

regulations authorize the planning board to decide whether a

special permit is required in the first place. See McDonald's

Corp. v. Seekonk, 12 Mass. App. Ct. 351, 352-353 (1981) ("under

 7 General Laws c. 40A, § 8, states that "[a]n appeal to the
permit granting authority as the zoning ordinance or by-law may
provide, may be taken . . . by any person . . .aggrieved by an
order or decision of the inspector of buildings, or other
administrative official . . . . " General Laws c. 40A, § 1A,
defines "permit granting authority" as "the board of appeals or
zoning administrator." The town's bylaw also defines "permit
granting authority" as the zoning board of appeals.
 8 The bylaw designates the zoning board of appeals as the
granting authority for other special permits.
  9

the statute and by-law," planning board had "no role" in

determining whether intended use was permissible).

 Consistent with this allocation of authority, the planning

board never took a position on whether CRG's proposed warehouse

requires a special permit. When the planning board approved

CRG's initial sit

leads.caseName: GSD Contracting, LLC v. All American Builders & Debris Removal, Inc.
leads.court: District Court of Appeal of Florida
leads.text:
DISTRICT COURT OF APPEAL OF THE STATE OF FLORIDA 
FOURTH DISTRICT 

GSD CONTRACTING, LLC, 
Appellant, 

v. 

ALL AMERICAN BUILDERS & DEBRIS REMOVAL, INC., 
Appellee. 

No. 4D2024-3286 

[October 14, 2026] 

Appeal from the Circuit Court for the Seventeenth Judicial Circuit, 
Broward County; John B. Bowman, Judge; L.T. Case No. 
062021CA012822AXXXCE. 

Andrew V. Cobbe, Douglas J. Clarke, and Oscar E. Soto of Soto Law 
Group, P.A., Fort Lauderdale, for appellant. 

Wayne R. Atkins of Xander Law Group, P.A., Miami, for appellee. 

L
EVINE, J. 

 Appellant GSD Contracting, LLC (“GSD”) appeals a final judgment 
requiring it to pay appellee All American Builders & Debris Removal, Inc. 
(“All American”) a total of $116,882.98 for breach of contract. We find no 
error in awarding to All American a $71,582.98 retainage in accordance 
with the plain language of the subcontract. Thus, we affirm as to this 
amount. However, we reverse that portion of the judgment that awarded 
$45,300 for work that had not yet been performed. In fact, All American 
concedes this amount was never sought and was not recoverable under 
the subcontract’s plain language. 

All American was a subcontractor hired to provide framing, drywall, 
insulation, and acoustical ceiling tiles on a five-story hotel project. After 
the original general contractor was terminated, GSD was hired as the 
replacement general contractor. 

The pertinent sections of the subcontract include section 16.6, which 
contained a termination for convenience provision: 

2 

Termination for Convenience. Contractor reserved the right 
to terminate this Subcontract and all rights and obligations 
hereunder, without cause, and at Contractor’s sole discretion 
and convenience. In the event of a termination pursuant to 
this section, Subcontractor shall be entitled to recover its 
partial and final payment for all Subcontract Work 
performed through the date of termination, as well as costs 
incurred due to the termination (demobilization) but in no 
event shall be entitled to payment for any Subcontract 
Work not performed, including profit that would have been 
realized on the Work not yet performed. 

(emphasis added). Additionally, section 11.3 of the subcontract, which 
addressed the retainage, stated: 

Partial Payments. Partial payments for or on account of the 
Subcontract Work shall be made by the Contractor to 
Subcontractor as the Subcontract Work progresses, in 
accordance with the payment schedule set forth in this 
Section. . . . In making any partial payments, there shall be 
retained ten percent (10%) of the estimate on which partial 
payment is made until ninety (90) days after the final 
completion of the Project. 

(emphasis added). 

At the time GSD took over, All American had completed approximately 
93.9% of its contractual work, and All American was owed a $71,582.98 
retainage. All American had not finished its work because other trades 
needed to complete their work first. 

At some point before the work was completed, the project suffered from 
significant mold issues due to water intrusion. All American then refused 
to complete the remainder of the work unless the mold was properly 
remediated to ensure the safety of its workers. GSD claimed that it 
performed sufficient remediation by removing certain areas of drywall and 
completing limited mold testing. All American believed GSD’s remediation 
efforts were insufficient because GSD never hired an industrial hygienist 
or prepared a formal remediation plan. GSD ultimately terminated All 
American from the project and never paid All American a $71,582.98 
retainage for work already performed. 

All American sued GSD for breach of contract, seeking the $71,582.98 
retainage. During trial, All American’s owner testified that All American 
3 

was seeking to recover only the retainage amount and was not seeking the 
$45,300 for unperformed work. The trial court found GSD breached the 
subcontract by (1) failing to pay All American for work performed as 
required under the subcontract, and (2) failing to properly remediate the 
mold as required by an exhibit to the subcontract. Nevertheless, the trial 
court awarded All American $116,882.98, which consisted of the 
$71,582.98 retainage plus $45,300 in unperformed work. This appeal 
follows. 

The interpretation of a contract is reviewed de novo. Klinow v. Island 
Ct. at Boca W. Prop. Owners’ Ass’n, 64 So. 3d 177, 180 (Fla. 4th DCA 
2011). “Where the language of a contract is clear and unambiguous, the 
court can give to it no meaning other than that expressed.” Flaim v. Flaim, 
417 So. 3d 1, 3 (Fla. 4th DCA 2025) (quoting Nawaz v. Universal Prop. & 
Cas. Ins. Co., 91 So. 3d 187, 188 (Fla. 4th DCA 2012)). 

GSD argues the trial court erred in finding that GSD breached the 
subcontract. Contrary to GSD’s contention, the plain language of the 
subcontract supports the trial court’s finding that GSD breached the 
subcontract by failing to pay All American the $71,582.98 retainage for 
work it completed before its termination. Section 11.3 of the subcontract 
expressly provides that 10% of each partial payment “shall be retained . . 
. until ninety (90) days after the final completion of the Project.” Because 
the project was completed in 2023, the 90-day period has long since 
expired, making the $71,582.98 retainage immediately payable. 

Significantly, the subcontract does not contain a termination for cause 
provision or any other pertinent provision permitting GSD to withhold or 
retain All American’s retainage following a termination. Section 11.3 
establishes when the retainage becomes payable—90 days after final 
completion of the project—while section 16.6 expressly provides that All 
American “shall be entitled to recover its partial and final payment for all 
Subcontract Work performed through the date of termination . . . .” 
Nothing in the subcontract provides that GSD may thereafter withhold the 
retainage based on an alleged default by All American. Thus, the 
subcontract provides no contractual basis for GSD to keep the $71,582.98 
retainage.
1 

Because we affirm based on GSD’s breach by failing to pay for work 
performed, we need not reach the merits of whether GSD in fact also 
breached the subcontract by failing to sufficiently remediate the mold 

1 Our analysis could be different if there was a provision for cause in the contract, 
thus allowing the party to terminate based upon such proof. 
4 

issue. See Kelley v. Mutnich, 481 So. 2d 999, 1000 (Fla. 4th DCA 1986) 
(stating that where a final judgment is based on several grounds, 
affirmance is warranted if the record supports any one of those grounds). 

Finally, reversal is nevertheless warranted as to the trial court’s award 
of $45,300 for unperformed work. The complaint sought only $71,582.98 
in damages for the nonpayment of the retainage. Additionally, as All 
American concedes, All American’s owner testified to seeking only the 
retainage, and the subcontract prohibits recovery for unperformed work. 
Specifically, we note section 16.6 of the subcontract provides that All 
American shall not “be entitled to payment for any Subcontract Work not 
performed, including profit that would have been realized on the Work not 
yet performed.” 

In summary, we affirm the trial court’s finding of breach of contract by 
GSD for failing to pay All American the $71,582.98 retainage, reverse as 
to the $45,300 in unperformed work, and remand for the trial court to 
enter a final judgment consistent with this opinion. 

Affirmed in part, reversed in part, and remanded. 

K
LINGENSMITH and LOTT, JJ., concur. 

* * * 

Not final until disposition of timely-filed motion for rehearing.

leads.caseName: Pilac Management, Ltd., Etc. v. Parque Towers Developers, LLC, Etc.
leads.court: District Court of Appeal of Florida
leads.text:
Third District Court of Appeal 
State of Florida 

Opinion filed October 14, 2026. 
Not final until disposition of timely filed motion for rehearing. 

________________ 

No. 3D25-1698 
Lower Tribunal No. 22-2219-CA-01 
________________ 

Pilac Management, Ltd., etc., et al., 
Appellants, 

vs. 

Parque Towers Developers, LLC, 
Appellee. 

 An Appeal from the Circuit Court for Miami -Dade County, William 
Thomas, Judge. 

 Reiner & Reiner, P.A., and David P. Reiner, II, for appellants. 

 Law Offices of Robert Frankel, P.A ., and Robert P. Frankel; Lauri 
Waldman Ross, P.A., and Lauri Walman Ross, for appellee. 

Before LOGUE, LINDSEY, and GOODEN, JJ. 

 LOGUE, J. 

 2 
The Appellants are various purchasers of pre- construction 
condominium units . Under their purchase and sale agreements, the 
developer, Parque Towers Developers, LLC, contracted to return deposits 
that exceeded 15% of the units’ purchase price if the purchasers failed to 
close. In an earlier stage of Appellants’ litigation with the developer, they 
obtained a judgment for the return of their entire deposits due to the 
developer’s failure to timely complete the construction. On appeal, however, 
we reversed in part , finding the developer’s delay in construction did not 
violate the purchase agreements. Parque Towers Devs., LLC v. Pilac Mgmt., 
Ltd., 395 So. 3d 189 (Fla. 3d DCA 2024) (“Parque I”). 
In the litigation now under review, the trial court refused the purchasers’ 
claim for return of their deposits in excess of 15% provided by the purchase 
agreements even though the developer had sold the units at or above the 
contracted prices. The trial court reasoned that, although “unfair and 
inequitable,” this result was mandated by res judicata . In doing so, the 
seasoned trial judge overlooked the line of authority that allows res judicata 
to be overridden when its mechanical application would work an injustice . 
Accordingly, we reverse and remand for further proceedings. 

 3 
BACKGROUND 
The underlying matter concerns a dispute over the pre -construction 
sale of five condominium units. The developer contracted to sell 
condominium units to five different sets of purchasers: (1) Pilac 
Management, Ltd.; (2) Rebecca Christina Vallias and Hugo Kawasaki; (3) 
Josh Kurzban and Michelle Kurzban ; (4) Marcio Silveira Kogut; and (5) 
Francisco Alimari Netto and Nely Rachel Delicato Alimari. 
All five sets of purchasers individually sued the developer and another 
defendant in five separate actions seeking rescission of their purchase 
agreements and the immediate return of their deposit money with interest. In 
their operative complaints, the p urchasers alleged that the developer 
breached the purchase agreements by failing to substantially complete the 
units by the estimated completion date of December 31, 2017 . The 
purchasers alleged that they had formally notified the developer of its default 
and that they were “rescinding and cancelling the [a]greement[s] and 
demanding the immediate return of the deposit money paid thereunder.” The 
developer counterclaimed, alleging that the purchasers breached the 
purchase agreements by failing to close. 
The cases were consolidated, and following a non -jury trial, the trial 
court entered a final judgment in each of the five cases. On the breach of 
 4 
contract claims for failure to substantially complete the units, the trial court 
found in favor of the purchasers and determined that the p urchasers were 
“entitled to the return of [their] deposits as damages[.]” The trial court also 
found in favor of the purchasers on the developer’s counterclaim. 
The developer appealed all five final judgments but challenged only 
the trial court’s judgment in favor of the purchasers on their breach of 
contract claims. It did not appeal the trial court’s finding in favor of the 
purchasers on its counterclaim. As to the breach of contract claims, the 
developer argued the trial court erred by interpreting the purchase 
agreement to require the units be completed by December 31, 2017. We 
consolidated these appeals and reversed in part. Parque I, 395 So. 3d at 
190. In reversing, we held that “the agreements did not create an affirmative 
obligation for the developer to complete the units by a date certain or 
otherwise make time of the essence.” Id. In so doing, we noted that “we t[ook] 
no position on any other remedy the Purchasers may have exercised had 
they desired to exit the contract prior to the notice of closing.” Id. at 192 n.3. 
On remand, the purchasers sought leave in the trial court to assert 
supplemental claims “for damages and statutory recission regarding the 
disputed deposit amounts.” The trial court denied the motion, finding that it 
“only ha[d] jurisdiction to enforce the mandate.” Pursuant to the mandate, the 
 5 
trial court vacated the final judgment on the breach of contract claim and 
entered a final judgment in favor of the developer. 
Thereafter, the purchasers commenced five separate new actions 
against the developer, alleging two causes of action: (1) breach of contract 
for failure to return deposits as required by Section 13 of the purchase 
agreement; and (2) rescission for failure to comply with section s 
718.202(1)(a) and (5), Florida Statutes.1 
Pertinent to this appeal, Section 13 of the purchase agreements 
provided, in relevant part, as follows: 
Upon Purchaser’s default (and the expiration of any cure period, 
if applicable), all Purchaser’s rights under this Agreement will 
terminate and Seller can resell the Unit without any accounting 
to Purchaser. . . . If Purchaser defaults or breaches this 
Agreement after Purchaser has paid fifteen percent (15%) of 
the purchase price of the Unit , excluding any interest owed 
under this Agreement, the Seller shall refund to the Purchaser 
any amount which remains in excess of (a) fifteen percent 
(15%) of the purchase price of the Unit, excluding any 
interest owed under the Agreement, or (b) the amount of 
damages incurred by the Seller as a result of such breach, 

1 These statutes provide: “If a buyer properly terminates the contract 
pursuant to its terms or pursuant to this chapter, the funds shall be paid to 
the buyer together with any interest earned.” § 718.202(1)(a), Fla. Stat. “The 
failure to comply with the provisions of this section renders the contract 
voidable by the buyer, and, if voided, all sums deposited or advanced under 
the contract shall be refunded with interest at the highest rate then being paid 
on savings accounts, excluding certificates of deposit, by savings and loan 
associations in the area in which the condominium property is located. ” § 
718.202(5), Fla. Stat. 

 6 
whichever is greater, from the amount paid by Purchaser with 
respect to the purchase price of the Unit. . . . The amount of the 
deposit and any interest earned on it which remains after 
subtracting the amount of the refund to which Purchaser is 
entitled as provided above in t his paragraph, shall be paid to 
Seller. 

(emphasis added). 
The operative complaints referenced the prior consolidated actions, 
alleging that “[t]he parties’ competing claims for breach of contract have both 
been denied; however, [the developer] nevertheless sold the [u]nit[s] to . . . 
third part[ies].” On the breach of contract claim, the purchasers sought return 
of the excess deposit amounts under Section 13 of the purchase 
agreements, alleging: (1) during trial in the prior actions, the developer’s 
representative testified that its damages were still ongoing and continuing; 
(2) the developer sold the units to a third parties; (3) as a result of this Court’s 
opinion in Parque I, the developer’s damages became ascertainable and 
calculable; and (4) the developer “failed or refused to calculate its damages 
and to refund the excess deposit amounts pursuant to Section 13 of the 
Purchase Agreement[s].” Of note, the purchasers cited to the portion of 
Section 13 concerning the buyer’s breach, not the seller’s breach. On the 
recission claim, the purchasers sought return of the deposits with interest, 
alleging that “[p]ursuant to the Third DCA Opinion, [ the developer’s] course 
of conduct in selling the [u]nit[s] to a third part [ies], and the denial of [ the 
 7 
developer’s] counterclaim for breach of contract, the Purchase Agreement[s] 
ha[ve] been properly terminated” and that the developer has failed to return 
the funds as required by section s 718.202(1)(a) and (5). For our purposes 
here, section 718.202(1)(a) concerns the return of funds after a buyer’s 
termination of the contract, not the seller’s. 
The developer moved to dismiss the new actions based on res 
judicata. The cases were then consolidated, and the purchasers filed their 
consolidated response to the developer’s motions to dismiss. The 
purchasers argued res judicata did not bar their claims because there was a 
subsequent breach of the purchase agreements. They also argued the 
doctrine of res judicata was inapplicable where it worked an inequity. The 
purchasers alleged that during the pendency of the prior actions, the 
developer sold the five units for a total of $6,440,000, more than the original 
total contract price of $6,265,000, and that the developer had also retained 
the purchasers’ deposits, which totaled $3,144,500, resulting in a windfall to 
the developer. 
The trial court thereafter entered the order on appeal, which dismissed 
the purchasers’ consolidated actions with prejudice. The order found that 
while “it would appear unfair and inequitable for [the developer] to be able to 
keep all of the deposits paid by [the purchasers] when the contract between 
 8 
the parties appears to express otherwise,” “Plaintiffs’ consolidated actions 
are barred by res judicata, ” as the trial court was bound by this Court’s 
decision in Parque I. The instant appeal followed. 
STANDARD OF REVIEW 
“We review orders granting a motion to dismiss under a de novo 
standard of review.” Williams Island Ventures, LLC v. de la Mora, 246 So. 3d 
471, 475 (Fla. 3d DCA 2018). “The de novo standard of review further applies 
to a trial court ’s ruling that relief is barred on the grounds of res judicata or 
collateral estoppel.” Fernandez v. Cruz, 341 So. 3d 410, 412 (Fla. 3d DCA 
2022). 
ANALYSIS 
The issue before this Court is whether the purchasers’ underlying 
actions were barred by res judicata. “The doctrine of res judicata prevents 
the re-litigation of a claim that was brought or could have been brought in 
prior litigation.” Claims Holding Grp., LLC v. AT&T Mobility, LLC, 347 So. 3d 
412, 414 (Fla. 3d DCA 2022). See also Mabson v. Christ, 140 So. 671, 671-
72 (Fla. 1932) (“The general rule is that a judgment on the merits, rendered 
in a former suit between the same parties or their privies, on the same cause 
of action, by a court of competent jurisdiction, operates as an estoppel, not 
only as to every matter which was offered and received to sustain or defeat 
 9 
the claim, but as to every other matter which might with propriety have been 
litigated and determined in that action.”). The doctrine “ is founded upon the 
sound proposition that there should be an end to litigation and that in the 
interest of the State every justiciable controversy should be settled in one 
action in order that the courts and the parties will not be pothered for the 
same cause by interminable litigation.” Gordon v. Gordon, 59 So. 2d 40, 44 
(Fla. 1952). “For res judicata to apply, four identities must exist between the 
former suit and the suit in which res judicata is to be applied: ‘(1) identity of 
the thing sued for; (2) identity of the cause of action; (3) identity of th e 
persons and parties to the action; and (4) identity of the quality or capacity 
of the persons for or against whom the claim is made.’” Claims Holding Grp., 
347 So. 3d at 414 (quoting Pearce v. Sandler, 219 So. 3d 961, 966 (Fla. 3d 
DCA 2017)). 
There exists some

leads.caseName: C&B Development, LLC v. Maxatawny Twp. ZHB.
leads.court: Commonwealth Court of Pennsylvania
leads.text:
IN THE COMMONWEALTH COURT OF PENNSYLVANIA 

C&B Development, LLC, : 
 Appellant : 
 : 
 v. : No. 982 C.D. 2025 
 : 
Maxatawny Township Zoning : Argued: September 14, 2026 
Hearing Board, Maxatawny Township : 
Board of Supervisors, State System : 
of Higher Education and Kutztown : 
University, Steve D. Wilson, Nicholas : 
Prikis, and Sophie Pittas : 

BEFORE: HONORABLE PATRICIA A. McCULLOUGH, Judge 
 HONORABLE STACY WALLACE, Judge 
 HONORABLE STELLA M. TSAI, Judge 

OPINION NOT REPORTED 

MEMORANDUM OPINION 
BY JUDGE McCULLOUGH FILED: October 14, 2026 

 C&B Development, LLC (Landowner) appeals from the July 14, 2025 
Order of the Court of Common Pleas of Berks County (trial court), which affirmed (1) 
the Maxatawny Township Zoning Hearing Board ’s (ZHB) determination that the 
proposed private road/access drive to Landowner’s proposed warehouse facility is an 
impervious surface subject to the provisions of Section 593(c) of Maxatawny Township 
Zoning Ordinance Number 2022-08 (Zoning Ordinance Number 2022-08)1 and (2) the 

1 Zoning Ordinance Number 2022-08 modified, revised and/or amended certain provisions of 
the Maxatawny Township Zoning Ordinance of 2 012 (Zoning Ordinance of 2012) , with the 
amendments taking effect on October 13, 2022. We reference each zoning ordinance separately where 
appropriate. 

2 
ZHB’s denial of Landowner’s alternative request for a dimensional variance . After 
careful review, we affirm. 
I. Factual and Procedural Background 
 Landowner is the equitable owner of a 75.5-acre tract of land (Property) 
currently improved with a restaurant, mobile home park , and airport.2 It has frontage 
only on Kutztown Road. The Property contains portions that are located in three 
different zoning districts: C-1 (Commercial District), L-I (Light Industrial District) and 
AP-1 (Agricultural Preservation District). The area surrounding the Property contains 
a mix of commercial and residential uses and the Kutztown University campus. 
 Landowner seeks to demolish all existing uses and buildings and construct 
a commercial building and a 709,000-square-foot warehouse facility on the L-I District 
portion of the Property. Warehouses are a permitted use in the L-I District subject to 
conditional use approval from the Maxatawny Township Board of Supervisors. The 
portion of the Property zoned L-I, where the proposed warehouse would be located, 
can only be accessed from the Property’s sole frontage on Kutztown Road via a 
proposed private road (Road A) that would need to be constructed from Kutztown Road 
through the C-1 District. 
 As part of Landowner’s construction planning process, it submitted a 
Conditional Use Plan to the Maxatawny Township Zoning Officer on July 28, 2023, 
and a Land Development Plan on August 14, 2023. Based on the positioning of the 
proposed warehouse and its proximity to residential structures, there was no possibility 
the proposed road, Road A (which connects the warehouse to Kutztown Road), could 
be located more than 500 feet from those residences. 

2 Landowner owns the Property by way of a purchase agreement dated August 23, 2022. 
Nicholas Prikis and Sophie Pittas (Prikis and Pittas) are the record owners. 

3 
 Christopher Falenki, Township Engineer and Alternate Zoning Officer, 
submitted a review of the Conditional Use Application on August 14, 2023, raising

Zoning Ordinance Number 2022 -08, § 593(c) ; Supplemental Reproduced Record

 On August 16, 2023, Zoning Officer Christopher Paff and Jerome

Further discussion o n site accessibility issues shall be

the Preliminary Subdivision and Land Development Plan 
Application. 

4 
(Reproduced Record (R.R.) at 5a.)3 
 On August 31, 2023, Zoning Officer Paff sent Landowner a Zoning

and receive a zoning variance from the ZHB before continuing with the conditional use 
application. Zoning Officer Paff explained in his August 31, 2023 Zoning 
Determination Letter, that:

31a (discovery motion); 246a-372a; 373a-81a (discovery dispute); 394a (discovery order). The law 
is well settled that an appellate court may not consider documents that are not part of the certified

4 “Impervious surface” is defined as a “surface which prevents the percolation of water into 
the ground ( i.e. roads, buildings, sidewalks, drives, loading areas, parking areas, stone and paved 
recreation courts).” Zoning Ordinance of 2012, § 202; S.R.R. at 265b. 

5 “Accessory use” is defined as “a use customarily incidental and subordinate to the principal

2012, § 202; S.R.R. at 270b. 

5 
Both the Preliminary Plan and the [Conditional Use] Plan 
show property lines to suggest 3 lots. The unlabeled 3rd lot 
contains proposed new Road “A”. Proposed new Road “A”, 
whether part of proposed Lot 1 or a new stand -alone lot or 
proposed new right of way, is necessary and required to 
provide access to the new Lot 2 . Proposed Road “A” is less 
than 500-feet from existing, residential uses, and as such, the

of [Zoning Ordinance] 2022-08. 

Road “A” is a proposed new impervious surface capable of 
extending vehicular access to the proposed warehouse use on 
proposed new Lot 2. As proposed, Road “A” requires Zoning 
Relief in the form of a variance from Section 593(c)(1) of 
[Zoning Ordinance] 2022-08. 

 * * * 
We are sending this Zoning determination letter so that you 
may have the opportunity to request to continue, to a later

Id. at 13a (emphasis in original). 
 On September 6, 2023, Landowner appealed to the ZHB, asking it to (1) 
overturn Zoning Officer Paff’s determination that Road A is an “accessory use” to the

 The ZHB conducted public hearings regarding Landowner’s application. 
Public hearings were held on October 24, 2023, November 20, 2023, and January 4,

 On January 15, 2024, the ZHB issued a written decision sustaining Zoning
